cards.q: Common Errors/Cues for RDL/Deadlift
cards.a: RDL - All Reps Begin And End With Knees Slightly Flexed - Bar Remains Close To Body, Hips Move Backward - Bar Should Be Lowered To Just Below Knees Or Until Neutral Spine Cannot Be Maintained Deadlift - Hips lower than shoulders - Bar 1 inch from shins and over middle of feet (laces) - Shoulders over or slightly ahead of the bar - Hips and knees extend at same rate

cards.q: Common Errors/Cues for Forward Step Lunge
cards.a: LEAD KNEES DO NOT GO PAST TOES OF LEAD FOOT | EVENLY DISTRIBUTE WEIGHT

cards.q: Overreaching (functional overreaching)
cards.a: intentionally programming a drastic increase in volume, intensity and/or duration

cards.q: Overtraining (nonfunctional overreaching)
cards.a: consistent training at high volumes/intensities/durations without the appropriate amounts of rest and recovery -Thus, eventually leading to decreases in performance

cards.q: Overtraining Syndrome
cards.a: A decline in performance lasting multiple months or more

cards.q: what is catastrophe theory?
cards.a: a relationship between the level of arousal and manifestation of cognitive anxieties once crossing the arousal threshold, which changes focus to what cannot be executed in competition and thus a decline in performance

cards.q: how can specificity of loading help bone health?
cards.a: external stimuli increasing bone density in specific joints likely to experience bone loss or mineral thinning

cards.q: what are the implications of greater tendon stiffness?
cards.a: greater stiffness = greater force required for transmission to a muscle to produce a recoil response, and useful for transmitting forces through tendons and into muscles at a high rate under strain – either from high velocity or from an opponent; essential in improving performance in some sports

cards.q: what is the end goal of exergonic reactions?
cards.a: to perform some kind of work via released energy

cards.q: when does catabolism occur?
cards.a: heavy training volumes, reduced caloric intake, and times of high life stress

cards.q: what are the adaptations to aerobic exercise?
cards.a: increased cardiac output, reduced heart rate at rest, and (during submaximal exercise intensities) increased stroke volume per heartbeat, and a significant increase in density in the microvasculature

cards.q: what is a side effect of creatine supplementation?
cards.a: acute effects that include gastrointestinal issues such as gas or mild bloating

cards.q: what function does oyxgen deficit provide?
cards.a: insight into contributions of the anaerobic energy system during intense bouts of exercise, plus weaknesses in individual athletes that can be improved via training

cards.q: what is the contractile phase of the cardiac cycle?
cards.a: systole

cards.q: for what purposes does the systole phase eject blood?
cards.a: either delivering oxygen-rich blood to working tissues or sending blood into the lungs to be oxygenated

cards.q: what kind of muscle fibers are fast oxidative and glycolytic?
cards.a: type IIa

cards.q: how does the GTO inhibit tension overload?
cards.a: emitting electrical signals from its sensory neuron to an inhibitory neuron in the spinal cord, which inhibits the motor neuron in the same muscle.

cards.q: what is the primary neurotransmitter involved in muscular contraction?
cards.a: acetylcholine

cards.q: what causes excitation of the sarcolemma?
cards.a: an action potential releases and arrives at a nerve terminal, then acetylcholine is released from the nerve terminal and diffuses across the neuromuscular junction (a muscle contraction will occur when enough acetylcholine is released and an action potential is released across the sarcolemma)

cards.q: what is troponin responsible for?
cards.a: initiating the movement of troponin from the myosin binding site after Ca+ has initiated a conformational change (then the myosin cross bridge can be carried out, allowing contraction)

cards.q: what kind of chemical cascade takes place during muscular contraction?
cards.a: a chemical cascade causes a conformational change in tropomyosin that allows for the myosin filament to bind with the actin filament

cards.q: how does the tropomyosin position relative to troponin and the actin filament?
cards.a: the head of tropomyosin wraps helically around troponin on the actin filament, thereby preventing formation of the myosin cross bridge

cards.q: reciprocal inhibition allows an athlete to achieve what?
cards.a: allows for maximal contraction to occur in an agonist muscle group while inhibiting and actually forcing relaxation to occur in the antagonist muscle group, which then allows an athlete to achieve relaxation and enhance mental focus by alternating through relax-contract cycles throughout the body

cards.q: what concentration of hemoglobin is oxygen carried through circulation with?
cards.a: 3mL per liter of plasma

cards.q: during exercise, how is carbon dioxide transported?
cards.a: out of the cell via diffusion and into the plasma for transport to the lungs for clearance – buffering CO2 relies on bicarbonate and water, which requires catalyzation by carbonic anhydrase in order to buffer the hydrogen ions accumulating in the blood.

cards.q: how is the buffering of CO2 supported?
cards.a: through the natural acid-base buffering capacity of hemoglobin in order to maintain blood pH balance. once exercise intensity reaches a level where aerobic metabolism is insufficient to maintain pH balance, lactic acid accumulates and is referred to as OBLA

cards.q: what is diffusion?
cards.a: movement of gases from areas high concentration to areas of lower concentration

cards.q: what is the cause of diffusion?
cards.a: due to the partial pressure exerted by each molecule of gas; during exercise, the partial pressure of the gases are altered depending on their location in the circulatory system.

cards.q: what are the gas pressures at the alveolus level and venous level respectively?
cards.a: alveolus: PO2 = 100 mm Hg and PCO2 = 40 mm Hg; venous: PO2 = 40 mm Hg and PCO2 = 46 mm Hg (after unloading into muscle tissue)

cards.q: what determines whether the gases (CO2/O2 or PCO2/O2) move into or out circulation during exercise?
cards.a: the changes in pressures

cards.q: what is the carbohydrate recommendations for aerobic and anaerobic athletes respectively?
cards.a: aerobic: 8g to 10g / kg; anaerobic: 5g to 6g / kg

cards.q: what is a benefit of a process goal?
cards.a: causes an athlete to engage in the behaviors necessary day to day without becoming too focused on the result

cards.q: what kinds of muscle striations are there and why?
cards.a: smooth muscle, obliquely striated muscle and striated muscle (striated contains actin and myosin; others don't)

cards.q: what does optimal functioning theory state?
cards.a: individuals will have different levels of anxiety and arousal that let them perform at their optimal abilities; there is a standardized mood state evaluation, such as state anxiety inventory, to quantify arousal state and correlate info to the physical performance of the athlete

cards.q: what does association refer to?
cards.a: normally refers to connections between different states, but in sport psychology it refers to being aware of the body's physical status during competition or training; maintaining focus on the task

cards.q: what does dissociation refer to?
cards.a: an athlete disconnecting from the physical tasks in order to block out fatigue, discomfort and pain; leads to decreased physical performance however, in one sense due to increased anxiety about fatigue or pain or task performance

cards.q: what is counterconditioning?
cards.a: the use of somatic and cognitive responses in order to reduce an athlete's performance-related anxiety; this is achieved through systematic desensitization where an athlete visualizes a stressful competitive situation and in order to counter the stress response engages in progressive muscle relaxation; over time application of this to situations causing mild anxiety can be effective in combating anxiety

cards.q: what does metabolic acidosis refer to?
cards.a: a condition that occus when the body produces too much acid

cards.q: what induces metabolic acidosis?
cards.a: rapid decrease in blood pH due to increased H+ ions; this response can be used to determine training capacities

cards.q: what is lactate a byproduct of?
cards.a: anaerobic glycolysis

cards.q: in what organs is lactate used as a fuel source?
cards.a: heart and brain

cards.q: when does anaerobic glycolysis occur?
cards.a: in a state of reduced oxygen availability

cards.q: what drives fast glycolysis?
cards.a: the conversion of pyruvate into lactate

cards.q: what does reaching lactate threshold imply for muscular contraction?
cards.a: slowing of muscular contractions (possibly until cessation of movement) until lactate can be cleared and homeostasis restored

cards.q: what is required for aerobic glycolysis?
cards.a: pyruvate to enter mitochondria, then when oxygen is present the pyruvate is oxidized and enters into the krebs cycle

cards.q: what governs the differentiation between the two types of glycolysis?
cards.a: what takes place in the mitochondrion -- if oxygen is present, aerobic glycolysis will take place through oxidative phosphorylation, but if oxygen isn't available the pyruvate will undergo fermentation to produce sufficient ATP

cards.q: what is an action potential?
cards.a: an electrical impulse that is triggered by the rapid depolarization of the cell membrane of a neuron

cards.q: what are the four segments of sarcomere?
cards.a: A-band, H-zone, I-band, and Z-line

cards.q: what does the A-band contain?
cards.a: actin and myosin filaments

cards.q: where is the H-zone and what does it contain?
cards.a: center of sarcomere, contains only myosin

cards.q: what is the I-band made of and what does it contain?
cards.a: made of two continguous sarcomeres, contains only actin

cards.q: where is the Z-line located?
cards.a: middle of the I-band

cards.q: what are the essential features of the sarcoplasmic reticulum?
cards.a: pumping Ca+ ions into the muscle when an action potential is released into sarcomere (for muscle contraction), and storing calcium ions there

cards.q: what is negative punishment?
cards.a: the removal of something highly valued to deter undesired behavior; the antithesis of positive reinforcement

cards.q: function of arterioles?
cards.a: controlling factor of blood flow in and out of capillary beds.

cards.q: what are synonyms for reducing blow flow and allowing greater blood flow?
cards.a: vasoconstriction and vasodilation respectively

cards.q: when is the lactate threshold thought to occur?
cards.a: at 4mL per dL of blood

cards.q: what is diastole?
cards.a: period of the cardiac cycle when the heart fills with blood

cards.q: which kind of veins carry deoxygenated blood, and which carry oxygenated blood?
cards.a: systemic: deoxygenated, pulmonary: oxygenated

cards.q: what is the smallest division of the blood vessel?
cards.a: capillary; role is to exchange gases, fluids, nutrients, hormones, electrolytes and others

cards.q: what does the atrioventricular node's delay of the sinoatrial node's signal do?
cards.a: allows for the complete ejection of blood from the atria into the ventricles, prior to the contraction of ventricles that sends blood from the heart to the lungs or body

cards.q: what does the sinoatrial do for heart rhythm?
cards.a: establishes normal heart rhythm, referred to as sinus rhythm

cards.q: why is there an increase in signal velocity from the atrioventricular bundle toward the ventricles?
cards.a: out of necessity as the left and right branches communicate directly with the purkinje fibers + the signals are directly responsible for the contraction of the left+right ventricles, which eject blood systemically or into lungs

cards.q: where is the signal from the atrioventricular node sent and why is this necessary?
cards.a: to the left and right bundle branches, necessary because this is a point of conduction between the atria and the ventricles; crucial in maintaining cardiac rhythm

cards.q: what does the parasympathetic regulate?
cards.a: mental acuity, focus, heart rate, and others

cards.q: what are arteries?
cards.a: muscular blood vessels that function to take blood away from the heart (systemic) or to the lungs (pulmonary)

cards.q: why do arteries operate under varying rates of pressure?
cards.a: due to the cardiac cycle of systole (high pressure) and diastole (low pressure)

cards.q: why are arteries significant for determining blood pressure and pulse rate?
cards.a: proximity to contractions of the heart

cards.q: what is the electron transport chain?
cards.a: the process of electrons being moved from electron donors to electron acceptors

cards.q: how does the electron transport chain generate energy during oxidative phosphorylation?
cards.a: the formation of a pH gradient along with the electron potential that can move across the inner mitochondrial membrane

cards.q: how is energy resynthesized in the electron transport chain during oxidative phosphorylation?
cards.a: through the activity of ATP synthase, which converts electrical activity into mechanical energy and results in the phosphorylation of adenosine diphosphate into ATP

cards.q: pyruvate is a product of what?
cards.a: anaerobic glycolysis

cards.q: in anaerobic glycolysis, one molecule of glucose is reduced to what?
cards.a: two pyruvate molecules, which can produce energy through two separate mechanisms

cards.q: in anaerobic glycolysis, what is one mechanism pyruvate can produce energy?
cards.a: via conversion into acetyl-coenzyme A, which is the primary means of entering Krebs cycle

cards.q: in anaerobic glycolysis, what is the other mechanism pyruvate can produce energy?
cards.a: via conversion to oxaloacetate in order to produce intermediaries involved in the Krebs cycle

cards.q: the oxidative system can utilize all three macros as substrate but is predominantly oriented to what?
cards.a: using fats while at rest (about 70%) and carbs during low-moderate exercise intensities

cards.q: when will the oxidative system convert proteins to glucose via gluconeogenesis?
cards.a: rarely; generally during periods of starvation and exercise bouts greater than 90 minutes

cards.q: how many molecules of ATP will oxidative phosphorylation generate?
cards.a: 40, after two rotations through Krebs, using one molecule of glucose

cards.q: the sarcomere is defined by what?
cards.a: the area occurring between two z-lines; they can be thought of as the location where all muscular contractions take place

cards.q: what does substrate-level phosphorylation refer to?
cards.a: reactions that are enzymatically driven and lead to the generation of ATP

cards.q: what is another name for substrate-level phosphorylation?
cards.a: anaerobic glycolysis or fast phosphorylation

cards.q: how does substrate-level phosphorylation operate?
cards.a: via the transfer and direct donation of a phosphoryl (PO3) group to adenosine diphosphate to form ATP

cards.q: where does substrate-level phosphorylation occur?
cards.a: in the cytoplasm of the cell as part of glycolysis, and can also be active in mitochondria as part of the krebs cycle

cards.q: can substrate-level phosphorylation only be active during anaerobic glycolysis?
cards.a: no, can be active during anaerobic and aerobic activities

cards.q: how is the onset of blood lactate defined?
cards.a: the point in which exercise intensity causes blood lactate to accumulate at a rate faster than can be buffered

cards.q: how is onset of blood lactate caused?
cards.a: first, release of H+ ions into blood due to ATP hydrolysis. second, reduction of available bicarbonate in the blood due to increased physical activity

cards.q: what does the P-wave represent?
cards.a: atrial depolarization, which involves the electrical signal from the sinoatrial node to the atrioventricular node and spreading from the right to the left atrium (this can cause atrial contraction)

cards.q: how is atrial contraction caused during atrial depolarization?
cards.a: electrical signal moves from the sinoatrial node to the atrioventricular node and spreading from the right to the left atrium

cards.q: what is the pulmonary division of the arteries responsible for?
cards.a: delivering deoxygenated blood from the heart to the lungs and returning oxygenated blood back to the heart

cards.q: what is the systemic division of the arteries responsible for?
cards.a: carrying oxygenated blood away from the heart and returning deoxygenated blood back to the heart

cards.q: in terms of deoxygenated blood, what is the role of pulmonary and systemic arteries?
cards.a: pulmonary: deliver dexoygenated from heart to lungs, systemic: return deoxygenated blood back to the heart

cards.q: lactate deydrogenase is the catalyst for what?
cards.a: conversion of pyruvate to lactate and back

cards.q: other than the conversion of pyruvate, what is the role of lactate dehydrogenase?
cards.a: conversion of NADH to NAD+

cards.q: what is the significance of lactate dehydrogenase?
cards.a: without it, the system would be strictly oxygen dependent, which would limit the intensity of possible physical activities

cards.q: what does the T-wave represent?
cards.a: the repolarization of the left and right ventricles of the heart

cards.q: abnormalities in cardiac rhythm would be indicated by what kind of test?
cards.a: EKG

cards.q: why is the T-wave in an EKG of primary interest?
cards.a: because electrical impulses (positive and negative) that occur here can be used as leading indicators for early detection

cards.q: a hyper acute T-wave is possibly the first manifestation of what kind of issue?
cards.a: acute myocardial infarction or heart attack

cards.q: what does ischemia mean?
cards.a: ischemia = "stopping blood" or not having enough blood, coronary ischemia = not having enough blood in coronary arteries

cards.q: what is an indicator for coronary ischemia?
cards.a: inverted T-wave

cards.q: why is the pleura an essential anatomical structure in lung anatomy?
cards.a: it's heavily involved in reducing surface tension via a small amount of pleural fluid, which makes breathing easier and helps inflate alveoli to potentiate gas exchange

cards.q: how does the pleura help potentiate gas exchange?
cards.a: by improving the oppositional proximity of the lungs to the chest wall, which provides flexibility in all the various breathing patterns that can ocur -- and assists with gas exchange

cards.q: what is ATP composed of?
cards.a: an adenine group, a ribose group, and three molecules of inorganic phosphates

cards.q: how is glycolysis driven?
cards.a: by enzymes, similar to PCr; glycolysis can supply greater energy over time because more available energy-generating resources from stored glycogen or free floating glucose are in the blood stream

cards.q: what are mitochondria responsible for?
cards.a: aerobic metabolism; they are where pyruvate is converted to acetyl CoA via pyruvate dehydrogenase, which can go to Krebs after

cards.q: how many strands may a muscle fiber (fasciculi covered by perimyseum) consist of?
cards.a: 150 individiual strands

cards.q: where does a motor neuron transmit signals from and what is it the site of?
cards.a: from the spinal cord to the muscles; it's the site of an action potential release into the neuromuscular junction

cards.q: what is adenosine triphosphatase responsible for?
cards.a: catalyzing the decomposition of ATP to ADP

cards.q: what does the dephosphorylation of ATP to ADP do?
cards.a: releases energy into a system in order to carry out additional chemical reactions

cards.q: do the enzymes that dephosphorylate ATP have multiple reactions?
cards.a: no, each enzyme has a specific effect and generally only does a single reaction

cards.q: what kinds of insights would biological age provide to a trainer?
cards.a: sexual development, structural musculoskeletal age, and neurological maturity through movement assessments

cards.q: how does the krebs cycle generate energy?
cards.a: through the oxidation of acetyl CoA derived from the three macros

cards.q: what insights does oxygen uptake provide?
cards.a: overall work capacity, rate of fatigue, anaerobic/aerobic thresholds

cards.q: what is the cori cycle?
cards.a: metabolic pathway in which lactate produced from anaerobic glycolysis is moved to the liver, converted to glucose, and returned to working muscles to be used as energy and again converted to lactate via gluconeogenesis

cards.q: why is the cori cycle utilized?
cards.a: to prevent lactic acidosis, which is a form of metabolic acidosis

cards.q: why is the sarcoplasm analogous to the cytoplasm of other organisms?
cards.a: this is where elements of muscular contraction are located such as glycogen, fat, various enzymes, mitochondria, and the sarcoplasmic reticulum

cards.q: why are the bonds of ATP molecules broken down via hydrolysis?
cards.a: to utilize the energy from these bonds

cards.q: what does hydrolysis require to break down the bonds of ATP molecules?
cards.a: one molecule of water and several enzymes

cards.q: how does ATP changed after hydrolysis?
cards.a: reduces ATP from the original eergy state to adenosine diphosphate and ends with adenosine monophosphate

cards.q: what is the bronci's relation to conduction?
cards.a: primary bronchi are part of the conducting zone in the respiratory system

cards.q: how are the primary bronchi formed?
cards.a: from the trachea, and divided into left and right branches

cards.q: why does no gas exchange takes place in the primary bronchi?
cards.a: they serve as the primary conductor for air passage into the bronchioles

cards.q: what are the side effects of caffeine?
cards.a: restlessness, trouble sleeping/insomnia, hyperactivity, heart palpitations or arrythmias, and frequent urinations, reductions in performance over time due to overstimulation of nervous system

cards.q: how do beta-adregenergic agonists increase energy expenditure?
cards.a: by increasing heart rate, blood pressure, rate of respitation, increased activity of cyclic-AMP

cards.q: why may beta-adrenerergic agonists be problematic for athletes?
cards.a: HR, blood pressure, heart conditions due to abnormal cardiac rhythm

cards.q: does anabolism build up neutral materials?
cards.a: no, anabolism builds up materials that have been reduced from catabolic processes to meet the organism's homeostatic needs

cards.q: how does anabolism generate new muscle tissue?
cards.a: form new amino acids from previously catabolized amino acids

cards.q: why are acute adapations to altitude training necessary?
cards.a: to stabilize respiration and heart rate, while chrnic adaptations primarily impact cellular function

cards.q: what are the acute adaptations to altitude?
cards.a: increase in pulmonary ventilation and cardiac output in resting and exercising states

cards.q: what are the chronic adaptations to altitude training?
cards.a: oriented toward delivering sufficient oxygen to the working tissues which requires increased myoglobin concentrations (5-15%), greater diffusion capacity though pulmonary membranes, increased capillary density in trained muscle, and increased buffering capacity of lactate through hyperventilation and greater availability of bicarbonate

cards.q: what are the drawbacks to altitude training?
cards.a: length of time the chronic adaptations persist -- they generally normalize after a month?

cards.q: what are endergonic reactions initiated by?
cards.a: previously released energy being absorbed by reactants in order to initiate a status change

cards.q: are anabolic processes endergonic or exergonic?
cards.a: they require the release of energy to begin the process of amino acid assimilation and tissue rebuilding, so endergonic

cards.q: is muscular contraction endergonic or exergonic?
cards.a: the release of energy substrate is required to initiate the biochemical cascade that causes muscular contraction, so endergonic

cards.q: for how long does EPOC cause a significant change in resting metabolic rate?
cards.a: 6-12 hours after training

cards.q: why does the endocrine system secrete hormones?
cards.a: to assist neuro restoration, blood glucose regulation, tissue growth, and muscular recovery

cards.q: reducing practice time due to improved performance is an example of what kind of reinforcement?
cards.a: negative reinforcement

cards.q: increasing a desired activity is an example if what kind of reinforcement?
cards.a: positive reinforcement

cards.q: what is a limitation of lock-and-key theory?
cards.a: cannot take into account allosteric binding and cross reactivity

cards.q: what functions are steroid hormones involved with?
cards.a: water balance, inflammatory responses, metabolic control, and immunity

cards.q: how are peptides synthesized?
cards.a: in the nucleus of the cell from various proteins, which are utilized as a signal or template precursors for other hormones or cascades

cards.q: allosteric binding sites?
cards.a: non-primary binding sites that allow for other non-hormonal substances to bind on a receptor and either increase or decrease activity at the site

cards.q: how do allosteric binding sites encourage or discourage binding?
cards.a: using homeostatic feedback (feedback pertaining to homeostasis)

cards.q: functions of growth hormone?
cards.a: maintain blood glucose, uptake of amino acids, release of fatty acids from adipose, stimulate muscle and bone growth

cards.q: most significant side effect of growth hormone use?
cards.a: acromegaly

cards.q: how is bioenergetics defined?
cards.a: conversion of macronutrients from food ingestion into useable energy substrates that allow the organism and its systems to perform work

cards.q: potential downside of a coach attending to mechanical advantage?
cards.a: overlook the development of weaknesses by overemphasizing mechanical advantage

cards.q: cardiomyocytes are?
cards.a: specialized muscle cells that allow for cardiac signals to be conducted quickly and consistently, which allows the heart to maintain constant rhythm

cards.q: what is minute ventilation responsible for?
cards.a: increasing or decreasing the rate of ventilation based on the amount of carbon dioxide in the blood when exercising

cards.q: how does minute ventilation clear CO2 from blood?
cards.a: respiration must increase and once levels have been normalized or exercise has ceased the rate of ventilation will decrease

cards.q: what does the QRS complex represent?
cards.a: rapid depolarization of the left and right ventricle

cards.q: why is the signal segment in the QRS complex much larger in amplitude than the P-wave?
cards.a: because of the larger mass of the ventricles of the hearts in comparison to the atria

cards.q: causes of overtraining?
cards.a: training too often, excessive volume and intensity, poor nutrition / reduced calorie intake, inadequate rest provisions

cards.q: physiological symptoms of overtraining?
cards.a: frequent illness, minor injuries that don't resolve, extreme fatigue

cards.q: calcium ATPase is what?
cards.a: enzymatic regulator of calcium movement into and out of the sarcoplasmic reticulum, which causes muscular relaxation

cards.q: in muscular contraction, the removal of CA+2 from the cell reduces the number of fibers that can cross bridge for contraction -- why?
cards.a: to induce muscular relaxation

cards.q: what kind of things should youth be taught?
cards.a: movement variety, work capacity development, guarding against overtraining or overuse

cards.q: why are women shorter than men?
cards.a: reduced growth cycles during puberty

cards.q: during the adolescent growth phase, what are the primary sites of growth?
cards.a: along the diaphysis of a long bone and in the growth cartilage

cards.q: during the adolescent growth phase, along the long bone, where are the three surfaces?
cards.a: at the joint surfaces, the apophyseal insertions of muscle tendons, and along the epiphyseal plates

cards.q: what causes bone growth to cease in the adolescent growth phase?
cards.a: ossification of the epiphyseal plates

cards.q: what kind of factors will taking into account training age benefit?
cards.a: guarding against overuse or injury, assessing acclimation to program

cards.q: what are the primary program considerations to minimize structural differences of female athletes?
cards.a: injury prevention for knee, improving upper body strength

cards.q: why do female athletes have a greater risk of knee injury?
cards.a: angle of the femur formed from the hip to the knee -- this creates natural sheer forces at the knee and can lead to a variety of injuries

cards.q: sarcopenia?
cards.a: natural occurrence in a reduction in cross-sectional muscle fiber mass as a result of aging; most significantly impacts older adult women

cards.q: how does sarcopenia occur?
cards.a: result of reduced or complete inactivity, which results in a loss of neural drive to the type II fast twitch motor units

cards.q: what are the primary factors affecting sarcopenia?
cards.a: activity levels over time, reduced neural capacity, poor nutrition, and hormonal alterations

cards.q: how is mean arterial pressure assessed?
cards.a: MAP = [(SDP-DBP)/3] + DBP

cards.q: what use does mean arterial pressure serve?
cards.a: an indicator for the rate of perfusion throughout the cardiac cycle, either at rest or during activity

cards.q: what is an athlete's benefit of knowing mean arterial pressure?
cards.a: to know if there are issues with moving blood into working tissues; can alert to possible disease if perfusion issue is identified

cards.q: what is alveolar pressure?
cards.a: pressure when the glottis is open and there is no air movement in or out of the lungs

cards.q: how does alveolar pressure change?
cards.a: pressure must drop below atmospheric pressure during inspiration and above atmospheric pressure during expiration

cards.q: what is the electron transport chain?
cards.a: a component of the oxidative system that uses redox reactions that transfer electrons from donors to acceptors via an electrochemical gradient

cards.q: what chemicals does the electron transport chain produce ATP with?
cards.a: NADH and FADH2

cards.q: how many molecules of ATP does NADH produce?
how many molecules of ATP does FADH2 produce?
why is the ETC important?
cards.a: maintaining the necessary ATP stores during aerobic exercise

cards.q: primary difference between overreaching and overtraining?
cards.a: duration of the time period that the training state persists; functional overreaching can force athlete beyond ability to adapt and recover, producing overstressing on all physiological systems, which causes supercompensation

cards.q: what is total peripheral resistance?
cards.a: the measure of the vascular resistance in the systemic circulation

cards.q: what is total peripheral resistance caused by?
cards.a: the opening and closing of vessels throughout the systemic circulation (vasoconstriction and vasodilation)

cards.q: how is total peripheral resistance determined?
cards.a: via the equation of [total peripheral resistance] = (mean arterial pressure - mean vascular pressure) / Q where Q = (cardiac output)

cards.q: in physical terms, how is work defined?
cards.a: the product of the application of force on an object and the distance it's displaced in the direction the force is applied

cards.q: quantifying work helps a coach gauge what training variables?
cards.a: levels of volume, loading intensity, and specific movement patterns

cards.q: how does quantifying work help across athletic populations?
cards.a: a larger athlete may perform considerably more work than a smaller athlete due to the size differential

cards.q: how is valsalva perrformed?
cards.a: forced exhalation against a closed glottis, which prevents air from leaving lungs, causes abdominals and ribcage to contract, and causes air pressure to increase in the upper torso

cards.q: what is a concentration gradient
cards.a: the process of particles, which are sometimes called solutes, moving through a solution or gas from an area with a higher number of particles to an area with a lower number of particles. (the areas are typically separated by a membrane.)

cards.q: how does the diffusion of gases (through respiratory exchange) occur?
cards.a: diffusion of CO2 and O2 through the alveoli in the lungs occurs according to a concentration gradient.

cards.q: how is the respiratory concentration gradient formed?
cards.a: formed by molecules from a higher concentration region into a region with a lower concentration of those molecules, which is dictatedby partial pressure of the gases as well as concentrations in capillaries and alveoli. this process does not occur actively; it's passively driven by the motion of molecules as they transition from regions of higher/lower concentration.

cards.q: what is a moment arm
cards.a: distance from a muscle's line of action to the joint's center of rotation, oriented in the direction of the force being produced

cards.q: the humerus and biceps acting on the resistive force of a dumbbell during a bicep curl is an example of what?
cards.a: moment arm

cards.q: why is pleural pressure significant?
cards.a: it maintains the tension between the chest wall and the pleura of the lungs, allowing fro inspiration and expiration

cards.q: why is pleural pressure slightly negative?
cards.a: to compensate for the expansion capacities of the lungs while also allowing the lungs to maintain pressures below atmospheric level

cards.q: why should pleural pressure never equal or exceed atmospheric pressure?
cards.a: the lungs will collapse, which is referred to as pneumothorax (defined as "an abnormal collection of air in the pleural space between the lung and the chest wall")

cards.q: what are alveoli?
cards.a: the terminal ends of the respiratory tree

cards.q: where is the primary site for gas exchange in the respiratory system?
cards.a: alveolar ducts and sacs; the alveolar membrane serves as the gas exchange surface

cards.q: where are alveoli located?
cards.a: alveolar sacs and alveolar ducts

cards.q: systemic circulation does what to deoxygenated blood?
cards.a: returns it from the rest of the body via alveolar blood vessels; through passive diffusion the carbon dioxide that has been carried from the body's tissue is unloaded; concurrently the oxygen is being diffused into the red blood cells and will be carried into working tissues via pulmonary circulation

cards.q: what is a fulcrum?
cards.a: simple point of rotation for a lever

cards.q: how is length of a moment arm dictated?
cards.a: length of a fulcrum, which dictates total force required to overcome resistive force

cards.q: how is mechanical advantage determined?
cards.a: fulcrum position

cards.q: what are the resistive forces that can act on the body?
cards.a: gravity, and static and kinetic frictions during activities such as running/swimming/jumping

cards.q: leg extensions and bicep curls occur in what plane of movement?
cards.a: saggital

cards.q: what is torque?
cards.a: capacity of a force to generate rotation on a fulcrum

cards.q: what is increasing the rate of torque dependent on?
cards.a: rate of force production, which requires a range of training interventions incl. speed/acceleration training and higher loading intensities

cards.q: what are the synergists of a barbell curl?
cards.a: brachialis and brachioradalis, as well as stabilizing muscles along the scapula that work to maintain structural and force integrity of the humerus and scapula

cards.q: what processes does metabolism include?
cards.a: muscle growth, hormona balance, fat loss, and literally any process undertaken to maintain homeostasis. it's the result of all activities, or LACK thereof, taken part of by an athlete.

cards.q: how should female athletes be programmed for?
cards.a: not much different than male ones bc after correcting for body mass differences total power output and strength is similar

cards.q: what benefits do risk assessments provide coaches?
cards.a: contraindications, training limits, and whether or not medical clearance is necessary

cards.q: what kind of fibers will contract first in a contraction?
cards.a: smaller, lower force, fatigue-resistant units (size principle)

cards.q: the hamstring action during a squatting movement provides what kind of muscle action?
cards.a: antagonist via stabilization

cards.q: first class lever?
cards.a: muscle force and resistive force on opposite sides of fulcrum

cards.q: second class lever?
cards.a: requires muscular and resistive forces to occur on the same side of the fulcrum

cards.q: third class lever?
cards.a: muscular and resistive forces on same side of fulcrum, through a distance shorter than distance trhough which resistive force is acting

cards.q: structural changes that change within muscle in response to resistance training?
cards.a: increased myofibrillar volume, increased density of cytoplasm, increased sarcoplasmic and t-tubule density, increased enzyme activity; also due to muscular growth -- reduced mitochondria density, reduced capillary density, increased lactate buffering capacity

cards.q: what are the primary connective tissue adaptations from demand on tissues in response to increased strength/growth?
cards.a: tendon junctions that occur between two bony surfaces, body of the tendon and ligament, fascia covering a hypertrophied muscle thickening and stiffening

cards.q: what is oxygen uptake?
cards.a: amount of oxygen transported and unloaded into working tissues

cards.q: what factors influence oxygen uptake?
cards.a: training intensity, selected exercise method, duration of session

cards.q: why does exercise selection influence oxygen uptake measurement?
cards.a: chosen method may involve smaller muscle groups (arm ergometer) or larger groups (treadmill) that require varying amount of oxygen to supply tissues worked

cards.q: METS = ?
cards.a: metabolic equivalent of task, used to assess energy expenditure of various tasks

cards.q: what is a limitation of METS?
cards.a: assumptions are made wrt a specific individual; cannot account for differences which include fat mass, fat free mass, exercise intensity, and overall conditioning of the person

cards.q: movements that occur in the frontal plane?
cards.a: pull-ups, dips, and squats

cards.q: how is VO2max evaluated?
cards.a: graded exercise test where the amount of work performed is gradually increased over time until a maximum oxygen value is reached

cards.q: why is maximal oxygen uptake the best measure of cardiovasc. fitness?
cards.a: it indicates the upper limit capacities for the endurance athlete across varying heart rates and workloads

cards.q: what is the use of VO2max for anaerobic athletes?
cards.a: indicative of the anaerobic lactate threshold and aerobic potential

cards.q: osteopenia presents with symptoms of thinning bones. what considerations must be made for trainees with this ailment?
cards.a: osteopenia is not a limiting factor when considering movements of the client, b/c weight-bearing exercises will help reduce the rate of bone loss and has been seen to reverse the process

cards.q: where does mechanical loading model new bone cells?
cards.a: along the surfaces between bone cells, which occur primarily on the surface of bone to increase density

cards.q: an athlete with uncorrected bilateral deficit is likely to face what issue?
cards.a: imbalanced force relationships, poor length-tension relationships, possible injury

cards.q: what is the force-velocity curve?
cards.a: the representative curve of force and velocy along an x- and y- axis

cards.q: what does the force-velocity curve depict?
cards.a: an athlete's ability to contract with a range of qualities including high total force and low velocity -- maximal strength -- and high velocity and low total force -- speed

cards.q: how can the force-velocity curve benefit the strength athlete?
cards.a: to develop sport-specific training characteristics and correct individual weaknesses

cards.q: what does the fick equation assess?
cards.a: maximal oygen uptake

cards.q: what are the essential components of the fick equation?
cards.a: cardiac output (Q), arterial oxygen content (a), and venous oxygen content (VO2). to properly assess maximal oxygen content, you must be able to calculate the difference in arterial and venous oxygen content

cards.q: why in the fick equation is it essential to know the difference in arterial and venous oxygen content?
cards.a: because the difference is the volume unloaded into working tissues. you must also know how hard the heart is working to pump the oxygen into the working tissues, which is why cardiac output is essential

cards.q: what are the three types of joints in the body?
cards.a: uniaxial, biaxial, multiaxial

cards.q: the elbow is an example of what kind of joint?
cards.a: hinge joint / uniaxial

cards.q: the ankle and wrist are examples of what kind of joint?
cards.a: biaxial joints; joints that allow movement about two perpendicular planes

cards.q: the hip is an example of what kind of joint?
cards.a: multiaxial or ball and socket

cards.q: why is blood flow constricted to certain tissues during exercise?
cards.a: to maximize blood volume for the active tissue sites that need oxygen, and to reduce the functions of certain systems during exercise e.g. digestion

cards.q: what is ventilatory equivalent?
cards.a: the ratio of minute ventilation and oxygen uptake during exercise

cards.q: how is ventilatory equivalent expressed?
cards.a: VE/VO2 for oxygen consumption and VE/VCO2 when evaluating carbon dioxide output

cards.q: when does ventilation rate increase disproportionate to rate of oxygen uptake in tissues?
cards.a: the onset of lactate accumulating more rapidly than can be effectively buffered

cards.q: what variables does EKG/ECG test?
cards.a: rate and frequency of heartbeats + size and position of heart's chambers

cards.q: what would EKG/ECG test for athletes?
cards.a: detection of left ventricular hypertrophy, congential heart defects, other cardiac rhythm distortions, sudden death

cards.q: why are lactate threshold and ventilatory equivalent connected?
cards.a: because of the necessity of clearing excess lactate and CO2 from the body

cards.q: the frank-sterling mechanism refers to?
cards.a: the forceful contraction of the heart in response to increase stroke volume which over time stretches the left ventricle

cards.q: why is the frank-sterling mechanism significant?
cards.a: primarily responsible for the increased ejection fraction (measurement of the percentage of blood leaving your heart each time it contracts), which means greater blood volume ejected due to frank-sterling

cards.q: law of mass action / mass action effect?
cards.a: specific to the concentrations of reactants and products in solution; the concentration of a reactant or product is entirely depenedent on establishing equilibrium within the system

cards.q: why is the law of mass action significant for exercise?
cards.a: for enzyme driven reactions, establishing equilibrium is specific to maintaining ATP threshold to perform the work; therefore, the enzymatic activities must continue throughout the exercise section to maintain threshold ATP levels; once the stimulus is reduced or ceased, these processes discontinue

cards.q: what is venous return?
cards.a: the volume of blood returning to the heart from the periphery

cards.q: why does venous return increase in response to aerobic conditioning?
cards.a: over time the volume of the left ventricle will increase to accommodate the increased blood flow from the right atrium; this leads to greater volumes of blood being ejected from the left ventricle, enhancing aerobic performance

cards.q: where are steroid hormones secreted from?
cards.a: adrenal cortex and gonads. steroids = transported across sarcolemma; polypeptide = bind to receptor cells.

cards.q: what are the three major divisions of the bronchioles?
cards.a: lesser bronchioles, terminal bronchioles, and respiratory bronchioles

cards.q: what does the division of bronchioles represent?
cards.a: the end of the conduction zone in human respiration and can be identified with the occurrence of alveoli, which represents the beginning of the respiration zone

cards.q: what percent of total gas exchange from respiratory bronchioles?
major functions of catecholamines?
cards.a: neural upregulation, vasodilation, vasoconstriction, enhancing enzyme activity in skeletal muscle; increase muscle contraction, elevate blood pressure, increase blood flow, improve testosterone secretion re: resistance training

cards.q: how does testostone affect pituitary gland?
cards.a: increases growth hormone production there

cards.q: how does testosterone affect CNS adaptations to resistance training?
cards.a: increasing neuronal receptor availability, increasing neurotransmitter activity and availability, altering structural proteins that facilitate muscular contraction

cards.q: what are chronic adaptations to resistance exercise?
cards.a: hypertrophy of high-threshold motor units, increased importation and affinity for nutrients in muscle tissue, increased insulin sensitivity, increased androgen receptor count

cards.q: what does adenylate kinase do?
cards.a: converts two ADP molecules into ATP+AMP; this is significant b/c it maintains cellular energy homeostasis and stimulates glycolysis via elevating AMP

cards.q: where does the phosphagen get its ATP?
cards.a: local muscle stores and breakdown of creatine phosphate

cards.q: how does the phosphagen system resynthesize ATP?
cards.a: adding an inorganic phosphate group (creatine phosphate or phosphocreatine, same thing) to an existing ADP molecule via an enzymatic process with creatine kinase

cards.q: end-diastolic volume?
cards.a: volume of blood available to be pumped after diastole

cards.q: why is end-diastolic volume significant for stroke volume?
cards.a: this is what will be pumped from the heart to the rest of the body and during exercise, thereby working muscle

cards.q: what adaptations can an athlete have regarding end-diastolic volume?
cards.a: over time the muscle fibers of the heart become stretched, which allows for greater end-diastolic volume and increases the volume of blood during systole

cards.q: what are the adaptations to aerobic training?
cards.a: hypertrophy of type I fibers, increased mitochondria, increased myoglobin activity

cards.q: why is greater mitochondrial density significant for athletes?
cards.a: leads to greater ATP production / is significant in enhancing aerobic capacity

cards.q: why is increased myoglobin significant for athletes?
cards.a: myoglobin is the protein responsible for transporting oxygen into the muscle cell; more myoglobin increases the amount of oxygen available for energy production in working muscle

cards.q: memories of missing an important free throw in high school when attempting a free throw in college is an example of what?
cards.a: cognitive anxiety

cards.q: which ventricle does bradycardia continge on?
cards.a: hypertrophy of the left ventricle, which increases stroke volume capacity (more volume = less need to beat)

cards.q: elderly populations/athletes might want to be concerned about bradycardia why?
cards.a: could be indications of decreased electrical activity in sinoatrial node; if symptoms unrelated to exercise, refer to physician

cards.q: how does an athlete perform autogenic training?
cards.a: get into relaxed setting/lying position/other and begin to visualize/sensationalize the relaxation of individual muscles or limbs by emphasizing the warmth and increasing heaviness of the limbs (this approach may cause a shift from sympathetic neural dominance to parasympathetic and reduced arousal)

cards.q: how will increasing muscle buffering capacity benefit an anaerobic athlete?
cards.a: increase the physiological capacity to buffer H+ ions from lactate to better maintain rate of work, esp. at high intensity

cards.q: how many macronutrients, minerals, and vitamins are in the Dietary Reference Intake, and how does the DRI help athletes?
cards.a: 18 macronutrients, 18 minerals, 14 vitamins; DRI helps athletes by being aware of baseline needs

cards.q: how does reaching peak bone mass benefit aging?
cards.a: there is a higher percentage of bone loss that can be lost before a harmful threshold is reached

cards.q: what do athletes/populations who want to reduce bone aging effects have to account for?
cards.a: maintaining activity levels across the aging cycle

cards.q: what is successive approximation and how does it benefit athletes?
cards.a: establishing a series of short-term goals that increase in difficulty, and, as athlete progresses, more resemble final behavior; can eliminate bad habits or dangerous motor patterns as well as improve adherence

cards.q: an athlete reduces their soda intake gradually, until eventually reaching zero. what is this strategy called?
cards.a: successive approximation

cards.q: what factors must an athlete pay attention to for manipulating their breathing?
cards.a: awareness of the body, levels of tension or stress, and specific elements in response to these techniques; this can positively impact recovery from training

cards.q: what factors should be evaluated in older clients?
cards.a: body composition and anthropometrics; cardiovascular, flexibility, and strength training

cards.q: what is the function of myosin-heavy chain protein?
cards.a: remodeling and regeneration of muscle tissue after heavy resistance training; this can alter fiber typing by impacting gene expression, increasing protein synthesis, and retarding protein loss

cards.q: what do proteolytic enzymes do?
cards.a: hydrolize peptide bonds that link proteins and amino acid groups together in order for these proteins to be assimilated into other amino acids or proteins; therefore they can be utilized in other cells or tissues

cards.q: what is the site of ATP hydrolysis?
cards.a: the myosin fiber

cards.q: when is the energy required for cross-linking between actin and myosin available?
cards.a: when phosphate has been released onto the myosin fiber

cards.q: a coach assessing an athlete's possible physical limitations should conduct what kind of test?
cards.a: movement analysis

cards.q: an athlete drills their fingers to get in the zone before a free throw. this is an example of what?
cards.a: preparatory routine

cards.q: what is the risk of an athlete who is extrinsically motivated?
cards.a: inconsistency; an intrinsically motivated athlete will be more consistent

cards.q: what conversion does the neuromuscular junction represent?
cards.a: electrical --\> biochemical --\> mechanical

cards.q: functions of growth hormone?
cards.a: increase in cellular amino acid uptake; increased availability of glucose and amino acids in circulation; increased lipolysis; can strengthen immune response

cards.q: how would a coach benefit from arteriovenous oxygen difference?
cards.a: it's the primary means of evaluating the amount of oxygen being unloaded into active tissues during exercise, and crucial to determining aerobic fitness because this component is crucial to the fick equation.

cards.q: when do cartilaginous joints allow the body flexibility and elasticity?
cards.a: during growth or respiration

cards.q: the knee will have what kind of joint?
cards.a: synovial

cards.q: pubic symphysis is an example of what kind of joint?
cards.a: cartilaginous

cards.q: what is inorganic phosphate composed of and why does this matter?
cards.a: adenine, ribose, and two molecules of inorganic phosphate; ADP can convert into ATP with the addition of an inorganic phosphate group from the creatine phosphate system

cards.q: what is myosin ATPase responsible for?
cards.a: catalyzing the actomyosin cross-bridging response in muscular contraction, which creates free energy needed for the contraction

cards.q: what does creatine kinase do?
cards.a: potentiate the activity of replenishment of ATP molecules for energy utilization in the phosphagen system

cards.q: why should athletes be concerned about creatine kinase elevation in tests?
cards.a: indicative of muscle damage -- possibly from heart attack, or kidney failure, or rhabdomyolysis

cards.q: under what timespan can rhabdomyolysis occur?
cards.a: immediately to the course of a training week

cards.q: cardiac output?
cards.a: volume of blood pumped through the heart specifically by a right/left ventricle in one minute

cards.q: what are the factors of cardiac output?
cards.a: stroke volume (ml/min), heart rate (BPM)

cards.q: what does sodium-potassium ATPase do?
cards.a: maintain cellular sodium potassium balance by pumping sodium out of a cell and potassium into the cell. (2 K+ ions into the cell = 3 Na+ ions out of the cell)

cards.q: why is the pumping activity of sodium-potassium ATPase necessary?
cards.a: maintain proper fluid resting potential, maintain fluid balance in cells

cards.q: sarcolemma?
cards.a: cell membrane of striated muscle tissue, responsible for separation of each muscle fiber; essential for conducting and receiving stimuli from connecting nerve fibers (allows its t-tubules to release Ca2+ into sarcoplasm)

cards.q: what is a function of cortisol?
cards.a: cortisol is a glucocorticoid that converts amino acids into carbohydrates and is involved as a signaling hormone in carbohydrate metabolism (related to glycogen storage)

cards.q: smooth muscle functions?
cards.a: one nucleus/no striations, comprising walls of blood vessels/organs of urinary/digestive/respiratory/reproductive tracts, also for peristalsis (moving food through digestive tract)

cards.q: bioenergetic diff. between type I and type II?
cards.a: type I = low myosin ATPase, slower calcium handling, reduced glycolytic capacity, large mitochondria

cards.q: difference between IIa and IIb fibers?
cards.a: IIa = moderate aerobic/anaerobic capacity, fast-oxidative+glycolytic, high myosin ATPase activity, greater number of capillaries than IIx fibers. IIb = fast glycolytic, less capacity for aerobic energy therefore more fatigable

cards.q: number of skeletal muscles in the body?
cards.a: over 500

cards.q: what are the twelve muscle groups by function?
cards.a: (1) facial expression (2) mastication (3) head/vertebral column movement (4) pectoral girdle movement (5) arm movement (6) forearm movement (7) hand movement (8) abdominal wall movement (9) pelvic outlet movement (10) thigh movement (11) leg movement (12) foot movement

cards.q: muscles responsible for arm/shoulder flexion?
cards.a: pectoralis major, anterior delt, coracobrachialis

cards.q: muscles responsible for arm/shoulder extension?
cards.a: teres major, lat dorsi, posterior delts

cards.q: muscles responsible for arm abduction?
cards.a: supraspinatus and deltoid muscles

cards.q: muscles responsible for arm rotation?
cards.a: subscapularis, infraspinatus, teres minor

cards.q: muscles responsible for elbow flexion?
cards.a: biceps, brachialis, bracioradialis

cards.q: muscles responsible for elbow/forearm extension?
cards.a: triceps, anconeus

cards.q: muscles responsible for forearm rotation?
cards.a: supinator, pronator teres, and pronator quadratus

cards.q: muscles responsible for wrist/hand flexion?
cards.a: flexor carpi radialis, flexor carpi ulnaris, palmaris longus, flexor digitorum profundus, flexor digitorum superficialis

cards.q: muscles responsible for knee flexion?
cards.a: bicep femoris, semitendinosus, semimembranosus (the hamstring muscles) and sartorius

cards.q: muscles responsible for knee extension?
cards.a: quadriceps femoris (rectus femoris, vastus lateralis, vastus medialis, and vastus intermedius)

cards.q: muscles responsible for dorsiflexion?
cards.a: fibularis tertius, extensor digitorum longus, extensor hallucis longus, and tibialis anterior

cards.q: muscles responsible for ankle plantarflexion?
cards.a: plantaris, flexor digitorum longus, gastrocnemius, soleus

cards.q: superior (cranial)?
cards.a: near/toward upper part of body, toward head

cards.q: antonym of cranial?
cards.a: caudal (inferior)

cards.q: ventral/dorsal are other words for what?
cards.a: anterior/posterior

cards.q: medial?
cards.a: near body’s midline

cards.q: lateral - relationship to medial?
cards.a: away from body’s midline

cards.q: bilateral?
cards.a: on either side of central axis or midline

cards.q: ipsilateral?
cards.a: on or affecting the same side of the body

cards.q: contralateral?
cards.a: on or affecting opposite sides of the body

cards.q: intermediate?
cards.a: located between two structures -- e.g. one medial and one lateral, or one superior/inferior

cards.q: proximal?
cards.a: location of the origin or point of attachment toward the trunk and away from appendages

cards.q: distal?
cards.a: location of origin or point of attachment away from the body

cards.q: superficial (external)
cards.a: near the outside or surface of an object or body

cards.q: deep (internal)
cards.a: inside, away from surface or body

cards.q: axial
cards.a: associated with the center of the body (head/neck/trunk = axial skeleton)

cards.q: appendicular
cards.a: body's appendages (legs/arms)

cards.q: abduct
cards.a: movement away from body's midline

cards.q: adduct
cards.a: movement toward the body's midline

cards.q: in terms of orientation/direction, where is the clavicle in relation to the iliac crest?
cards.a: superior to

cards.q: in terms of orientation/direction, where is the talus in relation to the patella?
cards.a: talus is inferior to patella

cards.q: in terms of orientation/direction, where is the sternum in relation to the spine?
cards.a: sternum is anterior to the spine

cards.q: in terms of orientation/direction, where is the spine in relation to the sternum?
cards.a: spine is posterior to the sternum

cards.q: in terms of orientation/direction, where is nose in relation to the ears?
cards.a: nose is medial to the ears

cards.q: in terms of orientation/direction, where are the ears in relation to the nose?
cards.a: ears are lateral to nose

cards.q: what are the body's bilateral structures?
cards.a: legs, eyes, lungs

cards.q: what are the body's isolateral structures?
cards.a: hands and feet

cards.q: what is an example of contralateral action?
cards.a: a stroke on the right side of the brain may affect the function of the left arm

cards.q: a stroke on the left side of the brain may affect the movement of the right leg -- this is an example of what?
cards.a: contralateral effect

cards.q: in terms of orientation/direction, where is the knee relative to the hip?
cards.a: intermediate

cards.q: in terms of orientation/direction, where is the thigh relative to the ankle?
cards.a: proximal

cards.q: in terms of orientation/direction, where is the ankle relative to the knee?
cards.a: distal

cards.q: the first phase of jumping jacks -- what kind of movement is this?
cards.a: abduct

cards.q: the second phase of jumping jacks -- what kind of movement is this?
cards.a: adduct

cards.q: what is the action of the ilicostalis (lateral), longissimus (intermediate), and spinalis (medial)?
cards.a: prime mover of back extension; each side consists of three columns

cards.q: how do the origin and insertion differ in mobility?
cards.a: insertion is movable, origin is immovable

cards.q: where is the origin and insertion of the trapezius muscle?
cards.a: ORIGIN: occipital bone, ligamentum nuchae, and spines of C7 and all thoracic vertebrae INSERTION: continuous insertion along acromion and spine of scapula and lateral third of clavicle

cards.q: what is the origin and insertion of the rhomboids?
cards.a: ORIGIN: spinous processes (T7-T5), INSERTION: medial border of scapula

cards.q: what is the action of the rhomboid major?
cards.a: retracts, elevates, and rotates scapula

cards.q: what is the action of the rhomboid minor?
cards.a: retracts and elevates scapula

cards.q: what is the action of the pectoralis minor?
cards.a: abducts scapula pulling it forward and downward; draws rib cage superiorly (raises ribs)

cards.q: what is the origin and insertion of the pectoralis minor?
cards.a: ORIGIN: anterior surface of ribs 3-5, INSERTION: coracoid process of scapula

cards.q: what is the action of the pectoralis major?
cards.a: prime mover of arm flexion; rotates arm medially, adducts humerous; pulls arm across chest

cards.q: what is the origin and insertion of the pectoralis major?
cards.a: ORIGIN: medial 1/2 of clavicle, sternum, and costal cartilages of ribs one through six INSERTION: greater tubercle of humerus

cards.q: what is the action of the teres major?
cards.a: posteromedially extends, medially rotates, and adducts humerus; synergist of latissimus dorsi

cards.q: what is the origin and insertion of the teres major?
cards.a: ORIGIN: posterior surface of scapula at inferior angle INSERTION: intertubercular groove of humerus

cards.q: what is the action of the latissimus dorsi?
cards.a: prime mover of arm extension; arm adductor; medially rotates humerus at shoulder

cards.q: what is the origin and insertion of the latissimus dorsi?
cards.a: ORIGIN: spines of lower six thoracic vertebrae, lumbar vertebrae, lower three to four ribs, and iliac crest INSERTION: intertubercular groove of humerus

cards.q: what is the action of the deltoids?
cards.a: prime mover of arm abduction (at shoulder); extends and flexes arm

cards.q: what is the origin and insertion of the deltoids?
cards.a: ORIGIN: spine of scapula, acromion, and lateral 1/3 of clavicle INSERTION: deltoid tuberosity of humerus

cards.q: what muscles comprise the rotator cuff?
cards.a: supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor, subscapularis

cards.q: what is the action of the rotator cuff (supraspinatus/infraspinatus/teres minor/subscapularis)?
cards.a: medially or laterally rotate arm at shoulder; supraspinatus assists abduction; stabilizes shoulder joint, helping to prevent downward dislocation of humerous

cards.q: what is the action of the biceps brachii?
cards.a: flexes elbow joint and supinates forearm and hand

cards.q: what is the origin and insertion of the biceps brachii?
cards.a: ORIGIN: short head -- caracoid process of scapula, long head -- tubercle above glenoid cavity of scapula INSERTION: radial tuberosity of radius

cards.q: what is the action of the brachialis?
cards.a: flexes elbow

cards.q: what is the origin and insertion of the brachialis?
cards.a: ORIGIN: anterior, distal 1/2 of humerus INSERTION: coronoid process of ulna

cards.q: what is the action of the brachioradialis?
cards.a: flexes forearm at elbow

cards.q: what is the origin and insertion of the brachioradialis?
cards.a: ORIGIN: lateral supercondylar ridge at distal end of humerus, INSERTION: base of styloid process at radius

cards.q: what is the action of the triceps brachii?
cards.a: extends forearm at elbow

cards.q: what is the origin and insertion of the triceps brachii?
cards.a: ORIGIN: long head -- infraglenoid tubercle of scapula, lateral head -- posterior humerus above radial groove, medial head -- posterior humerus below INSERTION: all three heads -- olecranon process of ulna

cards.q: what is the action of the external obliques?
cards.a: tenses abdominal wall and compresses abdominal contents

cards.q: what is the origin and insertion of the external obliques?
cards.a: ORIGIN: outer surfaces of lower eight ribs INSERTION: outer lip of iliac crest and linea alba

cards.q: what is the action of the internal obliques?
cards.a: tenses abdominal wall and compresses abdominal contents

cards.q: what is the origin and insertion of the internal obliques?
cards.a: ORIGIN: lumbar fascia, iliac crest, and inguinal ligament INSERTION: cartilages of lower ribs, linea alba, and crest of pubis

cards.q: what is the action of the transverse abdominis?
cards.a: compresses abdominal components

cards.q: what is the origin and insertion of the transverse abdominis?
cards.a: ORIGIN: inguinal ligament, lumbar fascia, cartilages of the last six ribs, iliac crest INSERTION: linea alba and crest of pubis

cards.q: what is the action of the rectus abdominis?
cards.a: flexes and rotates lumbar region of vertebral column; fixes and depresses ribs, stabilizes pelvis when walking; tenses abdominal wall, increases intra-abdominal pressure

cards.q: what is the origin and insertion of the rectus abdominis?
cards.a: ORIGIN: crest of pubis and symphysis pubis INSERTION: xiphoid process and costal cartilages of ribs five through seven

cards.q: what is the origin and insertion of the psoas major (iliopsoas)?
cards.a: ORIGIN: lumbar intevertebral discs, bodies and transverse processes of lumbar vertebrae INSERTION: femur on and immediately below lesser trochanter of femur via ilipsoas tendon

cards.q: what is the action of the iliacus (iliopsoas)?
cards.a: prime mover for flexing thigh or for flexing trunk on thigh during a bow

cards.q: what is the origin and insertion of the iliacus (iliopsoas)?
cards.a: ORIGIN: iliac fossa and crest, INSERTION: femur on and immediately below lesser trochanter of femur via iliopsoas tendon

cards.q: what is the action of the gluteus maximus?
cards.a: major extensor of thigh; generally inactive during walking and standing, laterally rotates and abducts thigh

cards.q: what is the origin and insertion of the gluteus maximus?
cards.a: ORIGIN: sacrum, coccyx, and posterior surface of ilium INSERTION: posterior surface of femur and fascia of thigh

cards.q: what is the action of the piriformis?
cards.a: abducts and rotates thigh laterally, stabilizes hip joint

cards.q: what is the origin and insertion of the piriformis?
cards.a: ORIGIN: anterior surface of sacrum INSERTION: superior border of greater trochanter of femur

cards.q: what is the action of the hamstring group (bicep femoris, semitendinosus, semimembranosous)?
cards.a: extends thigh and flexes knee, laterally or medially rotates leg, especially when knee is flexed

cards.q: what is the origin and insertion of the hamstring group (bicep femoris, semitendinosus, semimembranosus)?
cards.a: ORIGIN: ischial tuberosity INSERTION: varies on muscle

cards.q: what is the action of the quadricep group (vastus lateralis, vastus medialis, vastus intermedius, rectus femoris)?
cards.a: extends and stabilizes knee

cards.q: what is the origin and insertion of the quadricep group (vastus lateralis, vastus medialis, vastus intermedius, rectus femoris)?
cards.a: ORIGIN: varies on specific muscle INSERTION: patellar ligament to tibial tuberosity

cards.q: what is the action of the gastrocnemius?
cards.a: plantar flexion of foot, flexes knee

cards.q: what is the origin and insertion of the gastrocnemius?
cards.a: ORIGIN: lateral and medial condolytes of femur INSERTION: posterior surface of calcaneus

cards.q: what is the action of the soleus?
cards.a: plantar flexion of foot

cards.q: what is the origin and insertion of the soleus?
cards.a: ORIGIN: head and shaft of fibula and posterior surface of tibia INSERTION: posterior surface of calcaneus

cards.q: of the actin/myosin combo, which is responsible for splitting ATP?
cards.a: myosin

cards.q: how is the distance of Z-lines in the sarcomere reduced?
cards.a: by actin/myosin sliding past each other, causing the overlap of filament to increase

cards.q: when is minimal calcium in the myofibril?
cards.a: under resting conditions

cards.q: what are the phases of sliding filament theory?
cards.a: resting phase, excitation-coupling phase, recharge phase, relaxation phase

cards.q: why are isometric muscle contractions not able to contract concentrically?
cards.a: they result from when the resistance force is greater than that generated by the muscle

cards.q: what does a motor neuron consist of?
cards.a: motor neuron (cell body), axon, dendrites

cards.a: elbow extension

cards.q: tricep push down is an example of what kind of body movement?
cards.a: elbow extension

cards.q: football punting is an example of what kind of body movement?
cards.a: hip flexion

cards.q: leg raises are an example of what kind of body movement?
cards.a: hip flexion

cards.q: diving (tuck dive) is an example of what kind of body movement?
cards.a: knee flexion

cards.q: leg curl is an example of what kind of body movement?
cards.a: knee flexion

cards.q: swimming (breaststroke) is an example of what kind of body movement?
cards.a: shoulder adduction

cards.q: wide grip lateral pull down is an example of what kind of body movement?
cards.a: shoulder adduction

cards.q: resisted inversion is an example of what kind of body movement?
cards.a: ankle inversion

cards.q: soccer dribbling is an example of what kind of body movement?
cards.a: ankle inversion

cards.q: standing adduction machine is an example of what kind of body movement?
cards.a: hip adduction

cards.q: soccer side step is an example of what kind of body movement?
cards.a: hip adduction

cards.q: basketball pivot movement is an example of what kind of body movement?
cards.a: hip internal rotation

cards.q: resisted internal rotation is an example of what kind of body movement?
cards.a: hip internal rotation

cards.q: baseball batting is an example of what kind of body movement?
cards.a: lower back left rotation

cards.q: medicine ball side toss is an example of what kind of body movement?
cards.a: lower back left rotation

cards.q: golf swing is an example of what kind of body movement?
cards.a: lower back right rotation

cards.q: torso machine is an example of what kind of body movement?
cards.a: lower back right rotation

cards.q: what is force?
cards.a: the interaction of two objects that have both magnitude and direction

cards.q: an athlete has fewer actin and myosin crossbridges. how will this affect force production?
cards.a: decrease, because number of cross bridges = force production ability.

cards.q: how to fix an athlete who is strong but not fast?
cards.a: more time training at lower force intensity (e.g. back squats at 30% RM) + faster velocity

cards.q: an athlete who is trying to develop explosiveness would benefit from what calculation?
cards.a: rate of force development (change in force divided by change in time)

cards.q: momentum?
cards.a: velocity \* mass; both velocity and momentum are vector quantities without direction

cards.q: an athlete is concerned about injury risk from contact. what calculation would benefit?
cards.a: momentum

cards.q: impulse?
cards.a: product of time required to generate a force

cards.q: a coach is trying to figure out how much intensity/volume an athlete can handle. which equation is beneficial?
cards.a: work. (force \* distance)

cards.q: how is COP (center of pressure) defined?
cards.a: point of application of ground reaction force whihc is the force that is exerted by the supporting surface (eg ground) on body

cards.q: what sports are COP calculations especially relevant for?
cards.a: sports like tennis where player may shift COP medially and laterally as when a player moves side to side before receiving serve

cards.q: movement of ball-and-socket joint?
cards.a: rotation and movement in all planes (ex: hip)

cards.q: movement of condylar joint?
cards.a: no rotation, variety of movement in different planes (ex: joints between phalanges and metacarpals)

cards.q: movement of plane joint?
cards.a: twisting or sliding (ex: joints between various bones of the ankle and wrist)

cards.q: movement of hinge joint?
cards.a: flexion and extension (ex: elbow)

cards.q: movement of pivot joint?
cards.a: rotation (ex: joint between the proximal ends of the ulna and radius)

cards.q: movement of saddle joint?
cards.a: variety of movements, primarily in two planes (ex: joint between carpal and metacarpal of thumb)

cards.q: work done through isometric/isotonic muscle contractions?
cards.a: no work is done bc distance is zero

cards.q: neutralizers pull against and cancel out movement from agonist muscles. example?
cards.a: when elbow is flexed, supination is often undesirable, so the pronator teres counteracts the supination of the biceps so that only elbow flexion results

cards.q: what is the stabilizer of pelvis in an abdominal exercise?
cards.a: contraction of the hip joint

cards.q: in elbow flexion, what are the roles of biceps/triceps/delts/brachioradialis?
cards.a: biceps: agonist, triceps: antagonist, deltoid: stabilizer, brachioradialis: neutralizer

cards.q: fascia, bone, and cartilage will contain what strengthening quality?
cards.a: bundles of crosslinked collagen fibers

cards.q: what kind of collagen are bones/ligaments/tendons composed of?
cards.a: type I

cards.q: what kind of collagen is cartilage composed of?
cards.a: type II

cards.q: what is bone marrow composed of?
cards.a: adipose tissue, vasculature, and the manufacturing site of blood vessels

cards.q: is the recovery time of tendons and ligaments due to the collagen that needs to be produced?
cards.a: no, it's due to the limited vasculature and circulation to those areas because they normally need little oxygen

cards.q: what is wolff's law?
cards.a: bone remodels according to the forces placed upon it

cards.q: assembling amino acids into structural proteins is an example of what mechanism?
cards.a: anabolism

cards.q: what is the difference between the USDA's mediterranean style eating pattern and the US style eating pattern?
cards.a: healthy mediterranean has more fruit and seafood but less dairy than US style

cards.q: what does the DASH eating plan emphasize?
cards.a: whole grains, poultry, fish, and nuts -- along with potassium, calcium, and magnesium; may need to gradually increase grains/fruit/veg though because more fiber can lead to bloating and diarrhea

cards.q: what is myplate's macro focus?
cards.a: low saturated fat, sodium, and added sugar intake

cards.q: what are food exchanges?
cards.a: used for meal planning purposes for people with diabetes and/or weight loss goals. divided into starches/breads, fruits, milk, vegetables, meat, and fat

cards.q: for how long does the body use carbohydrates as a source of energy during medium- and high- intensity exercise?
cards.a: up to 2 hours in duration

cards.q: about how many carbs can the body store?
cards.a: 15 grams per kg

cards.q: carbohydrate consumption recommendation for athletes?
cards.a: 6-10 grams per kg daily, depending on intensity and duration and frequency

cards.q: types of saturated fats?
cards.a: butyric, lauric, myristic, palmitic, and stearic acid

cards.q: fat recommendation?
cards.a: at least 15% of intake; as much as 30-40% can be ok, depending on health and age and needs. intake of 30% fat (10% saturated, 10% unsaturated, 10% monounsaturated) ensures adequate intake

cards.q: what is the crossover concept?
cards.a: at lower intensities, the body is primarily using fat as fuel but at higher intensities the contributon of ATP from carb metab. increases

cards.q: what is the duration effect?
cards.a: as duration increases, the more heavily the body relies on fat, although fitter athletes can use fat as fuel at higher intensities of exercise

cards.q: what are the electrolytes?
cards.a: sodium, potassium, chloride, iron, calcium, phosphorus, and magnesium

cards.q: functions of the electrolyte chloride?
cards.a: help fluid balance and nerve conductions

cards.q: functions of iron?
cards.a: helps transport/use oxygen

cards.q: functions of calcium?
cards.a: nerve conduction, muscle contraction, bone formation, vascular contraction and vascular dilation

cards.q: bodily functions of phosphorus?
cards.a: intramuscular oxidation

cards.q: what electrolytes primarily need to be replaced due to water loss?
cards.a: sodium, potassium, chloride, calcium and magnesium in that order

cards.q: an athlete should do what to keep triglycerides under 150mg per deciliter?
cards.a: limit refined sugary foods, replace saturated with unsaturated, increase fiber intake

cards.q: what is the upper limit for cholesterol for healthy levels?
cards.a: 200 mg per deciliter

cards.q: what population is at risk of calcium deficiency?
cards.a: postmenopausal women

cards.q: symptoms of calcium deficiency?
cards.a: muscle weakness, cramping, susceptibility to fractures

cards.q: how does iron help circulate oxygen?
cards.a: through hemoglobin, an iron-protein that increases oxygen transport 65x -- muscle myoglobin too

cards.q: how does anemia affect exercise performance?
cards.a: less iron = less oxygen to working tissues, leading to fatigue

cards.q: an athlete with brittle nails, sluggishness, headaches, pale skin, and dizziness likely has what deficiency?
cards.a: iron deficiency

cards.q: iron ratios for athletes and vegetarian athletes?
cards.a: athletes: 1.3-1.7x; veg athletes 1.8x

cards.q: RDA for iron?
cards.a: 18mg: women ages 19-50; 8mg: men over 18; 8mg: women over 51

cards.q: endurance athletes might need more iron why?
cards.a: foot-strike hemolysis, loss of hemoglobin in urine from strenuous training, and the small amount of iron lost in sweat

cards.q: nonheme sources of iron?
cards.a: oatmeal, lentils, dark green leafy vegetables, and fortified cereals

cards.q: what vitamin helps increase absorption of nonheme iron?
cards.a: vitamin C; increases it by 3x

cards.q: what percent water are men and women respectively?
side effects of dehydration?
cards.a: headaches, sluggishness, mood changes, loss of cognitive functioning, muscle cramping

cards.q: what kind of decrements occur at 2% and 3% body weight loss due to hydration?
cards.a: 2% -- decreased physical performance. 3% -- risk of heat illness. (less sweat to mitigate body temperature.)

cards.q: how much sweat can individuals can lose from exercise?
cards.a: 6-10% via sweating, depending on type and intensity

cards.q: fluids needed every 15-20 minutes for adequate hydration?
cards.a: 6-8oz

cards.q: macronutrient ratios when reducing body fat?
cards.a: 40-45% carbs, 30-35% protein, 25% fat

cards.q: cups of water per day for men and women?
cards.a: 13 cups for men (104oz) and 9 cups for women (72oz) -- 1 cup = 8oz

cards.q: how do athletes carb load?
cards.a: 1. deplete carb stores through reducing carb intake while maintaining volume and intensity about 5 days out from the event 2. increase carb intake (8-10 grams per kg) 3. taper training volume for several days just before the event

cards.q: recommendation of carbs before exercise?
cards.a: 8-10g per kg

cards.q: how many carbohydrates per hour during exercise?
cards.a: 30-60g per hour in 8-16oz every 15min

cards.q: what should an athlete consume during an activity who wants to support endurance and formation of glycogen after the activity?
cards.a: 3-4g of carbs per 1g of protein; carbs improve muscle glycogen, minimize muscle damage, and support strength efforts

cards.q: how long after exercise does ingestion of carb/protein help rebuild glycogen?
cards.a: within 30 minutes; ISSN recommends 8-10g per kg of carbs and 0.2g - 0.5g per kg of protein

cards.q: an athlete who skimps on carbs might have what side effects?
cards.a: no fuel for neurons or red blood cells, poor muscle contraction (state of positive energy balance is required to prevent muscle catabolism for energy)

cards.q: nine essential AAs?
cards.a: isoleucine, leucine, lysine, methionine, phenylalanine, threonine, tryptophan, valine, and histidine

cards.q: seven conditional AAs?
cards.a: arginine, cysteine, glutamine, proline, taurine, glycine, tyrosine

cards.q: five inessential AAs?
cards.a: alanine, asparagine, aspartic acid, glutamic acid, serine

cards.q: spelt, amaranth, and quinoa are what kind of food category?
cards.a: grains
