cards.q: tofu is what kind of food category for protein purposes?
cards.a: legume

cards.q: what is the difference between a seed, nut, legume, and drupe?
cards.a: Nuts have a hard outer shell that contains a dry fruit and one or two seeds; the shell does not separate when the fruit is ready to eat but must be practically pried off. Seeds are embryonic plants with a built in nutrient-rich seed coat; some seeds need their outer husk removed prior to eating and others do not -- f the outer husk is removed, it can usually be easily split by hand and removed. Drupes are fruits having a hard interior seed that may be discarded, as with rock fruit, or eaten, as with almonds and walnuts. Legumes have pods (shells, if you will) that contain multiple fruit, like pea pods or peanuts. (nuts are the hard-shelled "fruit" of certain plants; seeds are a small edible plant enclosed in a seed coat. most nuts are seeds, but not all seeds are nuts.)

cards.q: what caloric level marks risks of anorexia?
cards.a: 15% lower than would be healthy for age/sex

cards.q: other than calorie restriction, what marks anorexia?
cards.a: obsessive in attempts to adhere to rules

cards.q: night eating syndrome (recurring eating at night) is an example of what?
cards.a: other specified feeding/eating disorder (OSFED)

cards.q: what are the physical signs and symptoms other than weight loss that may be associated with anorexia nervosa?
cards.a: mineral/electrolyte imbalances, amenorrhea in females, decreased sex drive, fainting or dizziness, hypothermia, consistently feeling cold even in warm weather, bloating, constipation, food intolerances, fatigue, low energy level, changes in face (sunken eyes), development of fine hair on face/body

cards.q: side effects of bulimia?
cards.a: knuckle calluses, tooth decay, bad breath; chronic sore throat, bloating, constipation, food intolerances; amenorrhea, fainting/fizziness; tiredness

cards.q: health conditions associated with bulimia?
cards.a: dehydration, gastrointestinal reflux, heartburn, ulcers, slowed or irregular heart beat, electrolyte imbalances, heart failure

cards.q: less obvious conditions BED (binge eating) can lead to?
cards.a: kidney failure, osteoarthritis, stroke, gallbladder disease, irregular menstrual cycle, skin disorders, heart disease, some cancers

cards.q: what are the stages in the trans theoretical model of change?
cards.a: (1) precontemplation stage: athlete not thinking about making changes, do not see behavior as problematic, not ready for change. (2) contemplation stage: athlete recognizes problem, thinking about changing, usually getting ready for change (3) preparation stage: ready to make change, may actually begin small changes (4) action phase: making consistent apparent changes (5) maintenance: have made changes for sustained period, usually 6 months, working to prevent setbacks (6) termination: athlete has sustained maintenance for quite some time and has no desire to return to previous behavior

cards.q: what are the categories of ergogenic aids?
cards.a: nutritional, pharmacologic, physiologic, psychologic

cards.q: what percent of athletes have taken ergogenic aids?
cards.a: 76% and nearly all athletes engaged in strength building

cards.q: how to dose creatine?
cards.a: 0.3g per kg for at least 3 days; 3g to 5g per day to maintain stores. an additional 0.1g/kg added to protein may facilitate resistance training.

cards.q: function of HMB?
cards.a: prevention of proteolysis / protein breakdown

cards.q: function of carnisine and beta alanine?
cards.a: buffering agent in skeletal muscle; beta alanine increases carnosine content which helps improve performance in intense exercise by neutralizing acid production.

cards.q: dose of beta alanine?
cards.a: 3g to 6g for anaerobic athletes

cards.q: what is the allowed olympic dose of caffeine?
cards.a: up to 12 micrograms per ml of caffeine in urine; NCAA allows up to 15

cards.q: dosing of caffeine for performance enhancement?
cards.a: 3 to 6 milligrams of caffeine per kg of body weight

cards.q: what are the three categories of sports beverages?
cards.a: isotonic (sodium and sugar in physiologically similar levels), hypertonic (more sodium/sugar than the body), and hypotonic (less sodium/sugar than the body)

cards.q: what athletic demographics should not take sodium supplements?
cards.a: athletes with kidney disease or hypertension

cards.q: function of glutamine as an ergogenic?
cards.a: preventing illness/infection and reducing muscle soreness

cards.q: function of wazy maize as an ergogenic?
cards.a: high molecular weight carb that replenishes stores better than maltodextrin and dextrose. protein is also good with it.

cards.q: what is the carb amount and ingestion time athletes should take in sports drinks?
cards.a: 6-8% carbs, and 3oz-8oz every 10-20 minutes for activities \>90min

cards.q: why is the phosphagen system the initial source of energy generation?
cards.a: because of how long glycolysis and oxidative act -- glycolysis has ten steps and requires an investment of energy to drive early steps of pathway

cards.q: why can the glycolytic system produce more ATP than CP?
cards.a: because of the supply of glucose and glycogen

cards.q: what is a precondition for pyruvate going into mitochondria?
cards.a: oxygen has to be available, otherwise will be converted to lactate

cards.q: how much ATP yield does oxidative system produce vs substrate-level phosphorylation?
cards.a: oxidative: 90 percent, substrate level: 10 percent

cards.q: what is the gross energy production of a molecule of glucose?
cards.a: 40 ATP. this climbs to 463 ATP for one 18-carbon triglyceride molecule.

cards.q: during rest, how much ATP is produced by fat metabolism?
cards.a: approximately 70 percent; 30 percent comes from the breakdown of carbohydrates

cards.q: in high intensity, what is the energy contribution breakdown?
cards.a: nearly 100 percent comes from carbohydrates

cards.q: what does the law of mass action mean for bioenergetics?
cards.a: the reactions will continue until a lower intensity energy system can take over or until the exercise ends

cards.q: what is the work-to-rest ratio for phosphagen?
cards.a: 5-10 seconds; work to rest 1:12 to 1:20 (90-100 percent power)

cards.q: work-to-rest ratio for glycolytic pathway?
cards.a: 15-30 seconds, work to rest ratio 1:3 to 1:5 (75-90 percent power)

cards.q: work-to-rest ratio for combined glycolytic and oxidative?
cards.a: 1-3 minutes, 1:3 to 1:4, 30-75 percent of power

cards.q: work-to-rest ratio for oxidative system?
cards.a: greater than 3 min, work-to-rest ratio 1:1 to 1:3, 20-30 percent power

cards.q: other roles of growth hormone?
cards.a: decreasing glucose utilization and glycogen synthesis, increasing availability of glucose and amino acids, increasing collagen synthesis and cartilage growth, enhancing immune cell function

cards.q: principle role of cortisol?
cards.a: ensuring that energy is available. it increases the production of glucose in the liver and glycogen production in skeletal muscle.

cards.q: how to catecholamines affect muscle?
cards.a: increase blood flow from vasodilation, elevate BP, increase muscle contraction rate, increase energy availability, enhance metabolic enzyme activity, increase testosterone secretion rates

cards.q: 30 minutes, 1 hour, 3 hours -- which of these are how long anabolic hormones are elevated post-exercise?
cards.a: 30 minutes

cards.q: how does hemoglobin affect cell reactions / muscle buffering?
cards.a: regulates hydrogen ion concentration

cards.q: what are the biomechanics of heavy breathing?
cards.a: requires movement of the ribs to allow for expansion of the lungs, elevated by the external intercostals, sternocleidomastoids, anterior serrati, and scaleni

cards.q: when does exchange of respiratory gases occur?
cards.a: when oxygen diffuses from alveoli into pulmonary blood and carbon dioxide diffuses from blood into the alveoli

cards.q: risk of forceful muscle contraction?
cards.a: hernia

cards.q: for athletes with blood flow issues, how do muscular contractions greater than 20 percent affect blood flow?
cards.a: slows peripheral blood flow intra-set

cards.q: what is 1 MET?
cards.a: resting oxygen consumption = 3.5 ml/kg per minute = 1 metabolic equivalent

cards.q: physiological adaptations to aerobic training?
cards.a: increases in cardiovascular and muscular endurance, mitochondrial and capillary density, ventricular size and strength, metabolic stores of glycogen/ATP/triglycerides

cards.q: recovery time from FOR, NFOR, and overtraining?
cards.a: FOR: days to weeks NFOR: weeks to months OTS: months or longer (sometimes 6-12+ months)

cards.q: physiological changes from parasympathetic OTS?
cards.a: reduced glycogen availability, increased cortisol, greater sympathetic stress response, reduced levels of nocturnal and resting catecholamines

cards.q: an aerobic athlete wants to stop training or detrain. what kind of aerobic changes can they expect?
cards.a: 4-14% after 4 weeks of reduced training, 6-20% after more than 4 weeks (aerobic adaptations are most sensitive to inactivity)

cards.q: development v. maturation?
cards.a: development = progression that occurs from fetus to adult. maturation = process of the body becoming fully functional.

cards.q: gold method of biological age testing?
cards.a: x-rays or radiographs of the wrist or iliac crest to compare bone ossification to standard reference radiographs

cards.q: athletes with motive to achieve success like what kind of situation?
cards.a: 50/50 odds

cards.q: osteopenia is what BMD level?
cards.a: -1 to -2.5 standard deviations of BMD of young adults

cards.q: osteoporosis is what BMD level?
cards.a: 2.5 standard deviations below that of young adults

cards.q: sarcopenia?
cards.a: largely due to reduced physical activity -- it's loss of muscle mass and therefore strength and power.

cards.q: how can older clients offset risks, balance issues, and postural problems?
cards.a: (1) preactivation: increased muscle activity before contact with ground (2) cocontraction: muscle activity immediately following contact with the ground

cards.q: safety recommendations for training in older adults?
cards.a: same as usual; 5-10 min of warm up, stretching after exercise, allow 48-72hr between training

cards.q: how does estrogen affect body composition?
cards.a: increases fat deposition

cards.q: risk of ACL tears in female athletes?
cards.a: 6x greater than males

cards.q: amenorrhea threshold?
cards.a: 3 months no menstrual cycle

cards.q: how is systematic desensitization performed?
cards.a: verbalize situation that causes fear while using breathing and muscle relaxation techniques

cards.q: what are the three types of instruction?
cards.a: (1) explicit instruction: most information in prescriptive manner, often step by step (the exercise guidebook is this). (2) guided discovery: less information but provides holistic description of overall movement. (3) discovery: no instructions, but presents the overall goal of a movement.

cards.q: types of feedback?
cards.a: intrinsic feedback: provided by the body. augmented feedback: provided by external source, such as coach or technology.

cards.q: two types of augmented feedback?
cards.a: knowledge of results: how well the athlete did, knowledge of performance: how the athlete performed the task

cards.q: situation where an athlete would want to avoid part practice?
cards.a: archery or jump shot, where component movements are interrelated

cards.q: symptoms/characteristics of anxiety?
cards.a: characteristics: worry, nervousness, apprehension, fear. symptoms: increased heart rate, upset stomach

cards.q: an athlete predisposed to be anxious would be said to have what?
cards.a: trait anxiety

cards.q: why is reversal theory novel?
cards.a: (1) the athete's interpretation of arousal, not the amount felt, is important (2) the athlete has the ability to change negative interpretations of arousal

cards.q: what are the types of self confidence?
cards.a: performing physical skills, psychological skills, learning potential, and confidence in one's fitness/training

cards.q: what are the sources of self-efficacy?
cards.a: (1) past performance examples, (2) watching/modeling successful athletes, (3) encouragement from coaches/teammates/anything, (4) physiological arousal and emotional/mood states

title: ch3 - bioenergetics of exercise and training

cards.q: what is catabolism associated with?
cards.a: release of energy

cards.q: are exergonic reactions catabolic or anabolic or neither?
cards.a: catabolic

cards.q: what do endergonic reactions include?
cards.a: anabolic processes and the contraction of muscle

cards.q: through what intermediate molecule are exergonic and endergonic reactions derived?
cards.a: ATP

cards.q: what is atp composed of?
cards.a: adenosine and three phosphate groups

cards.q: adenosine is the combination of what chemicals?
cards.a: adenine (a nitrogen-containing base) and ribose (a five-carbon sugar)

cards.q: the breakdown of one molecule of ATP to yield energy is known as?
cards.a: hydrolysis, because it requires one molecule of water

cards.q: what is the hydrolysis of ATP catalyzed by?
cards.a: an enzyme called adenosine triphosphatase (ATPase)

cards.q: what is crossbridge recycling?
cards.a: the process that occurs after myosin ATPase catalyzes ATP hydrolysis

cards.q: what other enzymes catalyze ATP at other locations?
cards.a: calcium ATPase for pumping calcium into the sarcoplasmic reticulum, sodium-potassium ATPase for maintaining the sarcolemmal concentration gradient after depolarization

cards.q: what equation depicts the reactants (left), enzyme (middle), and products (right) of ATP hydrolysis
cards.a: ATP + H2O ADP + Pi + H+ + Energy

cards.q: hydrolysis of ADP does what?
cards.a: cleaves the second phosphate group and yields adenosine monophosphate

cards.q: how does ATP store energy?
cards.a: in the chemical bonds of the two terminal phosphate groups, which classifies it as a high-energy molecule

cards.q: where do ATP-producing processes occur?
cards.a: in the cell

cards.q: how does the glycolytic system depend on oxygen?
cards.a: it doesn’t, neither does the phosphagen system

cards.q: where do the glycolytic and phosphagenic systems occur?
cards.a: in the sarcoplasm of a muscle cell

cards.q: where do the oxidative and aerobic mechanisms occur in muscle cells?
cards.a: in mitochondria

cards.q: what do mitochondria require for aerobic mechanisms?
cards.a: oxygen as the terminal electron acceptor

cards.q: which of the three macronutrients can be metabolized for energy without oxygen?
cards.a: carbohydrate, which is critical during anaerobic metabolism

cards.q: which energy system is active during anaerobic exercise?
cards.a: all three energy systems are active at any given time, it’s an issue of contribution percentage (modulated by intensity and duration)

cards.q: what chemical process does the phosphagen system rely on?
cards.a: hydrolysis of ATP and breakdown of another high-energy phosphate molecule called creatine phosphate (CP), also called phosphocreatine (PCr)

cards.q: what enzyme catalyzes the synthesis of ATP from CP and ADP?
cards.a: phosphocreatine / creatine kinase

cards.q: what is the reaction for catalyzing the synthesis of ATP from CP and ADP?
cards.a: ADP + CP

cards.q: what does creatine phosphate do for the ADP–>ATP process
cards.a: supplies a phosphate group that combines with ADP to replenish ATP, a reaction that provides energy at a high rate

cards.q: what is the downside of the PCr reaction?
cards.a: because CP is stored in relatively small amounts, the phosphagen system cannot be the primary supplier of energy for continuous, long-duration activities

cards.q: how much ATP does the body store?
cards.a: approximately 80 to 100 g (about 3 ounces) of ATP at any given time, which does not represent a significant energy reserve for exercise

cards.q: what's the lowest ATP a body can have?
cards.a: not zero, because ATP stores cannot be completely depleted due to the necessity for basic cellular function

cards.q: how much ATP does the body store?
cards.a: 80 to 100 g (about 3 ounces) of ATP at any given time

cards.q: what are the implications of the amount of stored ATP?
cards.a: it does not represent a significant energy reserve for exercise, and ATP stores cannot be completely depleted due to the necessity for basic cellular function.

cards.q: When muscle fatigue causes ATP to be reduced by 50-60% of preexercise levels, how does phosphagen system fix this?
cards.a: by using the creatine kinase reaction to maintain the concentration of ATP; under normal circumstances, skeletal muscle concentrations of CP are four to six times higher than ATP

cards.q: which type of muscle fibers contain higher concentrations of CP?
cards.a: type II, therefore individuals with higher percentages of Type II fibers may be able to replenish ATP faster through the phosphagen system

cards.q: what is the adenylate kinase reaction?
cards.a: 2ADP ATP + AMP

cards.q: why is the adenylate kinase reaction important?
cards.a: because a product of the adenylate kinase (myokinase) reaction is AMP, and AMP is a powerful stimulant of glycolysis

cards.q: what are the reactions of the phosphagen system controlled by?
cards.a: the law of mass action / mass action effect

cards.q: what does the law of mass action / mass action effect control?
cards.a: the reactions of the phosphagen system

cards.q: what is a consequence of the phosphagen system having enzyme-mediated reactions?
cards.a: the rate of product formation is greatly influenced by the concentrations of the reactants

cards.q: as ATP is hydrolyzed to yield the energy necessary for exercise, there is a transient increase in what?
cards.a: ADP concentrations (as well as Pi/phosphorus) in the sarcolemma

cards.q: transient sarcolemma increases in ADP produces what effect?
cards.a: increases rate of the creatine kinase and adenylate kinase reaction to replenish the ATP supply

cards.q: for how long will the ATP hydrolysis to increase the rate of ADP concentrations in sarcolemma continue?
cards.a: the process will continue until (a) the exercise ceases or (b) the intensity is low enough that it does not deplete CP stores and it allows glycolysis or the oxidative system to become the primary supplier of ATP and rephosphorylate the free creatine

cards.q: after ATP hydrolysis ends and the exercise ceases or glycolysis/oxidative can become primary supplier of ATP (and rephosphorylate the free creatine), what occurs?
cards.a: the sarcoplasmic concentration of ATP will remain steady or increase, which will slow down or reverse the directions of the creatine kinase and adenylate kinase reactions. as a result, these reactions/equations are often referred to as near-equilibrium reactions that proceed in a direction dictated by the concentrations of the reactants due to the law of mass action

cards.q: why is the ATP resynthesis rate during glycolysis is not as rapid as with the single-step phosphagen system?
cards.a: because the process of glycolysis involves multiple enzymatically catalyzed reactions

cards.q: why is the capacity to produce ATP higher in the glycolytic system than in CP?
cards.a: due to a larger supply of glycogen and glucose compared to phosphagenic

cards.q: what is the end result of glycolysis?
cards.a: pyruvate

cards.q: what are the two ways pyruvate may proceed?
cards.a: 1. Pyruvate can be converted to lactate in the sarcoplasm. 2. Pyruvate can be shuttled into the mitochondria.

cards.q: how does ATP resynthesis occur at a faster rate when pyruvate is converted into lactate?
cards.a: via the rapid regeneration of NAD+

cards.q: what is a limitation of the ATP resynthesis (during pyruvate-->lactate) due to rapid regeneration of NAD+?
cards.a: limited in duration due to the subsequent H+ production and resulting decrease in cytosolic pH; this process is sometimes called anaerobic glycolysis (or fast glycolysis)

cards.q: what process is aerobic or slow glycolysis?
cards.a: when pyruvate is shuttled into the mitochondria to undergo the Krebs cycle, the ATP resynthesis rate is slower because of the numerous reactions, but can occur for a longer duration if the exercise intensity is low enough.

cards.q: At higher exercise intensities, what happens to pyruvate and NADH?
cards.a: they will increase above what can be handled by pyruvate dehydrogenase and will then be converted into lactate and NAD+

cards.q: why might the term aerobic/anaerobic glycolysis be inaccurate?
cards.a: because glycolysis itself does not depend on oxygen

cards.q: how do energy demands affect the use of pyruvate?
cards.a: the fate of pyruvate is ultimately controlled by the energy demands within the cell. if energy demand is high and must be transferred quickly, as during resistance training, pyruvate is primarily converted to lactate for further support of anaerobic glycolysis. if energy demand is not as high and oxygen is present in sufficient quantities in the cell, pyruvate can be further oxidized in the mitochondria.

cards.q: what catalyzes the formation of lactate from pyruvate?
cards.a: the enzyme lactate dehydrogenase

cards.q: what is a mistaken belief about the formation of lactate from pyruvate?
cards.a: that the end result is the formation of lactic acid.

cards.q: why is lactate, rather than lactic acid, the product of the lactate dehydrogenase reaction?
cards.a: due to the physiological pH (i.e., near 7) and earlier steps in glycolysis that consume protons

cards.q: what are the functions of proton (H+) accumulation during fatigue?
cards.a: reduces the intracellular pH, inhibits glycolytic reactions, and directly interferes with muscle's excitation-contraction coupling

cards.q: how might proton (H+ accumulation interfere with excitation-contraction coupling
cards.a: possibly by inhibiting calcium binding to troponin or by interfering with crossbridge recycling

cards.q: how does the decrease in pH affect cell energy systems?
cards.a: inhibits the enzymatic turnover rate of the cell's energy systems

cards.q: what is exercise-induced decrease in pH referred to?
cards.a: metabolic acidosis, and may be responsible for much of the peripheral fatigue that occurs during exercise, although the role of metabolic acidosis in peripheral fatigue has been questioned recently

cards.q: what other factors might play a role in peripheral fatigue?
cards.a: increased interstitial K+ concentration and Pi that impairs Ca++ release

cards.q: what other mechanisms might be responsible for H+ accumulation?
cards.a: the simple hydrolysis of ATP

cards.q: what alternate theory has been posed toward lactate?
cards.a: that lactate itself actually works to decrease metabolic acidosis rather than accelerate it

cards.q: how is lactate used as an energy substrate?
cards.a: in Type I and cardiac muscle fibers and in gluconeogenesis—the formation of glucose from noncarbohydrate sources—during extended exercise and recovery

cards.q: what is the resting concentration of lactate in blood and in muscle?
cards.a: normally there is a low concentration of lactate in blood and muscle. The reported normal range of lactate concentration in blood is 0.5 to 2.2 mmol/L at rest and 0.5 to 2.2 mmol for each kilogram of wet muscle (muscle that has not been desiccated).

cards.q: what factors affect lactate production?
cards.a: lactate production increases with exercise intensity and appears to depend on muscle fiber type. maximal rate of lactate production for Type II muscle fibers is 0.5 mmol•g−1•s−1 and for Type I muscle is 0.25 mmol•g−1•s−1 (so, type II = double type I)

cards.q: what might be the reason type II fibers produce so much more lactate than type I?
cards.a: a higher concentration or activity of glycolytic enzymes than in Type I muscle fibers

cards.q: what is the highest lactate accumulation, and at what point does severe fatigue occur?
cards.a: highest possible concentration of lactate accumulation is not known, and severe fatigue may occur at blood concentrations between 20 and 25 mmol/L; another showed blood lactate concentrations greater than 30 mmol/L following multiple bouts of dynamic exercise (so, between 20->30 mmol/L)

cards.q: what other factors affect lactate accumulation besides exercise intensity and fiber type?
cards.a: exercise duration, state of training, and initial glycogen levels

cards.q: what chemical state does blood lactate concentration reflect?
cards.a: the net balance of lactate production and clearance as a result of bicarbonate (HCO3−) buffering

cards.q: how does HCO3 − minimize the disruptive influence of H+ on ph?
cards.a: by accepting the proton (H2CO3)

cards.q: how do methods of oxidation involve lactate?
cards.a: lactate can be transported in the blood to other muscle fibers to be oxidized or it can be cleared by oxidation within the muscle fiber in which it was produced

cards.q: what is a hepatic method to clear lactate, what does it convert to, and what is this called?
cards.a: lactate can be transported in the blood to the liver, where it is converted to glucose. this process is referred to as the Cori cycle

cards.q: how long do blood lactate concentrations typically return to preexercise values?
cards.a: within an hour after activity, depending on the duration and intensity of exercise, training status, and type of recovery (i.e., passive versus active)

cards.q: what is the effect of light activity on lactate during the postexercise period?
cards.a: clears lactate faster; light activity during the postexercise period has been shown to increase lactate clearance rates. (for example, an active recovery following a 200-yard (182.9 m) maximal-effort swim resulted in the greatest lactate clearance in comparison to a passive recovery in competitive swimmers. in addition, both aerobically trained and anaerobically trained athletes have faster lactate clearance rates than untrained people.)

cards.q: when do peak blood concentrations occur?
cards.a: approximately 5 minutes after the cessation of exercise, a delay frequently attributed to the time required to buffer and transport lactate from the tissue to the blood

cards.q: given two scenarios: high intensity intermittent and low-intensity continuous, which would result in greater blood lactate accumulation?
cards.a: greater following high-intensity, intermittent exercise (e.g. resistance training, sprinting) than following lower-intensity, continuous exercise

cards.q: how would you infer that resistance training results in alterations of lactate response similar to those from aerobic training?
cards.a: trained people experience lower blood lactate concentrations than untrained people when exercising at an absolute workload (same resistance); these alterations include (1) lower blood lactate concentration at a given workload in trained individuals (2) higher blood lactate concentrations in trained individuals during maximal exercise

cards.q: what is the net reaction for glycolysis when pyruvate is converted to lactate?
cards.a: Glucose + 2Pi + 2ADP --> 2Lactate + 2ATP + H2O

cards.q: when would pyruvate not be converted into lactate?
cards.a: when oxygen is present in sufficient quantities in the mitochondria; pyrvuate is then transported there along with two molecules of reduced nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NADH) produced during glycolytic reactions (reduced refers to the added hydrogen)

cards.q: how does acetyl coenzyme A enter mitochondria?
cards.a: from pyruvate, which converts to acetyl CoA through the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex

cards.q: what is a consequence of the pyruvate --> acetyl CoA conversion?
cards.a: the loss of a carbon as CO2, and acetyl-CoA can then enter the Krebs cycle for further ATP resynthesis

cards.q: what happens after acetyl CoA enters the Krebs cycle?
cards.a: the NADH (nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide) molecules enter the electron transport system, where they can also be used to resynthesize ATP

cards.q: the net reaction for glycolysis when pyruvate is shuttled to the mitochondria may be summarized as what?
cards.a: Glucose + 2Pi + 2ADP + 2NAD+ --> 2Pyruvate + 2ATP + 2NADH + 2H2O

cards.q: what are the two primary mechanisms for resynthesizing ATP during metabolism?
cards.a: 1. Substrate-level phosphorylation 2. Oxidative phosphorylation

cards.q: what is phosphorylation?
cards.a: the process of adding an inorganic phosphate (Pi) to another molecule

cards.q: ADP + Pi --> ATP is what?
cards.a: the phosphorylation of ADP to ATP

cards.q: the resynthesis of ATP in the electron transport chain is also called what?
cards.a: oxidative phosphorylation

cards.q: substrate-level phosphorylation refers to what?
cards.a: direct resynthesis of ATP from ADP during a single reaction in the metabolic pathways.

cards.q: in glycolysis, what are the two steps that result in substrate-level phosphorylation of ADP to ATP?
cards.a: I. 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate + ADP + Pi phosphoglycerate kinase --> 3-phosphoglycerate + ATP II. Phosphoenolpyruvate + ADP + Pi + Pyruvate kinase---> Pyruvate + ATP

cards.q: what is the gross number of ATP molecules that are resynthesized as a result of substrate-level phosphorylation during glycolysis?
cards.a: four

cards.q: in glycolysis, the reaction that converts fructose-6-phosphate to fructose-1,6-bisphosphate is catalyzed by what?
cards.a: the enzyme phosphofructokinase [PFK]

cards.q: in glycolysis, what is required for the reaction that converts fructose-6-phosphate to fructose-1,6-bisphosphate to occur?
cards.a: the hydrolysis of one ATP molecule.

cards.q: in glycolysis, what are the two possible sources of glucose?
cards.a: blood glucose and muscle glycogen

cards.q: what are the requirements for when blood glucose enters the muscle cell?
cards.a: 1. it must be phosphorylated to remain in the cell and to maintain the glucose concentration gradient 2. the phosphorylation of one molecule of blood glucose, which is catalyzed by hexokinase, also requires the hydrolysis of one ATP

cards.q: how does glycogenolysis (breakdown of muscle glycogen) differ from blood glucose
cards.a: due to the help of the enzyme glycogen phosphorylase, the glucose is already phosphorylated, and it does not require the hydrolysis of ATP

cards.q: when glycolysis begins with one molecule of blood glucose, what is the net result?
cards.a: two ATP molecules are used and four ATP are resynthesized, which results in a net resynthesis of two ATP molecules

cards.q: what is the net resynthesis of ATP from muscle glycogen?
cards.a: only one ATP is used and four ATP are resynthesized, which yields a net resynthesis of three ATP molecules

cards.q: what is the function of stimulating the rate of glycolysis?
cards.a: the rate of glycolysis is stimulated to increase during intense muscle actions by high concentrations of ADP, Pi, and ammonia and by a slight decrease in pH and AMP, all of which are signs of increased ATP hydrolysis and a need for energy

cards.q: in contrast to the stimulation of glycolysis, how is glycolysis inhibited?
cards.a: glycolysis is inhibited by markedly lower pH, ATP, CP, citrate, and free fatty acids, which are usually present at rest (a slight decrease in pH increases glycolysis, but if pH continues to decrease significantly it will inhibit the rate of glycolysis)

cards.q: what more specific factors contribute to the regulation of glycolysis?
cards.a: the concentrations and turnover rates of three important glycolytic enzymes: hexokinase, PFK, and pyruvate kinase

cards.q: why are hexokinase, PFK, and pyruvate kinase regulatory enzymes in glycolysis?
cards.a: each has important allosteric (meaning "other site") binding sites

cards.q: when does allosteric regulation occur?
cards.a: when the end product of a reaction or series of reactions feeds back to regulate the turnover rate of key enzymes in the metabolic pathways. consequently, this process is also called end product regulation or feedback regulation

cards.q: when does allosteric inhibition occur?
cards.a: when an end product binds to the regulatory enzyme and decreases its turnover rate and slows product formation (in contrast, allosteric activation occurs when an "activator" binds with the enzyme and increases its turnover rate)

cards.q: how is glucose-6-phosphate phosphorylated?
cards.a: through catalyzation by hexokinase

cards.q: how is hexokinase allosterically inhibited?
cards.a: by the concentration of glucose-6-phosphate in the sarcoplasm

cards.q: what are the consequences of the higher concentration of glucose-6-phosphate?
cards.a: the higher the concentration of glucose-6-phosphate, the more hexokinase will be inhibited

cards.q: how does glucose move around a cell once it's been phosphorylated?
cards.a: it can't; the phosphorylation of glucose commits it to the cell so that it cannot leave

cards.q: what is the function of the PFK reaction (fructose-6-phosphate → fructose 1,6-bisphosphate)?
cards.a: commits the cell to metabolizing glucose rather than storing it as glycogen

cards.q: why is phosphofructokinase the most important regulator of glycolysis?
cards.a: because it is the rate-limiting step

cards.q: how does the activity of the glycolytic pathway decrease?
cards.a: through PFK activity

cards.q: how does PFK activity decrease the activity of the glycolytic pathway?
cards.a: reduces the conversion of fructose-6-phosphate to fructose 1,6-bisphosphate and, subsequently, decreases activity of the glycolytic pathway

cards.q: ATP is an allosteric inhibitor of what?
cards.a: phosphofructokinase

cards.q: how does PFK activity decrease?
cards.a: by elevated intracellular ATP concentrations

cards.q: what is the function of adenosine triphosphate as it relates to the PFK and the glycolytic pathway?
cards.a: Adenosine triphosphate is an allosteric inhibitor of PFK; therefore, as intracellular ATP concentrations rise, PFK activity decreases and reduces the conversion of fructose-6-phosphate to fructose 1,6-bisphosphate and, subsequently, decreases activity of the glycolytic pathway

cards.q: what is an allosteric activator of PFK?
cards.a: AMP, and it is also a powerful stimulator of glycolysis

cards.q: what is another way to stimulate phosphofructokinase aside from AMP?
cards.a: the ammonia produced during high-intensity exercise as a result of AMP or amino acid deamination (removing the amine group from the amino acid molecule) can also stimulate PFK

cards.q: what is the final regulatory enzyme in glycolysis?
cards.a: pyruvate

cards.q: how does the conversion of phosphoenolpyruvate to pyruvate (the final step) occur?
cards.a: through catalyzation by pyruvate kinase

cards.q: what is pyruvate kinase allosterically inhibited and activated by?
cards.a: allosterically inhibited by ATP and acetyl-CoA (the latter is a Krebs cycle intermediate), and allosterically activated by high concentrations of AMP and fructose-1,6bisphosphate

cards.q: what is the ventilatory threshold?
cards.a: the breaking point in the relationship between ventilation and VO2

cards.q: what does the lactate threshold represent and correspond with?
cards.a: a significantly increased reliance on anaerobic mechanisms for energy production to meet demand; the LT corresponds well with the ventilatory threshold (breaking point in the relationship between ventilation and VO2) and is often used as a marker of the anaerobic threshold.

cards.q: when does the lactate threshold typically begin?
cards.a: at 50% to 60% of maximal oxygen uptake in untrained individuals and at 70% to 80% in aerobically trained athletes

cards.q: what is the onset of blood lactate accumulation?
cards.a: a second increase in the rate of lactate accumulation at higher relative intensities of exercise.

cards.q: when does the OBLA occur?
cards.a: when the concentration of blood lactate reaches 4 mmol/L

cards.q: breaks in the lactate accumulation curve may correspond to what?
cards.a: points at which intermediate and large motor units are recruited during increasing exercise intensities (the muscle cells associated with large motor units are typically Type II fibers, which are particularly suited for anaerobic metabolism and lactate production)

cards.q: what would cause lactate accumulation to occur later at a higher exercise intensity?
cards.a: some studies suggest that training at intensities near or above the LT or OBLA pushes the LT and OBLA to the right

cards.q: why might training near LT or OBLA cause them to occur later?
cards.a: reduced catecholamine release at high exercise intensities and increased mitochondrial content that allows for greater production of ATP through aerobic mechanisms

cards.q: what might allow an athlete to perform at higher percentages of maximal oxygen uptake?
cards.a: shifting the LT or OBLA curves to the right

cards.q: what are the primary energy substrates of the oxidative system?
cards.a: primarily carbohydrate and fats as substrates

cards.q: when does use of protein occur by the oxidative system?
cards.a: during long-term starvation and long bouts (>90 minutes) of exercise

cards.q: what is the fat/carb ratio for ATP production at rest?
cards.a: at rest, approximately 70% of the ATP produced is derived from fats and 30% from carbohydrate

cards.q: how does substrate use shift as the intensity of exercise increases?
cards.a: there is a shift in substrate preference from fats to carbohydrate; during high-intensity aerobic exercise, almost 100% of the energy is derived from carbohydrate if an adequate supply is available, with only minimal contributions from fats and protein

cards.q: during prolonged, submaximal, steady-state work, how does energy substrate use shift?
cards.a: there is a gradual shift from carbohydrate back to fats, and to a very small extent protein

cards.q: NADH stands for what?
cards.a: nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide + hydrogen

cards.q: FADH2 stands for what?
cards.a: flavin adenine dinucleotide

cards.q: substrate-level phosphorylation is in contrast to what other kind?
cards.a: oxidative phosphorylation

cards.q: when does oxidative metabolism of blood glucose and muscle glycogen begin?
cards.a: with glycolysis.

cards.q: when would pyruvate not be converted to lactate but transported to mitochondria?
cards.a: if oxygen is present in sufficient quantities; it is converted into acetyl CoA then

cards.q: the citric acid cycle is also known as what?
cards.a: tricarboxylic acid cycle and the Krebs cycle

cards.q: what continues the oxidation of the substrate from glycolysis, and produces two ATP indirectly from guanine triphosphate (GTP)?
cards.a: the Krebs cycle / citric acid cycle, it does this via substrate-level phosphorylation for each molecule of glucose

cards.q: before one molecule of glucose is produced, what is produced from two pyruvate molecules?
cards.a: six molecules of NADH and two molecules of reduced flavin adenine dinucleotide (FADH2)

cards.q: what is the function of hydrogen atoms in FADH2 and NADH?
cards.a: these molecules transport hydrogen atoms to the ETC to be used to produce ATP from ADP

cards.q: what is the ETC's function of NADH and FADH2?
cards.a: the ETC uses the NADH and FADH2 molecules to rephosphorylate ADP to ATP

cards.q: how is a proton concentration gradient formed through hydrogen atoms?
cards.a: the hydrogen atoms from NADH and FADH are passed down a series of electron carriers known as cytochromes to form a proton concentration gradient; cytochromes are proteins with heme bonded to them

cards.q: what does the proton concentration gradient do?
cards.a: provides the energy for ATP production, with oxygen serving as the final electron acceptor (resulting in the formation of water)

cards.q: why would NADH and flavin adenine dinucleotide differ in their ability to produce ATP?
cards.a: because they enter the ETC at different sites

cards.q: what is the ATP produced by one molecule of NADH and one molecule of FADH2?
cards.a: one molecule of NADH can produce three molecules of ATP; one molecule of FADH2 can produce two molecules of ATP

cards.q: oxidative phosphorylation?
cards.a: the process in which ATP is formed as a result of the transfer of electrons from NADH or FADH2 to O2 by a series of electron carriers

cards.q: the oxidative system begins with what?
cards.a: glycolysis, and includes the Krebs cycle and ETC

cards.q: the oxidative system gets how much ATP from one molecule of blood glucose?
cards.a: approximately 38 ATP

cards.q: if the initiation of glycolysis by the oxidative system is in muscle glycogen, what is the net ATP production and why?
cards.a: 39, since the hexokinase reaction is not necessary with muscle glycogenolysis

cards.q: how much ATP synthesis does oxidative phosphorylation account for compared to substrate level?
cards.a: over 90% of ATP synthesis compared to substrate-level phosphorylation

cards.q: how are fats used by the oxidative system?
cards.a: triglycerides stored in fat cells can be broken down by an enzyme, hormone-sensitive lipase, to produce free fatty acids and glycerol

cards.q: breaking down triglycerides to produce free fatty acids and glycerol does what?
cards.a: releases a portion of the total free fatty acids from the fat cells into the blood, where they can circulate and enter muscle fibers and undergo oxidation

cards.q: how would fat cells undergo oxidation?
cards.a: by entering muscle fibers and circulating, which happens when the breakdown of triglycerides and glycerol releases a portion of the total free fatty acids from the fat cells into the blood

cards.q: how are intramuscular sources of free fatty acids produced?
cards.a: by storing limited quantities of triglycerides in the muscle along with a form of hormone-sensitive lipase

cards.q: what happens when free fatty acids enter the mitochondria?
cards.a: they undergo beta oxidation, a series of reactions in which the free fatty acids are broken down, resulting in the formation of acetyl-CoA and hydrogen protons

cards.q: what happens when acetyl CoA and hydrogen protons are formed from the breakdown of free fatty acids?
cards.a: the acetyl-CoA enters the Krebs cycle directly, and the hydrogen atoms are carried by NADH and FADH2 to the electron transport chain

cards.q: what is the result of beta oxidation carrying NADH and FADH to the electron transport chain
cards.a: hundreds of ATP molecules

cards.q: how can 300 ATP molecules be yielded by the oxidative system
cards.a: breakdown of a single triglyceride molecule containing three 16-carbon chain free fatty acids (palmitic acid) can be metabolized by beta oxidation to yield over 300 ATP molecules (>100 ATP per palmitic acid)

cards.q: what is the oxidative potential of fats, proteins, and carbs?
cards.a: proteins < carbs < fats, in this order (and fats are *way* higher)

cards.q: what is protein oxidation?
cards.a: the oxidative system's breakdown of protein to its constituent amino acids by various metabolic processes

cards.q: after protein is broken down into its constituent aminos by the oxidative system, how is it utilized?
cards.a: converted into glucose (gluconeogenesis), pyruvate, or various Krebs cycle intermediates to produce ATP

cards.q: is gluconeogenesis the production of glucose from protein?
cards.a: not quite; gluconeogenesis is the metabolic process by which organisms produce glucose for catabolic reactions from non-carbohydrate precursors

cards.q: what percentage of ATP do amino acids produce in short-term and long-term exercise?
cards.a: minimal during short-term exercise but 3% to 18% of energy requirements during prolonged activity

cards.q: what are the major amino acids that are oxidized in skeletal muscle?
cards.a: primarily leucine, isoleucine, and valine (BCAAs); alanine, aspartate, and glutamate may also be used

cards.q: how are nitrogenous waste products of amino acid degradation eliminated?
cards.a: through the formation of urea and small amounts of ammonia

cards.q: why is the elimination of nitrogenous waste products through ammonia significant?
cards.a: because ammonia is toxic and is associated with fatigue

cards.q: the rate-limiting step in the Krebs cycle is what?
cards.a: the conversion of isocitrate to a-ketoglutarate, a reaction catalyzed by the enzyme isocitrate dehydrogenase

cards.q: isocitrate dehydrogenase is stimulated and inhibited by what?
cards.a: stimulated by ADP and allosterically inhibited by ATP

cards.q: the reactions that produce NADH or FADH2 also influence what?
cards.a: the regulation of the Krebs cycle

cards.q: if NAD+ and FAD2+ are not available in sufficient quantities to accept hydrogen, what occurs?
cards.a: the rate of the Krebs cycle is reduced

cards.q: when GTP accumulates, what occurs?
cards.a: the concentration of succinyl CoA increases, which inhibits the initial reaction (oxaloacetate + acetyl-CoA → citrate + CoA) of the Krebs cycle

cards.q: what is the initial reaction of the Krebs cycle?
cards.a: oxaloacetate + acetyl-CoA → citrate + CoA

cards.q: the electron transport chain is inhibited and stimulated by what?
cards.a: inhibited by ATP and stimulated by ADP

cards.q: how is exercise intensity defined?
cards.a: a level of muscular activity that can be quantified in terms of power (work performed per unit of time) output

cards.q: what do short high intensity activities rely on?
cards.a: fast glycolysis and phosphagen energy system

cards.q: what do low intensity activities rely on?
cards.a: slow glycolysis and the oxidative energy system

cards.q: what is the range of time for athletic activities?
cards.a: 1 to 3 seconds (e.g., snatch and shot put) to more than 4 hours (long-distance triathlons and ultramarathons)

cards.q: does intensity matter more for energy system contribution, or does duration?
cards.a: the degree to which anaerobic and oxidative systems contribute to the energy being produced is determined primarily by the exercise intensity and secondarily by exercise duration

cards.q: what are energy substrates?
cards.a: molecules that provide starting materials for bioenergetic reactions

cards.q: what are the energy substrates?
cards.a: phosphagens (ATP and CP), glucose, glycogen, lactate, free fatty acids, and amino acids

cards.q: fatigue is associated with depletion of what energy substrates?
cards.a: phosphagens and glycogen; depletion of substrates such as free fatty acids, lactate, and amino acids typically does not occur to the extent that performance is limited

cards.q: creatine phosphate can decrease how much during the first stage of high-intensity exercise of short and moderate duration (5-30 seconds)?
cards.a: 50-70%, and almost completely depleted as a result of very intense exercise to exhaustion

cards.q: during experimentally induced fatigue, how might concentrations of ATP decrease from preexercise levels?
cards.a: might only slightly or might up to 50% to 60%

cards.q: how is intramuscular ATP concentration sustained during exercise?
cards.a: as a consequence of CP depletion and the contribution of additional ATP from the myokinase reaction and oxidation of other energy sources, such as glycogen and free fatty acids

cards.q: when does postexercise phosphagen repletion occur and how?
cards.a: in a relatively short period; largely as a result of aerobic metabolism, although glycolysis can contribute to recovery after high-intensity exercise

cards.q: complete postexercise resynthesis of ATP and CP occur when?
cards.a: ATP: within 3 to 5 minutes, CP: within 8 minutes

cards.q: how might aerobic endurance training affect resting concentrations of phosphagens?
cards.a: may increase resting concentrations of phosphagens and decrease their rate of depletion at a given absolute submaximal power output but not at a relative (percentage of maximum) submaximal power output.

cards.q: how have short-term studies of sprint and six months of resistance or explosive training affected resting phosphagens?
cards.a: have not shown alterations in resting concentrations of phosphagens, but total phosphagen content can be larger following sprint training due to increases in muscle mass, and resistance training has been shown to increase the resting concentrations of phosphagens in the triceps brachii after five weeks of training

cards.q: why might resting phosphagens increase in some resistance training studies but not others?
cards.a: due to selective hypertrophy of Type II fibers, which can contain a higher phosphagen concentration than Type I fibers

cards.q: how much glycogen is stored in the liver and muscle respectively?
cards.a: 70-100g in liver and 300-400g in muscle

cards.q: can training and dietary manipulations influence resting glycogen?
cards.a: yes, anaerobic training (including sprinting and resistance training) and stereotypical aerobic endurance training can increase resting muscle glycogen concentration with concomitantly appropriate nutrition.

cards.q: during high intensity exercise, which source of glycogen (liver or muscle) is used more?
cards.a: muscle, and the rate of glycogen depletion is related to exercise intensity

cards.q: when would liver glycogen be more important?
cards.a: during low-intensity exercise, and its contribution to metabolic processes increases with duration of exercise

cards.q: how does exercise intensity affect glycogenolysis (the breakdown of glycogen) at 50%, 75%, and 100% of maximal oxygen uptake?
cards.a: 0.7, 1.4, and 3.4 mmol * kg^-1 * min^-1, respectively

cards.q: when does glycogen become an increasingly important energy substrate?
cards.a: at relative intensities of exercise above 60% of maximal oxygen uptake; the entire glycogen content of some muscle cells can become depleted during exercise

cards.q: at what intensity are relatively constant glucose concentrations maintained and why?
cards.a: below 50% of maximal O2 uptake, as a result of low muscle glucose uptake

cards.q: when do blood glucose concentrations below 50% maximal O2 fall?
cards.a: as duration >90min, but rarely below 2.8mmol/L; when duration >90, liver glycogen depletion may result in substantially decreased blood glucose

cards.q: when might exercise-induced hypoglycemia occur?
cards.a: when blood glucose <2.5 mmol/L

cards.q: what does impact does blood glucose around 2.5 to 3.0 mmol/L have on carbohydrates?
cards.a: reduced liver carbohydrate stores and causes decreased carbohydrate oxidation and eventual exhaustion

cards.q: how much glycogen depletion does high intensity intermittent exercise cause?
cards.a: 20% to 60% with relatively few sets

cards.q: phosphagen is primarily the limiting factor in exercise with high resistance and few sets, but when is glycogen the limiting factor?
cards.a: resistance training with many total sets and larger total amounts of work

cards.q: how might glycogen limit performance despite not being there?
cards.a: selective muscle fiber glycogen depletion (more depletion in Type II fibers), which can also limit performance

cards.q: how are intensity and glycogenolysis related?
cards.a: generally the greater the intensity the faster the rate of glycogenolysis, BUT it appears that when the total work performed is equal the absolute amount of glycogen depletion is the same regardless of the intensity

cards.q: repletion of muscle glycogen during recovery is accomplished how?
cards.a: postexercise carbohydrate ingestion; repletion appears to be optimal if 0.7 to 3.0 g of carbohydrate per kilogram of body weight is ingested every 2 hours following exercise

cards.q: ingesting 0.7 to 3.0 g of carbohydrate per kilogram of body weight will replenish muscle glycogen when and at what rate?
cards.a: at 5 to 6 mmol/g of wet muscle mass per hour during the first 4 to 6 hours following exercise; muscle glycogen may be completely replenished within 24 hours, provided that sufficient carbohydrate is ingested

cards.q: what factors would make glycogen take longer to replenish?
cards.a: if the exercise has a high eccentric component (associated with exercise-induced muscle damage); more time may be required to completely replenish

cards.q: what bioenergetic factors may be limiting factors?
cards.a: for many activities glycogen; for primarily anaerobic activities, the effect of metabolic acidosis on limiting contractile force; increased intracellular inorganic phosphate, ammonia accumulation, increased ADP, and impaired calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum

cards.q: the ability of working tissues to use oxygen is called what?
cards.a: oxygen uptake

cards.q: how does oxygen uptake increase during low-intensity exercise with a constant power output?
cards.a: oxygen uptake increases for the first few minutes until a steady state of uptake (oxygen demand equals oxygen consumption) is reached

cards.q: what is oxygen deficit?
cards.a: at the start of an exercise bout, some of the energy must be supplied through anaerobic mechanisms because the aerobic system responds slowly to the initial increase in the demand for energy; this anaerobic contribution to the total energy cost of exercise is the oxygen deficit

cards.q: what terms exist for postexercise oxygen uptake?
cards.a: oxygen debt, recovery O2, and xcess postexercise oxygen consumption (EPOC). EPOC is the oxygen uptake above resting values used to restore the body to the preexercise condition.

cards.q: what is the relationship between oxygen deficit and EPOC?
cards.a: the oxygen deficit may influence the size of the EPOC, but the two are not equal

cards.q: when do aerobic mechanisms provide much of the energy for work?
cards.a: if the exercise intensity is above the maximal oxygen uptake that a person can attain

cards.q: if aerobic mechanisms are active, what can you infer about exercise duration?
cards.a: it will decrease

cards.q: what kind of sport requires maximal sustained effort to exhaustion or near-exhaustion?
cards.a: competitive middle-distance sprints (400 m to 1,600 m)

cards.q: what is the metabolic profile of most sports?
cards.a: very similar to those of a series of high-intensity, constantor near-constant-effort exercise bouts interspersed with rest periods, such as American football, basketball, and hockey. In this type of exercise, the required exercise intensity (power output) that must be met during each exercise bout is much greater than the maximal power output that can be sustained using aerobic energy sources alone

cards.q: what kind of benefit would aerobic power provide athletes in most sports?
cards.a: increasing aerobic power through primarily aerobic endurance training -- while simultaneously compromising or neglecting anaerobic power and anaerobic capacity -- is of little benefit to athletes in these sports (it would be of little benefit for a baseball player to run miles during training rather than focusing on exercises that improve anaerobic power and capacity)

cards.q: how does interval training work?
cards.a: emphasizes bioenergetic adaptations for a more efficient energy transfer within the metabolic pathways by using predetermined intervals of exercise and rest periods (i.e., work-to-rest ratios)

cards.q: what are the nine HIIT variables that can be manipulated to achieve the most precise metabolic specificity?
cards.a: 1. intensity of the active portion of each duty cycle, 2. duration of the active portion of each duty cycle, 3. intensity of the recovery portion of each duty cycle, 4. duration of the recovery portion of each duty cycle, 5. number of duty cycles performed in each set, 6. number of sets, 7. rest time between sets, 8. recovery intensity between sets, and 9. mode of exercise for HIIT.

cards.q: what factors should a S&C professional consider when designing a HIIT program?
cards.a: aerobic/anaerobic durations and intensities, desired training adaptations are periodization, number of exercise sessions per day and week, how to juggle HIIT sessions in conjunction with other training sessions (e.g. team practice)

cards.q: how would properly spaced work-to-rest intervals allow more work to be accomplished at higher exercise intensities with the same or
cards.a: less fatigue than during continuous training at the same relative intensity? in one study, 2:1, 1:1, and 1:2 work-to-rest ratios were used with the same running intensity for a total duration of 30 minutes, however, the subjects were able to complete 4.14 miles (6.66 km), 3.11 miles (5.00 km), and 2.07 miles (3.33 km), respectively, all while working aerobic capacity in a manner similar to that in the continuous running condition

cards.q: six sessions of four to seven 30-second maximum cycling efforts interspaced with 4 minutes of recovery is what work-to-rest ratio?
what improvements would interval training bring?
cards.a: muscle oxidative potential, muscle buffering capacity, muscle glycogen content, and time-trial performance, as well as doubled aerobic endurance capacity

cards.q: what's the summary of guidelines for work-to-rest ratios?
cards.a: few studies provide definitive guidelines; information of ratios between 40s:20s, 30s:30s, and 30s:20s is mixed. outcomes include total work, time to exhaustion, metabolic values (VO2Max/Lactate concentration).

cards.q: what variables are considered when determining proper work to rest ratio?
cards.a: knowledge of the time intervals, intensity of work, and recovery periods for each of the energy systems (e.g. complete resynthesis of CP may take up to 8 minutes, which suggests that short-duration, high-intensity exercise requires greater work-to-rest ratios due to the aerobic mechanisms that replete phosphagen stores)

cards.q: what are the most important HIIT factors to consider?
cards.a: the intensities and durations of the active and recovery portions of each duty cycle

cards.q: how should HIIT sessions be optimized?
cards.a: they should maximize the time spent at or near VO2max; specifically, the cumulative duration and intensity of the active portions of the duty cycles should equate to several minutes above 90% of VO2max

cards.q: what are the beneficial adaptations of HIIT?
cards.a: oxidative muscle fiber adaptation and myocardial hypertrophy. also increases in VO2max, proton buffering, glycogen content, anaerobic thresholds, time to exhaustion, and time-trial performance.

cards.q: what is an example of HIIT's comparable results?
cards.a: one study reported equivalent improvements in muscle buffering capacity and glycogen content for HIIT at 250% of VO2peak during four to six 30-second cycling sprints compared to continuous cycling for 90 to 120 minutes at 65% of VO2peak over six total training sessions. 750 kJ cycling time trials decreased in both groups by 10.1% and 7.5% in the HIIT and long, slow endurance training groups, respectively. Thus, HIIT provided performance and physiological adaptations equivalent to those of long, slow endurance training, but in a time-efficient manner.

cards.q: what is the pro/con of cross training / combination training?
cards.a: relationships in power recovery in the first 10 seconds of a cycling sprint, the resynthesis of PCr, and endurance fitness (VO2max); however, aerobic endurance training may reduce anaerobic performance capabilities, anaerobic energy production capabilities, and hypertrophy/strength gains (studies are mixed on all of this)

cards.q: what are the mechanisms by which combination training might inhibit gains?
cards.a: may increase training volume to a level that may result in overtraining in comparison to aerobic and anaerobic training alone; also might be by (a) decreasing rapid voluntary activation, (b) chronically lower muscle glycogen levels that can limit intracellular signaling responses during resistance training, and (c) and fiber type transition to slow-twitch fibers

title: ch1 - structure and functions of body system

cards.q: approximately how many bones are in the body?
what does the axial skeleton consist of?
cards.a: skull (cranium), vertebral column (vertebra C1 through the coccyx), ribs, and sternum

cards.q: what does the appendicular skeleton include?
cards.a: the shoulder (or pectoral) girdle (left and right scapula and clavicle); bones of the arms, wrists, and hands (left and right humerus, radius, ulna, carpals, metacarpals, and phalanges); the pelvic girdle (left and right coxal or innominate bones); and the bones of the legs, ankles, and feet (left and right femur, patella, tibia, fibula, tarsals, metatarsals, and phalanges)

cards.q: what are fibrous joints and what kind of movement do they allow?
cards.a: fibrous joints are e.g. sutures of the skull; they allow virtually no movement

cards.q: what kind of joints are cartilaginous joints and what kind of movement do they allow?
cards.a: cartilaginous joints are e.g. intervertebral disks and allow limited movement

cards.q: what kind of joints are synovial joints and what kind of movement do they allow?
cards.a: synovial joints are e.g. elbow and knee and they allow considerable movement

cards.q: in terms of joints, what is the order of least to most movement allowed?
cards.a: fibrous joints

cards.q: smooth hyaline cartilage covers what?
cards.a: articulating bone ends

cards.q: how does hyaline cartilage differ from other kinds of cartilage?
cards.a: enclosed in a capsule filled with synovial fluid

cards.q: how do uniaxial joints operate?
cards.a: joints such as the elbow operate as hinges, essentially rotating about only one axis

cards.q: joints such as the elbow are what kind of joint?
cards.a: uniaxial

cards.q: how is the knee improperly referred to?
cards.a: often referred to as a hinge joint, but its axis of rotation actually changes throughout the joint range of motion

cards.q: ankle and wrists are what kind of joints?
cards.a: biaxial joints

cards.q: what range of movements do biaxial joints (such as the ankle and wrist) allow?
cards.a: movement about two perpendicular axes

cards.q: shoulder and hip ball-and-socket are what kind of joints?
cards.a: multiaxial joints

cards.q: what kind of movement do multiaxial joints allow?
cards.a: movement about all three perpendicular axes that define space

cards.q: how are vertebrae grouped?
cards.a: into 7 cervical vertebrae in the neck region; 12 thoracic vertebrae in the middle to upper back; 5 lumbar vertebrae, which make up the lower back; 5 sacral vertebrae, which are fused together and make up the rear part of the pelvis; and 3 to 5 coccygeal vertebrae, which form a kind of vestigial internal tail extending downward from the pelvis.

cards.q: what does epimysium cover?
cards.a: the body’s more than 430 skeletal muscles

cards.q: what is the relationship of epimysium with tendons?
cards.a: epimysium is contiguous with the tendons

cards.q: what are tendons attached to?
cards.a: tendon is attached to bone periosteum, a specialized connective tissue covering all bones

cards.q: what is the diameter of muscle cells?
cards.a: about 50 to 100 µm in diameter (about the diameter of a human hair)

cards.q: how many fibers are in a fasciculi?
cards.a: fasciculi may consist of up to 150 fibers

cards.q: is endomyseum contiguous with skeletal muscle?
cards.a: not quite, it is contiguous with the fiber’s membrane, or sarcolemma

cards.q: what contiguity do the connective tissues (endo/peri/epi mysium) have in common?
cards.a: they are all contiguous with the tendon, therefore tension developed in a muscle cell is transmitted to the tendon and the bone to which it is attached

cards.q: what does the light I-band correspond with?
cards.a: the areas in two adjacent sarcomeres that contain only actin filaments

cards.q: where is the z-line located and what does it run through?
cards.a: in the middle of the I-band running longitudinally through the I-band

cards.q: where is the h-zone located?
cards.a: in the center of the sarcomere

cards.q: what is the composition of the h-zone?
cards.a: only myosin filaments

cards.q: how does the h-zone work during muscle contractions?
cards.a: the h-zone decreases as the actin slides over the myosin toward the center of the sarcomere

cards.q: what does the i-band do during contractions?
cards.a: the I-band also decreases as the Z-lines are pulled toward the center of the sarcomere

cards.q: where are the tubules sarcoplasmic reticulum located?
cards.a: parallel to and surrounding each myofibril, and terminates as vesicles in the vicinity of the Z-lines

cards.q: what is stored in the vesicles of the sarcoplasmic reticulum?
cards.a: calcium ions; regulation of calcium controls muscular contraction

cards.q: where are transverse tubules in relation to the sarcoplasmic reticulum?
cards.a: perpendicular to the sarcoplasmic reticulum and terminate in the vicinity of the Z-line between two vesicles

cards.q: why do action potentials arrive near-simultaneously from the surface to the depths of the muscle fiber?
cards.a: because the T-tubules run between outlying myofibrils and are contiguous with the sarcolemma at the surface of the cell (when this happens calcium is released throughout the muscle and produces a coordinated contraction)

cards.q: how do the actin filaments slide at each end?
cards.a: inward on myosin filaments, pulling the Z-lines toward the center of the sarcomere and thus shortening the muscle fiber

cards.q: what happens when actin filaments slide over myosin filaments?
cards.a: both the H-zone and I-band shrink

cards.q: why must rapid, repeated flexions must occur in many crossbridges throughout the entire muscle for measurable movement to occur?
cards.a: because only a very small displacement of the actin filament occurs with each flexion of the myosin crossbridge

cards.q: how much calcium is present in the myofibril at rest?
cards.a: little calcium is present in the myofibril at rest, most of it is stored in the sarcoplasmic reticulum, therefore few of the myosin crossbridges are bound to actin (becomes strong when the actin binding site is exposed after release of the stored calcium)

cards.q: in the excitation-contraction coupling phase, what must happen before myosin crossbridges can flex?
cards.a: they must first attach to the actin filament

cards.q: how does troponin affect the sarcoplasmic reticulum?
cards.a: when the sarcoplasmic reticulum is stimulated to release calcium ions, the calcium binds with troponin, a protein that is situated at regular intervals along the actin filament and has a high affinity for calcium ions

cards.q: where is tropomyosin?
cards.a: runs along the length of the actin filament in the groove of the double helix

cards.q: what occurs when calcium binds with troponin?
cards.a: myosin crossbridge now attaches much more rapidly to the actin filament, allowing force to be produced as the actin filaments are pulled toward the center of the sarcomere

cards.q: what is the amount of force produced by a muscle at any instant contingent on?
cards.a: the number of myosin crossbridges bound to actin filaments cross-sectionally at that instant in time (to reiterate: the number of crossbridges that are formed between actin and myosin at any instant in time dictates the force production of a muscle.)

cards.q: in the contraction phase of the excitation-contraction coupling phase, where does the energy for the power stroke come from?
cards.a: from hydrolysis (breakdown) of adenosine triphosphate (ATP) to adenosine diphosphate (ADP) and phosphate, a reaction catalyzed by the enzyme myosin adenosine triphosphatase (ATPase)

cards.q: what must occur for the head to detach from the active actin site and return to its original position?
cards.a: another molecule of ATP must replace the ADP on the myosin crossbridge globular head; this allows the contraction process to continue (if calcium is available to bind to troponin) or relaxation to occur (if calcium is not available)

cards.q: what other events in skeletal muscle besides contraction does calcium regulate?
cards.a: glycolytic and oxidative energy metabolism, as well as protein synthesis and degradation

cards.q: in the recharge phase, how does muscle shortening occur?
cards.a: only when this sequence of events—binding of calcium to troponin, coupling of the myosin crossbridge with actin, power stroke, dissociation of actin and myosin, and resetting of the myosin head position—is repeated over and over again throughout the muscle fiber muscle

cards.q: shortening can occur as long as what conditions are satisfied?
cards.a: as long as calcium is available in the myofibril, ATP is available to assist in uncoupling the myosin from the actin, and sufficient active myosin ATPase is available for catalyzing the breakdown of ATP.

cards.q: when does the relaxation phase occur?
cards.a: when the stimulation of the motor nerve stops

cards.q: what occurs chemically during the relaxation phase?
cards.a: calcium is pumped back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum, which prevents the link between the actin and myosin filaments. relaxation is brought about by the return of the actin and myosin filaments to their unbound state.

cards.q: what is the origin of the "twitch" in fast/slow twitch muscle fibers?
cards.a: relaxation time

cards.q: chemically, how are fast/slow twitch determined?
cards.a: histochemical staining for myosin ATPase content; another more specific method is to quantify the amount of myosin heavy chain (MHC) protein; the nomenclature for this is similar to that with the myosin ATPase methodology

cards.q: what makes type I/II fibers able to act that way?
cards.a: difference in the ability of the fibers to demand and supply energy for contraction and thus to withstand fatigue

cards.q: why do type I fibers have low force production?
cards.a: low myosin ATPase activity; reverse for type II

cards.q: how do type IIa and type IIx fibers differ?
cards.a: mainly in their capacity for aerobic-oxidative energy supply; type IIa fibers have greater capacity for aerobic metabolism and more capillaries surrounding them than Type IIx and therefore show greater resistance to fatigue

cards.q: how can muscular force be graded?
cards.a: (1) through variation in the frequency at which motor units are activated, if a motor unit is activated once, the twitch that arises does not produce a great deal of force. (however, if the frequency of activation is increased so that the forces of the twitches begin to overlap or summate, the resulting force developed by the motor unit is much greater. This method of varying force output is especially important in small muscles, such as those of the hand.) (2) an increase in force through varying the number of motor units activated, a process known as recruitment. in large muscles, such as those in the thigh, motor units are activated at near-tetanic frequency when called on.

cards.q: can fast twitch fibers be used for slow twitch purposes?
cards.a: if additional force is needed, as in a sprint at the end of a race, the fast-twitch motor units are called into play to increase the pace; unfortunately, exercise at such intensity cannot be maintained very long

cards.q: where are proprioceptors located?
cards.a: within joints, muscles, and tendons

cards.q: what does the sensitivity to pressure and tension do?
cards.a: relay information concerning muscle dynamics to the conscious and subconscious parts of the CNS

cards.q: what is the kinesthetic sense?
cards.a: conscious appreciation of the position of body parts with respect to gravity

cards.q: is proprioception more conscious or unconscious?
cards.a: unconscious so we do not have to dedicate conscious activity toward tasks such as maintaining posture or position of body parts.

cards.q: what is the word for normal muscle fibers?
cards.a: extrafusal fibers

cards.q: what are muscle spindles?
cards.a: proprioceptors that consist of several modified muscle fibers enclosed in a sheath of connective tissue

cards.q: what are intrafusal fibers?
cards.a: modified proprioceptive muscle fibers that run parallel to the normal, or extrafusal, fibers.

cards.q: what do muscle spindles do?
cards.a: provide information concerning muscle length and the rate of change in length; when the muscle lengthens, spindles are stretched

cards.q: how is the sensory neuron of muscle spindles activated?
cards.a: through deformation; the activation sends an impulse to the spinal cord, where it synapses (connects) with motor neurons, which results in the activation of motor neurons that innervate the same muscle

cards.q: in another sense, what do muscles indicate?
cards.a: the degree to which the muscle must be activated in order to overcome a given resistance -- as a load increases, the muscle is stretched to a greater extent, and engagement of muscle spindles results in greater activation of the muscle

cards.q: how do muscles for precise movements deal with spindles?
cards.a: they have many spindles per unit of mass to help ensure exact control of their contractile activity

cards.q: where to tap for knee jerk reflex?
cards.a: the tendon of the knee extensor muscle group below the patella stretches the muscle spindle fibers

cards.q: how does the kneejerk tap work?
cards.a: causes activation of extrafusal muscle fibers in the same muscle, and a knee jerk occurs as these fibers actively shorten, which then shortens the intrafusal fibers and causes their discharge to cease

cards.q: where are GTOs located?
cards.a: in tendons near the myotendinous junction

cards.q: how are GTOs arranged?
cards.a: in series -- attached end to end with extrafusal muscle fibers

cards.q: when are GTOs activated?
cards.a: when the tendon attached to an active muscle is stretched

cards.q: what occurs during discharge of GTOs?
cards.a: sensory neuron of the GTO synapses with an inhibitory interneuron in the spinal cord, which in turn synapses with and inhibits a motor neuron that serves the same muscle

cards.q: what is the result of GTO synapsing?
cards.a: a reduction in tension within the muscle and tendon

cards.q: what is the difference between spindles and GTOs?
cards.a: whereas spindles facilitate activation of the muscle, neural input from GTOs inhibits muscle activation

cards.q: what can override GTOs?
cards.a: the motor cortex

cards.q: does the cardiovascular systen regulate acid-base functions?
cards.a: yes

cards.q: composition of heart?
cards.a: two interconnected but separate pumps; the right side of the heart pumps blood through the lungs, and the left side pumps blood through the rest of the body. Each pump has two chambers: an atrium and a ventricle

cards.q: functions of atria?
cards.a: the right and left atria deliver blood into the right and left ventricles

cards.q: functions of ventricles?
cards.a: the right and left ventricles supply the main force for moving blood through the pulmonary and peripheral circulations, respectively

cards.q: what are the tricuspid and mitral/bicuspid valves called?
cards.a: atrioventricular [AV] valves

cards.q: what do atrioventricular valves do?
cards.a: prevent the flow of blood from the ventricles back into the atria during ventricular contraction (systole)

cards.q: what are the semilunar valves?
cards.a: the aortic and pulmonary vlave

cards.q: what do the semilunar valves do?
cards.a: prevent backflow from the aorta and pulmonary arteries into the ventricles during ventricular relaxation (diastole)

cards.q: how do the semilunar valves open?
cards.a: passively when a backward pressure gradient pushes blood back against it, and opening when a forward pressure gradient forces blood in the forward direction

cards.q: what is the composition of the heart?
cards.a: 1. the sinoatrial (SA) node—the intrinsic pacemaker—where rhythmic electrical impulses are normally initiated; 2. the internodal pathways that conduct the impulse from the SA node to the atrioventricular node; 3. the atrioventricular (AV) node, where the impulse is delayed slightly before passing into the ventricles; 4. the atrioventricular (AV) bundle, which conducts the impulse to the ventricles; and 5. the left bundle branch and right bundle branch, which further divide into the Purkinje fibers and conduct impulses to all parts of the ventricles

cards.q: where are electrical impulses initiated in the heart?
cards.a: sinoatrial node

cards.q: where are impulses conducted in the heart?
cards.a: internodal pathways, from the SA node

cards.q: what conducts impulses to all parts of the ventricles?
cards.a: left bundle branch and right bundle branch

cards.q: where are impulses delayed in the heart?
cards.a: atrioventricular node, before passing into ventricles

cards.q: what conducts the impulse into ventricles?
cards.a: atrioventricular bundle

cards.q: what divides into the purkinje fibers?
cards.a: left bundle branch and right bundle branch

cards.q: where is the SA located?
cards.a: in the upper lateral wall of the right atrium

cards.q: why does each electrical impulse that begins in the SA node normally spread immediately into the atria?
cards.a: the fibers of the node are contiguous with the muscle fibers of the atrium

cards.q: why do the atria have time to contract and empty blood into the ventricles before ventricular contraction begins?
cards.a: because the conductive system is organized so that the impulse does not travel into the ventricles too rapidly

cards.q: where is AV node located?
cards.a: in the posterior septal (dividing wall between the right and left sides) wall of the right atrium

cards.q: do the left and right bundle branches penetrate the AV barrier?
cards.a: only in their initial portion

cards.q: is the function of bundle branches similar or different to AV nodal fibers?
cards.a: opposite; they are large and transmit impulses at much higher velocity than AV nodal fibers

cards.q: what kind of fibers more completely penetrate ventricles?
cards.a: purkinje fibers

cards.q: why do impulses travel so quickly throughout the ventricular system, allowing both ventricles to contract?
cards.a: the penetration of purkinje fibers

cards.q: what is the discharge rate of the SA node?
cards.a: 60-80 times per minute

cards.q: what is the discharge rate of AV node?
cards.a: 40-60 times per minute

cards.q: what is the discharge rate of ventricular fibers?
cards.a: 15-40 times per minute

cards.q: AV node, ventricular fibers, SA node: least to most discharges?
cards.a: ventricular fibers, AV node, SA node

cards.q: what normally controls heart rhythmicity and why?
cards.a: SA node, due to discharge rate

cards.q: what happens each time the SA node discharges?
cards.a: the impulse is conducted into the AV node and the ventricular fibers, discharging their excitable membranes, and self-excitatory tissues are discharged before self-excitation can actually occur

cards.q: central is to peripheral as?
cards.a: arterial is to venous Arteries

cards.q: what are the functions of the capillaries?
cards.a: to facilitate exchange of oxygen, fluid, nutrients, electrolytes, hormones, and other substances between the blood and the interstitial fluid in the various tissues of the body

cards.q: are capillary walls permeable to nutrients, electrolytes, and hormones?
cards.a: yes, but not all, substances

cards.q: what is the function of venules?
cards.a: to collect blood from the capillaries and gradually converge into the progressively larger veins, which transport blood back to the heart

cards.q: why are the venous walls thin and muscular?
cards.a: because the pressure in the venous system is very low

cards.q: what does the low pressure / thin walls of venules allow?
cards.a: to constrict or dilate to a great degree and thereby act as a reservoir for blood, either in small or in large amounts

cards.q: what is the function of one-way valves?
cards.a: to help maintain venous return by preventing retrograde blood flow.

cards.q: what is the function of the cardiovascular system?
