cards.a: < 100 mg/dL

cards.q: desirable level of total cholesterol
cards.a: < 200 mg/dL

cards.q: at rest and during low intensity exercise, a high percentage of the energy produced comes from?
cards.a: fatty acid oxidation

cards.q: as intensity of exercise increases, there is a gradual shift from ____ to ____ as the preferred source of fuel
cards.a: fat to carbs

cards.q: aerobic training increases the muscle's capacity to use what?
cards.a: fatty acids

cards.q: the body adapts to using greater amounts of _____ for energy when a higher fat, lower carb diet is consumed over a period of time
cards.a: fat

cards.q: alcohol recommendations for men and women per day?
cards.a: up to 1 drink per day for women up to 2 drinks per day for men

cards.q: ________ should be avoided in the time period post exercise because it reduces muscle protein synthesis
cards.a: alcohol

cards.q: organic substances needed in very small amounts that perform specific metabolic processes
cards.a: vitamins

cards.q: vitamins that dissolve in water and are transported in the blood, excess amounts excreted in the urine
cards.a: water soluble vitamins

cards.q: examples of water soluble vitamins
cards.a: vitamin B and C

cards.q: vitamins that are carried by fat in the blood and stored in fat tissue in the body
cards.a: fat soluble vitamins

cards.q: adequate _____ intake prevents the use of protein and muscle break down for energy
cards.a: carb

cards.q: carbohydrate to protein ratio recommended after aerobic exercises
cards.a: 4:1 or 3:1 carb to protein ration

cards.q: why do athletes "hit a wall?"
cards.a: ran out of stored glycogen + relying on protein and fats for fuel

cards.q: restoring depleted _______ is important for athletic performance
cards.a: glycogen

cards.q: glycogen storage = ~_______ calories for the average person
cards.a: 1,500 calories

cards.q: restoring depleted ________ is important for athletic performance because it increases time to exhaustion, prevents the use of protein for energy, and decreases the potential for catabolic break down of tissue
cards.a: glycogen

cards.q: it is recommended that aerobic endurance athletes should ingest how many grams of carbs each hour of activity
cards.a: 30 to 90g EACH HOUR

cards.q: the body can digest about ____g of carbohydrates per minute
cards.a: 1g/min so 60g/hour (some say 28 to 144g/hour)

cards.q: optimizing glycogen storage pre competition by increasing carbohydrate intake several days prior to competition to improve endurance
cards.a: carbohydrate loading

cards.q: carbohydrate loading is most important for which type of athlete?
cards.a: endurance athletes (pulling from glycogen storage)

cards.q: nutrition recommendation for endurance athlete hours before competition?
cards.a: high carb low fat low fiber moderate protein

cards.q: fluid balance recommendation for athletes during training
cards.a: 4 to 8 oz per 15 minutes (some say 6 to 8 oz)

cards.q: carbs and electrolytes from sports drinks may improve what two things for high intensity athletes?
cards.a: performance and speed

cards.q: high intensity athletes need how many carbohydrates from sports drink per break in competition or training?
cards.a: 200 to 400mL per break

cards.q: what percentage range of carbohydrates maximizes digesting?
cards.a: 6 to 8%

cards.q: more than ____% of carbohydrate ingestion significantly decreases digestion
common sources of fiber
cards.a: nuts vegetables/fruit chia seeds

cards.q: athletes who do not train every day can restore glycogen within _____ hours
cards.a: 24 hours

cards.q: type of fatty acid that is more difficult for the body to break down and use for energy due to no double bonds between the carbon molecules
cards.a: saturated fatty acids

cards.q: types of fatty acid that is more efficient for the body to break down and use for energy
cards.a: mono and poly unsaturated fats

cards.q: essential structural component of cell membranes but high levels can lead to cardiovascular disease
cards.a: cholesterol

cards.q: total cholesterol =
cards.a: LDL + HDL

cards.q: micronutrients essential for metabolic regulation and cellular processes
cards.a: vitamins + minerals

cards.q: important for bone health, oxygen carrying capacity, and fluid electrolyte balance
cards.a: minerals

cards.q: important minerals needed in the body?
cards.a: calcium phosphorus magnesium iron

cards.q: important electrolytes needed in the body?
cards.a: sodium potassium chloride

cards.q: what two electrolytes are lost through sweat but replenished by sports drink?
cards.a: sodium and potassium

cards.q: mineral important for oxygen transport throughout the body
cards.a: iron

cards.q: iron deficiency common in female aerobic endurance athletes that impairs athletic performance due to decreased oxygen transport
cards.a: anemia

cards.q: what are some possible symptoms of anemia?
cards.a: muscle fatigue dizziness mood changes deceased concentration headache hair loss feeling cold

cards.q: mineral important for bone density and development + neuromuscular function
cards.a: calcium

cards.q: largest component of the body that is essential for regulating body temperature, regulating blood pressure, and nutrient transport
cards.a: water

cards.q: adequate daily fluid intake for water
cards.a: 3.7 L/day for men 2.7 L/day for women

cards.q: most prevalent nutrition deficiency in the world
cards.a: iron deficiency

cards.q: water represents what percentage of a person's body weight (range)
when sweat loss exceeds fluid intake
cards.a: dehydration

cards.q: athletes are more prone to dehydration and heat stress at what point of the season?
cards.a: beginning

cards.q: mild dehydration decreases performance, increases fatigue, and represents what % weight loss
cards.a: 2 to 3% weight loss

cards.q: help retain fluid, essential for muscle contractions and nerve transmission, and lost through sweat
cards.a: electrolytes

cards.q: drinking JUST water to replenish lost fluids can cause what?
cards.a: hyponatremia

cards.q: what is hyponatremia?
cards.a: dangerously low levels of blood sodium (<125 mmol/L)

cards.q: athletes should try to prevent water weight losses exceeding __% of body weight while also restoring _______ lost through sweat
cards.a: 2%, electrolytes

cards.q: quick and simple way to estimate hydration status
cards.a: measuring changes in body weight before and after a workout

cards.q: 1 pound lost = ___ oz of fluid
true or false: ingestion of multiple types of carbohydrate vs a single carb will lead to greater gastric emptying, carb absorption, oxidation, and performance
cards.a: true

cards.q: fear of weight gain restricted food intake repeated weighing
cards.a: anorexia

cards.q: eating excessively then purging through vomiting, intense exercise, or laxatives (likely to be normal weight)
cards.a: bulimia nervosa

cards.q: eating excessively without purging, likely overweight and eat alone due to anxiety and not wanting others to know
cards.a: binge eating

cards.q: calories burned per day doing nothing
cards.a: basal metabolic rate (BMR)

cards.q: largest contribution to total energy expenditure (65 to 70% of calories)
cards.a: BMR

cards.q: higher than BMR due to daily physical activity and thermic effect of food
cards.a: resting metabolic rate (RMR)

cards.q: how many calories are burned per day from activity?
cards.a: around 400 cal/day (25% on average)

cards.q: to stay hydrated post exercise, ____ L/kg of weight loss needs to be consumed
post aerobic workout, high _____ ______ carbs needs to be consumed
cards.a: glycemic index carbs

title: Chapter 8: Psychology of Athletic Preparation & Performance

cards.q: Following sports psychology training with the men’s volleyball team, the athletes report that during competition, time seemed to slow down, and they felt more focused. The athletes are: a: in the ideal performance state b: in an anxious state c: in the low-determination state
cards.a: a: in the ideal performance state

cards.q: Which of the following exercises is best coached using whole practice? a: snatch b: Turkish get up c: kettlebell swing
cards.a: c: kettlebell swing

cards.q: scientific field of study within sports medicine that seeks to understand the influences of behavioral processes and cognitions on movement
cards.a: sport psychology

cards.q: state that every athlete strives to be in where there is an absence of negative self talk, a strong feeling of efficacy, and an adaptive focus on task relevant cues (“letting it happen”)
cards.a: ideal performance state

cards.q: using only the amount of mental and physical energy required to perform the task
cards.a: physiological efficiency

cards.q: what are some characteristics that an athlete would report about the ideal performance state?
cards.a: no fear of failure no thinking about performance analysis narrow focus of attention sense of effortlessness sense of personal control time slows down

cards.q: true or false: the ability to maintain self control and manage energy in a performance environment is a critical skill for any performer
cards.a: true

cards.q: mental energy is generated, maintained, depleted, and refreshed via our _________
cards.a: emotions

cards.q: temporary feeling states that occur in response to events, have both physiological and psychological components
cards.a: emotions

cards.q: true or false: emotions can have both beneficial and detrimental effects of human performance
cards.a: true

cards.q: how can coaches best teach their athletes to reach the ideal performance state?
cards.a: tap into emotions but control them so that they do not interfere with performance

cards.q: athletic performance is frequently affected by what 3 things?
cards.a: arousal anxiety stress

cards.q: intensity of motivation at any given moment
cards.a: arousal

cards.q: true or false: arousal is always present in an individual to some degree
cards.a: true

cards.q: subcategory of arousal; negatively perceived emotional state characterized by nervousness, worry, apprehension, or fear
cards.a: anxiety

cards.q: psychological component of state anxiety that is caused by fear of failure or worrying
cards.a: cognitive state anxiety

cards.q: physical reaction of state anxiety such as butterflies, muscle tension, and heart racing
cards.a: somatic state anxiety

cards.q: what are some examples of somatic anxiety?
cards.a: tense muscles fast HR rapid breathing

cards.q: subjective experience of apprehension and uncontrolled arousal that leads to elevated neural outflow and increased endocrine activity
cards.a: state anxiety

cards.q: personality characteristic that leads the athlete to perceive situations as threatening
cards.a: trait anxiety

cards.q: athletes with high levels of _________ anxiety tend to use attentional capacity on task-irrelevant cognitions such as thoughts of failure or catastrophe
cards.a: trait anxiety

cards.q: true or false: athletes with high levels of trait anxiety can handle higher levels of pressure because of the decreased probability of engaging in such personal catastrophizing
cards.a: false, athletes with LOW levels can

cards.q: in a ___________ state, arousal is under the control of the athlete and can be elevated or lowered as needed
cards.a: non anxious state

cards.q: in the ________ state, arousal is uncontrolled
cards.a: anxious state

cards.q: arousal is typically too _____ during periods of ineffective state anxiety
cards.a: high

cards.q: imbalance between demand and response capability, under conditions where failure to meet demand has consequences
cards.a: stress

cards.q: environmental or cognitive event that causes stress
cards.a: stressor

cards.q: negative stress
cards.a: distress

cards.q: positive stress
cards.a: eustress

cards.q: true or false: the more skill an athlete has developed, the better he or she can perform during states of less than or greater than optimal arousal
cards.a: true

cards.q: true or false: the optimal arousal point is higher for less skilled athletes than for more advanced players
cards.a: false, LOWER

cards.q: should coaches increase or decrease the decision making responsibilities of developing athletes?
cards.a: decrease

cards.q: two things that influence the appropriate level of arousal to achieve optimal performance?
cards.a: skill level task complexity

cards.q: as an individual's arousal or state anxiety increases, so does performance (theory)
cards.a: drive theory

cards.q: when does drive theory become unproductive or destructive?
cards.a: when it is applied to complex movements

cards.q: arousal facilitates performance up to an optimal level, however further increases in arousal are associated with reduced performance (theory)
cards.a: inverted U theory

cards.q: athletes in different types of performances perform best with different levels of arousal (theory)
cards.a: individual zones of optimal functioning theory

cards.q: true or false: any specific emotion can be positively perceived by one athlete but negatively perceived by another
cards.a: true

cards.q: increases in physiological arousal occur in the presence of cognitive anxiety and a sudden drop in performance occurs, rather than gradual decline (theory)
cards.a: catastrophe theory

cards.q: the athlete's interpretation of arousal and anxiety affect performance, and he or she has the ability to reverse this interpretation (theory)
cards.a: reversal theory

cards.q: motivation that comes from within the athlete regardless of reward/punishment
cards.a: intrinsic motivation

cards.q: motivation that comes from an external source as opposed to internal
cards.a: extrinsic motivation

cards.q: intensity and direction of effort
cards.a: motivation

cards.q: true or false: athletes are rarely completely intrinsically or extrinsically motivation but rather move along a motivation continuum
cards.a: true

cards.q: a person's effort to master a task, achieve excellence, overcome obstacles, and engage in competition or comparison
cards.a: achievement motivation

cards.q: the capacity to experience pride in one's accomplishments and is characterized by a desire to challenge oneself and evaluate one's abilities
cards.a: motive to achieve success (MAS)

cards.q: the desire to protect one's ego and self esteem
cards.a: motive to avoid failure (MAF)

cards.q: true or false: MAF is not really about avoiding failure itself but more about avoiding the perception of shame that accompanies the failure
cards.a: true

cards.q: this type of practice engages the athlete in some decisions and enhances feelings of competence and autonomy
cards.a: self controlled practice

cards.q: increasing the probability that a behavior will occur
cards.a: reinforcement

cards.q: adding something to increase a behavior
cards.a: positive reinforcement

cards.q: target behavior
cards.a: operant

cards.q: taking something away to increase a behavior
cards.a: negative reinforcement

cards.q: what coaching style focuses attention on what the athlete is doing correctly?
cards.a: reinforcement (positive or negative)

cards.q: decreases the occurrence of a given operant
cards.a: punishment

cards.q: adding something to decrease a behavior
cards.a: positive punishment

cards.q: taking something away to decrease a behavior
cards.a: negative punishment

cards.q: processing both environmental and internal cues that come to awareness
cards.a: attention

cards.q: inhibiting awareness of some stimuli in order to process others
cards.a: selective attention

cards.q: attention style in which the athlete assesses the situation by looking at the environment and various elements within it
cards.a: broad external

cards.q: attention style in which the athlete processes information and develops a strategy
cards.a: broad internal

cards.q: attention style in which the athlete mentally rehearses the upcoming action
cards.a: narrow internal

cards.q: attention style in which the athlete specifically focuses on one or two external cues to generate action
cards.a: narrow external

cards.q: what form of breathing is a basic stress management technique that focuses attention on the process of breathing to clear the mind and increase concentration?
cards.a: diaphragmatic breathing

cards.q: technique where psychological and physical arousal are self regulated through the control of skeletal muscle tension and relaxation
cards.a: progressive muscle relaxation (PMR)

cards.q: technique that helps an athlete confront or reduce fear by replacing it with a relaxation response
cards.a: systematic desensitization (SD)

cards.q: designed to reduce physiological arousal and increase task relevant focus
cards.a: relaxation techniques

cards.q: how does an athlete achieve a new relaxation response to a formerly fear inducing stimuli?
cards.a: counter conditioning

cards.q: the athlete creating or recreating a mental experience of an athletic performance in his or her mind that uses all the senses
cards.a: imagery

cards.q: _______ __________ allows the athlete to get used to uncertain environments over longer periods of time despite minimal real world competitive opportunities
cards.a: mental imagery

cards.q: the belief that one can successfully perform a desired behavior
cards.a: self confidence

cards.q: the perception of one's ability to perform a given task in a specific situation
cards.a: self efficacy

cards.q: someone who is highly self ________ does not doubt his or her ability to succeed at a given task, even when failure is expected
cards.a: self efficacious

cards.q: inner dialogue we have with ourselves to enhance self efficacy and aid in directing focus
cards.a: self talk

cards.q: process of progressively challenging standards of performance to increase the likelihood of perceived success
cards.a: goal setting

cards.q: _______ goals focus on the actions the athlete has control over/must engage in during performance to execute the skill well
cards.a: process goals

cards.q: ______ goals that focus on the actions the athlete has little control over (example: winning)
cards.a: outcome goals

cards.q: goals that are directly related to current training or competition and can be attained in a short time frame
cards.a: short term goals

cards.q: goals that overarch the series of linked short term goals
cards.a: long term goals

cards.q: process that results in a relatively permanent change in the capability for a motor skill
cards.a: learning

cards.q: execution of the skill in the current environment
cards.a: performance

cards.q: ___________ can be affected by arousal or motivation and therefore may not be indicative of the skill capabilities of the individual
cards.a: performance

cards.q: practice that addresses the skill in its entirety
cards.a: whole practice

cards.q: practice that separates the skill into a series of components
cards.a: part practice

cards.q: tasks that are challenging but have low interrelatedness of the subcomponents are learned best with _____ practice
cards.a: part practice

cards.q: tasks with subcomponents that are highly interrelated are learned best with _____ practice
cards.a: whole practice

cards.q: when learning a lunge, would it be better to learn through whole practice or part practice?
cards.a: whole practice

cards.q: 2 ways to separate a task into subcomponents
cards.a: segmentation fractionalization

cards.q: breaking down a task into a series of subcomponents that have clear breaks between them
cards.a: segmentation

cards.q: a snatch can be learned through part practice by way of ______________
cards.a: segmentation

cards.q: breaking down a task into subcomponents that occur simultaneously
cards.a: fractionalization

cards.q: when learning a push press, the athlete can use ___________ by first practicing the press motion of the arms and then second the push motion of the legs independently
cards.a: fractionalization

cards.q: adjusting the difficulty of the tasks by changing task characteristics
cards.a: simplification

cards.q: practicing a snatch with a PVC pipe instead of a bar is an example of?
cards.a: simplification

cards.q: 3 ways to teach an athlete how to integrate the parts back into the whole skill
cards.a: pure part training progressive part training repetitive part training

cards.q: type of training that has the athlete practice each subcomponent of the skill multiple times independently
cards.a: pure part training

cards.q: another name for pure part training
cards.a: part whole method

cards.q: type of training that has the athlete practice the first two parts in isolation before practicing these parts together, progression continues until the whole skill has been reintegrated
cards.a: progressive part training

cards.q: type of training that has the athlete practice only the first part in isolation, then each subsequent part is added until the whole task is reintegrated
cards.a: repetitive part training

cards.q: skills are practiced in a ________ practice when the athlete practices the same skill multiple times before progressing to another
cards.a: blocked

cards.q: skills are practiced in a ________ practice when the athlete practices multiple skills in a random order during a given practice session
cards.a: random

cards.q: ________ practice includes variations of the same skill within a single practice session
cards.a: variable

cards.q: ________ practice is when a specific skill is repeated multiple times
cards.a: specific

cards.q: why is developing flexibility and sports specific skills from a combination of specific and variable practice so important for an athlete?
cards.a: sports require the athlete to perform in unfamiliar environments + modify a practice skill in response to an opponent

cards.q: practice through observation of the task or skill to be performed through videos or live demonstrations
cards.a: observational practice

cards.q: a coach can facilitate learning by varying the amount of detail provided in the __________ to the athletes' strongest learning style
cards.a: instructions

cards.q: prescriptive information that gives the athlete the "rules" for effectively executing the given task
cards.a: explicit instructions

cards.q: provides the athlete with instructions about the overall movement goal and important prompts for task accomplishment without explicitly telling the athlete how to accomplish the task
cards.a: guided discovery

cards.q: instructs the athlete on the overarching goal of the task and the athlete receives little to no direction
cards.a: discovery

cards.q: plays a significant role in motor skill acquisition by providing the athlete with information about the movement pattern and the associated goal, which can then be used to make appropriate adjustments to achieve the desired movement pattern and goal
cards.a: feedback

cards.q: feedback provided to the athlete from senses
cards.a: intrinsic feedback

cards.q: feedback provided to the athlete by either a coach or technology
cards.a: augmented feedback

cards.q: augmented feedback can be broken down into knowledge of ________ and knowledge of _______
cards.a: results and performance

cards.q: knowledge of _______ feedback provides the athlete with information about the execution of the task goal
cards.a: results

cards.q: knowledge of ___________ feedback provides the athlete with information about his or her movement pattern
cards.a: performance

cards.q: when the task goal is a __________ __________, there is an overlap between knowledge of results and knowledge of performance, and then they can become one and the same
cards.a: movement outcome

cards.q: the _______ and ________ of feedback have different influences on performance and learning
cards.a: timing and frequency

cards.q: what type of feedback is beneficial for competition?
cards.a: concurrent feedback

cards.q: delayed feedback that is initially frequent and decreases with time will facilitate learning of what type of movement pattern?
cards.a: complex

cards.q: what is the BEST predictor of task execution?
cards.a: self efficacy

cards.q: self determination and achievement are examples of what type of motivation?
cards.a: intrinsic

cards.q: trophies and social approval are examples of what type of motivation?
cards.a: extrinsic

cards.q: which theory accounts for trait anxiety in determining the optimal arousal level for performance?
cards.a: reversal theory

cards.q: how may arousal be measured?
cards.a: blood pressure heart rate catecholamine levels self reported measures

cards.q: true or false: concurrent feedback is good for performance but not for long-term learning
cards.a: true

cards.q: an athlete with which type of motivation is most likely to succeed when facing a challenging goal such as facing an opponent in a high-pressure playoff game?
cards.a: motivation to achieve success (MAS)

cards.q: according to the inverted-U theory, which sport is likely to have a lower arousal level at the point of optimal performance?
cards.a: golf

title: Chapter 17: Program Design for Resistance Training

cards.q: what are the 7 program design variables?
cards.a: needs analysis exercise selection frequency exercise order load and repetitions volume rest periods

cards.q: what three principles should be incorporated in resistance training programs for athletic populations?
cards.a: specificity overload progression

cards.q: athletes training in a specific manner to produce a specific adaptation or training outcome
cards.a: specificity

cards.q: how can specificity be incorporated into a resistance training program for athletes?
cards.a: specific muscles, movement patters, muscle actions, and energy systems involved in the sport

cards.q: what does the SAID principle stand for?
cards.a: specific adaptation to imposed demands

cards.q: principle that states the type of demand placed on the body dictates the type of adaptation that will occur
cards.a: SAID principle

cards.q: training at a greater intensity than the athlete is accustomed to
cards.a: overload

cards.q: what are some ways to overload?
cards.a: increase loads or reps add exercises simple to complex decrease rest periods add variables

cards.q: training program intensity becomes progressively greater to continue producing higher levels of performance
cards.a: progression

cards.q: two stage process that includes an evaluation of the requirements and characteristics of the sport and an assessment of the athlete
cards.a: needs analysis

cards.q: athletic programs should be periodized to move from _______ to _______
cards.a: general to specific

cards.q: what are the 4 variables of a physiological analysis?
cards.a: strength power hypertrophy muscular endurance

cards.q: what two things does a needs analysis assess?
cards.a: the athlete and their sport

cards.q: current condition or level of preparedness of the athlete
cards.a: training status

cards.q: what is determined after the needs analysis is complete?
cards.a: the athlete’s specific needs for their sport and the primary goal for their specific training program

cards.q: how many training goals should an athlete focus on per season?
cards.a: one

cards.q: what are core exercises?
cards.a: multijoint exercises that recruit large muscle group(s) and have direct application to the sport of the athlete

cards.q: what are assistance exercises?
cards.a: single joint exercises that recruit smaller muscle areas and are considered less important to improving sport performance

cards.q: why are assistance exercises commonly used for injury prevention and rehab?
cards.a: because they isolate a specific muscle or muscle group

cards.q: exercises that load the spine directly or indirectly, requiring muscular stabilization of posture during performance of the lifting movement
cards.a: structural exercises

cards.q: a structural exercises that is performed very quickly or explosively
cards.a: power exercise

cards.q: true or false: muscle balance includes equal strength
cards.a: false

cards.q: what are recovery exercises?
cards.a: exercises that do not place high stress on muscular and nervous systems in order to promote movement and restoration

cards.q: number of training sessions completed in a given period of time
cards.a: training frequency

cards.q: what is the general recommendation for training frequency for athletes to allow sufficient recovery between sessions?
cards.a: 3x/week

cards.q: what is the general recommendation for rest days between strength days?
cards.a: 0-2 rest days (no more than 3)

cards.q: how many sessions per week is recommended for an athlete that has a beginner training status?
how many sessions per week is recommended for an athlete that has a intermediate training status?
how many sessions per week is recommended for an athlete that has a advanced training status?
how many sessions per week is recommended for an athlete during the off season?
how many sessions per week is recommended for an athlete during the pre season?
how many sessions per week is recommended for an athlete when in season?
how many sessions per week is recommended for an athlete during the post season?
cards.a: 0-3 (active rest)

cards.q: max to near max loads will require _____ recovery times
cards.a: longer

cards.q: heavy upper body training may require _____ recovery than heavy lower body training
cards.a: less

cards.q: single joint exercise are _____ taxing than multi joint exercises
cards.a: less

cards.q: sequence of resistance exercises performed during one training session
cards.a: exercise order

cards.q: what is the most common exercise order?
cards.a: power > core lifts > assistance lifts

cards.q: what is circuit training?
cards.a: performing the exercises with minimal rest periods

cards.q: with exercise order, why do power lifts need to be performed first?
cards.a: power lifts require the highest level of skill/concentration and most affected by fatigue

cards.q: what are two ways to "alternate" exercise order?
cards.a: upper body/lower body push/pull

cards.q: two exercises performed in an alternating fashion that stresses opposing muscles or muscle areas
cards.a: superset

cards.q: sequentially performing two different exercises for the same muscle group
cards.a: compound set

cards.q: compound sets are generally performed for what training goal?
cards.a: muscle hypertrophy/fatigue

cards.q: amount of weight assigned to an exercise set
cards.a: load

cards.q: what is often characterized as the most critical aspect of a resistance training program?
cards.a: load

cards.q: force x displacement =
cards.a: mechanical work

cards.q: what is the volume-load?
cards.a: total work done

cards.q: what is the repetition-volume?
cards.a: volume of each rep

cards.q: volume load / rep volume =
cards.a: average weight lifted per rep per workout session

cards.q: reps and loads are ________ related, meaning when one goes up the other has to go down
cards.a: inversely

cards.q: what is the goal rep method?
cards.a: matching the RM testing to the rep range that will be trained in the training program

cards.q: power exercises should be limited to ___RM or less for RM testing
cards.a: 5 reps or less

cards.q: how much weight should be added to the bar when performing upper body 1RM testing?
cards.a: 10-20 pounds or 5-10%

cards.q: how much weight should be added to the bar when performing lower body 1RM testing?
cards.a: 30-40 pounds or 10-20%

cards.q: to increase strength, the athlete needs to handle loads of at least ____% of the 1RM for up to ___ reps/set
cards.a: 85% 6 reps/set

cards.q: what is the recommended sets, reps, and load (%1RM) to train strength?
cards.a: 2-6 sets of 6 reps or less at 85%+ load

cards.q: what is the recommended sets, reps, and load (%1RM) to train single effort power?
cards.a: 3-5 sets of 1-2 reps at 80-90% load

cards.q: what is the recommended sets, reps, and load (%1RM) to train multiple effort power?
cards.a: 3-5 sets of 3-5 reps at 75-85% load

cards.q: what is the recommended sets, reps, and load (%1RM) to train for hypertrophy?
cards.a: 3-6 sets of 6-12 reps at 67-85% load

cards.q: what is the recommended sets, reps, and load (%1RM) to train for muscular endurance?
cards.a: 2-3 sets of 12+ reps at 67% or less load

cards.q: true or false: certain RM emphasize a specific outcome but training benefits are blended at any given RM
cards.a: true

cards.q: what load percentage has been shown to create peak power?
________ power is achieved with moderate loads and intermediate velocities
cards.a: maximal

cards.q: what is the 2-for-2 rule?
cards.a: if the athlete can perform two or more reps over the rep goal in the last set in two consecutive workouts, weight should be added to that exercise next session

cards.q: total amount of weight lifted in a training session
cards.a: volume

cards.q: what is the estimated load increase for a weaker athlete training upper body?
cards.a: 2.5-5 pounds

cards.q: what is the estimated load increase for a weaker athlete training lower body?
cards.a: 5-10 pounds

cards.q: what is the estimated load increase for a stronger athlete training upper body?
cards.a: 5-10+ pounds

cards.q: what is the estimated load increase for a weaker athlete training lower body?
cards.a: 10-15+ pounds

cards.q: what is the rule of thumb for quantity of load increases for heavier and lighter lifts?
cards.a: greater load increases for heavier lifts smaller load increases for lighter lifts

cards.q: what is the relative load increase percentage range that can be used instead of the absolute values?
what is the rep-volume?
cards.a: reps per workout

cards.q: volume-load =
cards.a: (sets x reps) x load

cards.q: volume load x concentric displacement =

title: Chapter 6: Adaptations to Aerobic Endurance Training Programs

cards.q: the amount of blood pumped by the heart in liters per minute

cards.q: quantity of blood ejected with each heart beat

cards.q: cardiac output =

two physiological mechanisms that are responsible for the regulation of stroke volume

cards.q: volume of blood in the left ventricle at the end of the filling phase

cards.q: hormones of the sympathetic nervous system that produce a forceful ventricular contraction and greater systolic emptying of the heart
cards.a: epinephrine and norepinephrine (catecholamines)

cards.q: the myocardial fibers become more stretched with increased volume resulting in a more forceful reflexive contraction and increased cardiac output. this is known as the _______

cards.q: fraction of the end diastolic volume ejected from the heart

cards.q: how can athletes estimate maximal heart rate?

cards.q: the amount of oxygen consumed by the body’s tissues

cards.q: true or false: aerobic exercise involving a larger mass of muscle or a greater level of work is associated with a higher oxygen uptake

cards.q: the greatest amount of oxygen that can be used at the cellular level for the entire body

cards.q: the most widely accepted measure of cardiorespiratory fitness

cards.q: the difference in the oxygen content between arterial and venous blood

cards.q: to express oxygen uptake in its common SI unit, what do you divide by?

cards.q: rate pressure product (or double product) =

cards.q: pressure exerted against the arterial walls when no blood is being forcefully ejected through the vessels

cards.q: diastolic blood pressure can decrease with aerobic endurance exercise due to?

cards.q: average blood pressure throughout the cardiac cycle

cards.q: mean arterial pressure is usually more or less than the average of the systolic and diastolic pressures?

cards.q: mean arterial pressure =

cards.q: primary mechanics for regulating regional blood flow

________ exercise provides for the greatest impact on both oxygen uptake and carbon dioxide production as compared to other types of exercise

cards.q: volume of air breathed per minute

cards.q: amount of air inhaled and exhaled with each breath

cards.q: ratio of minute ventilation to oxygen uptake

cards.q: functional unit of the pulmonary system where gas exchange occurs

cards.q: areas of the respiratory passages that are not functional for gas exchange

cards.q: true or false: increasing tidal volume makes for more efficient ventilation than increasing frequency of breathing alone

cards.q: alveoli with impaired gas exchange due to poor blood flow, poor ventilation, or other problems with the alveolar surface
cards.a: physiological dead space

cards.q: certain types of lung disease can significantly reduce alveolar function and increase physiological dead space by as much as ___x the volume of anatomical dead space
the movement of oxygen and carbon dioxide across a cell membrane
cards.a: diffusion

cards.q: diffusion results from the movement of gas from ____ concentration to ____ concentrations
cards.a: high to low

cards.q: 2 ways that oxygen is carried in blood
cards.a: transported by hemoglobin dissolved in plasma

cards.q: 70% of carbon dioxide removal occurs through the process of carbon dioxide being delivered to the lungs in the form of _______?

cards.q: why does lactate not accumulate during low to moderate intensity exercise?

cards.q: cycle where muscle derived lactate is transported via the blood to the liver where it undergoes gluconeogenesis

cards.q: what occurs when aerobic metabolism is not sufficient to keep up with the formation of lactic acid during higher work intensities and levels begin to rise in the blood?

cards.q: increasing maximal _______ uptake is very important for optimal aerobic exercise performance
cards.a: oxygen

cards.q: normal discharge rate of SA node
cards.a: 60 to 80 times per minute

cards.q: bradycardia
cards.a: slower heart rate

cards.q: resting heart rates commonly range from ___ to ___ bpm in highly conditioned aerobic endurance athletes
cards.a: 40 to 60 bpm

cards.q: 2 most significant cardiovascular function increases due to long term aerobic endurance training
cards.a: cardiac output stroke volume

cards.q: most like muscle fiber type transition with long term aerobic endurance training
cards.a: type IIx to type IIa

cards.q: why do type IIx fibers change to type IIa fibers with long term aerobic endurance training?
cards.a: type IIa fibers have a greater oxidative capacity than type IIx fibers, making them more similar with type I fibers to contribute to aerobic endurance performance

cards.q: average cardiac output at rest
cards.a: 5 L of blood

cards.q: average cardiac output during exercise
cards.a: 25 L of blood

cards.q: true or false: max HR changes with training
cards.a: false

cards.q: true or false: max stroke volume increases with training
cards.a: true

cards.q: Max HR=
cards.a: 220 - age

cards.q: How do you calculate Heart Rate Reserve (HRR)
cards.a: HRMax - Resting Heart Rate (RHR)

cards.q: Karvonen Method Equation:
cards.a: Resting HR + (training % * HRR)

cards.q: ________ increases linearly in response to the oxygen demand of activity
cards.a: heart rate

cards.q: true or false: max HR is an adaptation that changes with training
cards.a: false

cards.q: true or false: max stroke volume increases with training
cards.a: true

cards.q: true or false: endurance trained athletes can pump more blood per heartbeat
cards.a: true

cards.q: what two things cause stroke volume to increase?
cards.a: increased end diastolic volume increased epinephrine + norepinephrine

cards.q: how does increased epinephrine and norepinephrine increase stroke volume and cardiac output?
cards.a: cause a more forceful ventricular contraction and more emptying

cards.q: what type of exercise increases the release of catecholamines?
cards.a: high intensity exercise

cards.q: what 3 mechanisms increase venous return to the heart?
cards.a: skeletal muscle pump respiratory pump vasoconstriction

cards.q: decreasing vein size to increase pressure/venous return, via sympathetic nervous system activation
cards.a: vasoconstriction

cards.q: true or false: the frank starling mechanism increases ejection fraction
cards.a: true

cards.q: maximal cardiac output is __x as much blood pumping through the body as at rest
cards.a: 4x as much

cards.q: females generally have around ____% lower stroke volume and cardiac output compared to men
why do women have a lower stroke volume compared to men?
cards.a: smaller heart so less blood volume

cards.q: true or false: HR rises linearly in response to demand of activity
cards.a: true

cards.q: HR is ______ proportional to VO2 max
cards.a: directly

cards.q: difference between maximal and resting heart rate
cards.a: heart rate reserve

cards.q: true or false: the karvonen method is always lower than the strict percentage of max HR
cards.a: false, always higher

cards.q: what is metabolic equivalent?
cards.a: resting oxygen uptake

cards.q: 1 MET = ____ mL/kg/min
true or false: a-vO2 difference decreases with increased capillary and mitochondrial density
cards.a: false, improves with increased density

cards.q: units for VO2 max
cards.a: mL/kg/min

cards.q: true or false: VO2 max can increase just by decreasing body weight
cards.a: true

cards.a: lower partial pressure of oxygen = less oxygen to the muscles

cards.q: acute adaptations from altitude training occur within how many days?
cards.a: 0-14 days

cards.q: two acute adaptations that increase with altitude training
cards.a: respiratory rate submax SV and CO

cards.q: what are some chronic adaptations that take place with altitude training?
cards.a: increased hemoglobin, RBCs, capilarization = overall increased oxygen delivery to muscles

cards.q: why is there more time spent in diastole than systole?
cards.a: it takes longer to fill than push blood out

cards.q: increased systolic BP at rest
cards.a: hypertension

cards.q: why does diastolic BP stay the same?
cards.a: to create gradient for oxygen delivery

cards.q: used to describe the amount of oxygen consumption or work that the heart has to do
cards.a: rate pressure product (double product)

cards.q: muscle fiber that hypertrophies with aerobic training
cards.a: type I

cards.q: oxidative enzyme upregulation takes place with what type of training?
cards.a: aerobic

cards.q: how does aerobic training effect fat burning?
cards.a: allows you to burn a higher percentage of fat at a given submaximal HR (which allows you to save carbs)

cards.q: how does aerobic training affect blood lactate?
cards.a: decreases blood lactate at a given submax intensity

cards.q: what three things do NOT adapt to aerobic training?
cards.a: respiratory capacity muscle hypertrophy max heart rate

cards.q: protein that transports oxygen within the cell
cards.a: myoglobin

cards.q: aerobic exercise training, especially long distance and high intensity intermittent exercise, results in an increase in the ______ capacity of type I fibers

cards.q: what does it mean when an athlete has exercise efficiency?

cards.q: __________ reduces the amount of oxygen that can be carried by hemoglobin and thus reduces the oxygen that can be provided to the working muscles

title: CSCS CH 1 Structure & Function of Body Systems

cards.q: Musculoskeletal system
cards.a: consists of bones, joints, muscles, & tendons configured to allow the great variety of movements characteristics of human acitivty

cards.q: Skeleton
cards.a: muscle attachment points, to cause bony levels to enforce pushing and pulling forces from muscles.

cards.q: Axial skeleton
cards.a: consists of the skull, vertebral column, ribs, & sternum

cards.q: Appendicular skeleton
cards.a: includes the shoulder girdle; bones of the arm, wrist & hands. The pelvic girdle; bones of the legs, ankles, & feet.

cards.q: Fibrous joints
cards.a: allow virtually no movement; EX) sutures of the skull.

cards.q: Cartilaginous joints
cards.a: Allow limited movement; EX) intervertebral disks.

cards.q: Synovial Joint
cards.a: Allow considerable movement. EX) elbow & knee

cards.q: Hyaline Cartilage
cards.a: Articulating bone ends are covered in.

cards.q: Synovial Fluid
cards.a: The entire joint is enclosed in a capsule filled of

cards.q: Uniaxial joints
cards.a: Allows 1 axis of movement. EX) Hinge joint, elbow or knee

cards.q: Biaxial Joints
cards.a: Allows movement in 2 perpendicular axes. EX) ankle & wrist

cards.q: multiaxial joints
cards.a: Allows movement in all three perpendicular axes; EX ball-n-socket joint, hip or shoulder

cards.q: Vertebral column make up
cards.a: Vertebral bones separated by flexible disks that allow movement to occur 7 cervical 12 Thoracic 5 Lumbar 5 fused sacral 3 to 5 coccygeal

cards.q: Epimysium
cards.a: fibrous connective tissue, covers the body’s more than 430 skeletal muscles

cards.q: tendon
cards.a: connective tissue that attaches muscle to bone

cards.q: Bone periosteum
cards.a: specialized connective tissue covering all bones

cards.q: proximal
cards.a: closer to the trunk

cards.q: distal
cards.a: farther from the trunk

cards.q: superior
cards.a: closer to the head

cards.q: inferior
cards.a: closer to the feet

cards.q: muscle fibers
cards.a: muscle cells; long, cylindrical cells; Nuclei situated on periphery of the cell

cards.q: Fasciculi
cards.a: bundles of muscle fibers under the epimysium may consist of 150 fibers

cards.q: perimysium
cards.a: fasciculi bundle being surrounded by this connective tissue

cards.q: endomysium
cards.a: connective tissue that surrounds each muscle fiber of fasciculi

cards.q: sarcolemma
cards.a: encircled & is contiguous with endomysium; inside a fasciculus

cards.q: Sarcoplasm
cards.a: interior structure of a muscle fiber. Cytoplasm of a muscle fiber, contains contractile components; protein filaments, other proteins, stored glycogen, enzymes, fat particles, mitochondria, the sarcoplasmic reticulum. Surrounds the myofibril

cards.q: myofibrils
cards.a: within the sarcoplasm; contains apparatus that contracts the muscle cells (myofilaments actin and myosin)

cards.q: myofilaments
cards.a: where the sarcomere is located actin and myosin

cards.q: motor neuron
cards.a: nerve cell located in central nervous system (CNS)

cards.q: neuromuscular junction
cards.a: where the motor neuron & muscle fiber meet & is innervated (motor end plate)

cards.q: motor unit
cards.a: a motor neuron & the muscle fiber it innervates contract together when stimulated by motor neuron

cards.q: cross-bridge
cards.a: myosin thick head protrudes away from myosin filament & connects to, innervates with, actin thin.

cards.q: sarcomere
cards.a: Smallest contractile unit of the skeletal muscle

cards.q: A-band
cards.a: Dark; corresponds with the alignment of the myosin and actin attachment point

cards.q: I-band
cards.a: Light; corresponds with the areas in two adjacent sarcomeres that contain only actin filaments

cards.q: Z-line
cards.a: middle of the I-band (actin) & appears as a thin, dark line running longitudinally through the I-band

cards.q: H-zone
cards.a: Area in the center of the sarcomere where only myosin filaments are present

cards.q: M-line
cards.a: Center of the A band & sarcomere.

cards.q: Action potential
cards.a: An electrical nerve impulse. Arrives nearly simultaneously from surface to all depths of the muscle fibers. Calcium is thus released throughout the muscle, producing a coordinated contraction

cards.q: Sliding-Filament theory
cards.a: States that the actin filaments at each end of the sarcomere slide inward on myosin filaments, pulling the z-lines toward the center of the sarcomere & shortening the muscle fiber.

cards.q: SFT; Resting Phase
cards.a: Resting conditions, little calcium is present in the myofibrils (stored in sarcoplasmic reticulum) very few myosin cross-bridges are bound to actin.

cards.q: SFT; Excitation-contraction coupling phase
cards.a: Before myosin cross-bridges can flex, they must first attach to the actin filaments

cards.q: troponin
cards.a: A protein that is situated at regular intervals along the actin filaments & has a high affinity for calcium ions.

cards.q: tropomyosin
cards.a: protein molecule that runs the length of the actin filament in the groove of the double helix. The myosin cross-bridge attaches more rapidly.

cards.q: SFT; contraction phase
cards.a: when calcium binds to troponin

cards.q: power stroke
cards.a: The energy of pulling action hydrolysis (breakdown) of adenosine triphosphate (ATP) to Adenosine diphosphate (ADP) & phosphate (P), catalyzed by enzyme myosin adenosine triphosphate (ATPase).

cards.q: SFT; Recharge phase
cards.a: measurable muscle shortening transpires only when this sequence of events binding of calcium to troponin, coupling of the myosin, cross-bridge with actin, power stroke, dissociation of actin & myosin, & resetting of the myosin head position. Repeated over & over again.

cards.q: SFT; Relaxation phase
cards.a: Occurs when the stimulation of a motor nerve stops. Calcium is pumped back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum, prevents binding between actin & myosin filaments

cards.q: Neuromuscular system
cards.a: muscle fibers are innervated by motor neurons that transmit impulses in the form of electrochemical signals from the spinal cord to the muscles

cards.q: Acetylocholine
cards.a: Arrival of the action potential at the nerve terminal causes release of this neurotransmitter. It diffuses across the neuromuscular junction causing excitation of the sarcolemma

cards.q: All-OR-none principle
cards.a: All of the muscle fibers in the motor unit contract & develop force at the same time. If none contract than there is no contraction

cards.q: Twitch
cards.a: Each action potential traveling down a motor neuron results in a short period of activation of the muscle fibers within the motor unit.

cards.q: Tentanus
cards.a: The stimuli may be delivered at so high a frequency that the twitches begin to merge & eventually completely fuse. Maximal amount of force the motor unit can develop.

cards.q: Fast-Twitch fibers
cards.a: A motor unit that develops force & also relaxes rapidly & has a short twitch time. Type IIa & IIx

cards.q: Slow-twitch fibers
cards.a: A motor unit that develops force & relaxes slowly & has a long twitch time. Type I

cards.q: Type I fibers
cards.a: efficient & fatigue resistant & have a high capacity for aerobic energy supply; limited potential for rapid force development. Low myosin ATPase activity & low anaerobic power

cards.q: Type II fibers
cards.a: Inefficient & Fatigable & have low aerobic power; rapid force development high myosin ATPase activity & high an anaerobic power.

cards.q: Type IIa
cards.a: Have greater capacity for aerobic metabolism & more capillaries surrounding them. Great resistance to fatigue

cards.q: Type IIx
cards.a: Less capacity for aerobic metabolism & less capillaries surrounding. Less resistance to fatigue.

cards.q: Proprioception
cards.a: specialized sensory receptors located within joints, muscles, & tendons sensitive to pressure & tension

cards.q: Muscle spindles
cards.a: proprioceptors that consist of several modified muscle fibers enclosed in a sheath of connective tissue. Intra & extrafusal fibers.

cards.q: Intrafusal fibers
cards.a: muscle spindles-sensory receptors for muscle control & movement.

cards.q: Extrafusal fibers
cards.a: Build up the muscle mass, generate force & execute movements.

cards.q: Golgi Tendon Organs (GTOs)
cards.a: Proprioceptors located in tendons near the myotendinous junction & are in series, attached end to end with extrafusal muscle fibers. Activated when the tendon attached to an active muscle is stretched inhibitory process thought to provide a mechanism that protects against excessive tension

cards.q: Atrium
cards.a: chambers Left & right deliver blood into the left & right ventricles

cards.q: Ventricle
cards.a: Supply the main force for moving blood through the pulmonary & peripheral circulations. Let & Right ventricle

cards.q: Tricuspid valve & mitral valve
cards.a: Atrioventricular (AV) valves prevent the flow of blood from the ventricles back into the atria's during ventricular contraction.

cards.q: Systole
cards.a: Ventricular contraction

cards.q: Aortic valve & pulmonary valve
cards.a: semilunar valves, prevent backflow from the aorta & pulmonary arteries into the ventricles during ventricular relaxation

cards.q: Diastole
cards.a: Ventricular relaxation

cards.q: Sinoatrial (SA) node
cards.a: intrinsic pacemaker, where rhythmic electrical impulses are normally initiated.

cards.q: atrioventricular (AV) node
cards.a: where the impulse is delayed slightly before passing into the ventricles

cards.q: atrioventricular (AV) bundle
cards.a: conduct the impulse to the ventricles

cards.q: Left & right bundle branch
cards.a: conducts impulses to all parts of the ventricles

cards.q: Purkinje fibers
cards.a: continuation of the right bundle branch

cards.q: myocardium
cards.a: The heart muscle

cards.q: autonomic nervous system
cards.a: involuntary contractions from the Central Nervous system. Splits into sympathetic and parasympathetic nervous systems.

cards.q: Sympathetic Nervous system
cards.a: Fight or Flight. Causes depolarization of SA node to make heart beat faster.

cards.q: Parasympathetic Nervous System
cards.a: Rest or Digest. Slows the SA node. Slows the heart rate.

cards.q: Bradycardia
cards.a: Fewer than 60 beats/min

cards.q: Tachycardia
cards.a: more than 100 beats/min

cards.q: Electrocardiogram (ECG)
cards.a: electrical activity of the heart can be recorded at the surface of the body. A graphic representation of activity.

cards.q: P-Wave
cards.a: generated by the changes in the electrical potential of cardiac muscle cells that depolarize the atria & results in atrial contraction.

cards.q: QRS complex
cards.a: Q-wave, R-wave, & S-wave. Generated by the electrical potential that depolarized the ventricles & results in ventricular contraction.

cards.q: T-wave
cards.a: electrical potential generated as the ventricle recover from the state of depolarization

cards.q: Repolarization
cards.a: Occurs in ventricular muscle shortly after depolarization.

cards.q: Arterial system
cards.a: carries blood away from the heart to supply oxygenated blood to the body.

cards.q: Venous system
cards.a: Returns deoxygenated blood toward the heart

cards.q: Arteries
cards.a: rapidly transport blood pumped from the heart. Strong muscular walls

cards.q: arterioles
cards.a: Small branches of arteries. act as control vessels through which blood enter the capillaries.

cards.q: capillaries
cards.a: facilitate exchange of oxygen, fluid, nutrients, electrolytes, hormones, & other substances between the blood & the interstitial fluid in the various tissue of the body. Very thin & very permeable.

cards.q: Venules
cards.a: collect blood from the capillaries & gradually converge into large veins

cards.q: Veins
cards.a: transport blood back to the heart. Low pressure, thin walls, although muscular.

cards.q: Hemoglobin
cards.a: transport of oxygen, iron-protein molecule carried by the red blood cells.

cards.q: Red blood cells
cards.a: Major component of the blood, contains carbonic anhydrase, catalyzes carbon dioxide & water for carbon removal.

cards.q: Respiratory System
cards.a: Primary Function of the respiratory system is the basic exchange of oxygen & carbon dioxide.

cards.q: Trachea
cards.a: first-generation respiratory passage

cards.q: Bronchi
cards.a: second-generation respiratory passage.

cards.q: Bronchioles
cards.a: The next generation of branches.

cards.q: Alveoli
cards.a: Where gases are exchanged in respiration.

cards.q: Pleural pressure
cards.a: pressure in the narrow space between the lung pleura & the chest wall pleura.

cards.q: Pleura
cards.a: Membranes enveloping the lungs & lining the chest wall.

cards.q: Alveolar pressure
cards.a: pressure inside the alveoli when the glottis is open & no air is flowing into or out of the lungs.

cards.q: Diffusion
cards.a: simple random motion of molecules moving in opposite directions through the alveolar capillary membrane.

title: Chapter 1 - The Structure and Function of Body Systems

cards.q: A-Band
cards.a: The section of the sarcomere that corresponds with the alignment of myosin and actin filaments.

cards.q: Acetylcholine
cards.a: A neurotransmitter released when an action potential arrives at the nerve terminal. The Acetylcholine diffuses across the neuromuscular junction causing excitation of the sarcolemma.

cards.q: Actin
cards.a: A protein that forms actin myofilaments. Actin filaments consist of two thin strands about 6nm in diameter arranged in a double helix.

cards.q: Action potential
cards.a: An electrical impulse from a motor nerve that signals the release of calcium from the sarcoplasmic reticulum into the myofibril, causing tension development in the muscle.

cards.q: All-or-none principle
cards.a: The phenomenon that a stimulus from the motor neuron will cause all fibers in that motor unit to contract. As such, stronger action potentials do not result in bigger contractions.

cards.q: Alveolar pressure ​
cards.a: Pressure inside the alveoli when the glottis is open and no air is flowing into or out of the lungs.

cards.q: Alveoli
cards.a: The final passages in the respiratory system where gases are exchanged from the lungs.

cards.q: Aortic valve
cards.a: Valve in the heart that prevents backflow of blood from the aorta into the ventricle.

cards.q: Appendicular skeleton
cards.a: Bones of the shoulder/pectoral girdle (left and right scapula and clavicle), bones of the arms, wrists, and hands (left and right humerus, radius, ulna, carpals, metacarpals, and phalanges); the pelvic girdle (left and right coxal or innominate bones), and the bones of the legs, ankles, and feet (left and right femur, patella, tibia, fibula, tarsals, metatarsals, and phalanges). (ESC p. 2)

cards.q: Arterial system
cards.a: System of tubes that carries blood away from the heart. Due to the high pressure of the blood from the heart, arteries have strong walls.

cards.q: Arteriole
cards.a: Smaller branches of the arterial system that deliver blood to the capillaries.

cards.q: Artery
cards.a: Strong tubes that rapidly transport blood from the heart.

cards.q: Atrioventricular (AV) bundle
cards.a: Conducts the impulse in the heart to the ventricles.

cards.q: Atrioventricular (AV) node
cards.a: Node in the heart that slightly delays the impulse from the SA node.

cards.q: Atrioventricular (AV) valves
cards.a: One-way valves that prevent the backflow of the blood from the ventricles into the atria.

cards.q: Atrium
cards.a: Chambers of the heart that receive blood and pump it to the ventricles. The left and right atria pump blood to the left and right ventricle, respectively.

cards.q: Axial Skeleton
cards.a: Bones of the skull (cranium), vertebral column (C1-coccyx), ribs, and sternum.

cards.q: Biaxial joints
cards.a: Joints such as the ankle and wrist that allow movement around two perpendicular axes.

cards.q: Bone periosteum
cards.a: A specialized connective tissue covering all bones. The tendons attach to the bone periosteum.

cards.q: Bradycardia
cards.a: Heart rate less than 60 bpm.

cards.q: Bronchi
cards.a: Second generation passages in the respiratory system that deliver air to the bronchioles.

cards.q: Bronchiole
cards.a: The third generation passages in the lungs that deliver air to the alveoli, where gases are exchanged.

cards.q: Capillary
cards.a: Small end-tubes of the arterial system that facilitate exchange of oxygen, fluid, nutrients, and other substances between the blood and other fluids in various body tissues.

cards.q: Cartilaginous joints
cards.a: joints that allow limited movement - i.e. intervertebral disks. (ESC p. 2).

cards.q: **Crossbridge**
cards.a: The connections between the globular heads on myosin filaments that bind with actin. The strength of a muscle contraction is directly related to the number of myosin crossbridges bound to actin.

cards.q: **Depolarization**
cards.a: The reversal of the heart membrane electrical potential and results in contraction of the atria or ventricles in the case of the P-Wave and QRS complex, respectively.

cards.q: **Diastole**
cards.a: Ventricular relaxation.

cards.q: **Diffusion**
cards.a: The simple random motion of molecules moving in opposite directions through the alveolar-capillary membrane.

cards.q: Distal
cards.a: The attachment of a limb muscle that is further from the trunk relative to the proximal attachment.

cards.q: **Electrocardiogram (ECG)**
cards.a: Graphic representation of heart electrical activity.

cards.q: **Endomysium**
cards.a: The connective tissue that surrounds each muscle fiber and is contiguous with the muscle fiber membrane known as the sarcolemma.

cards.q: **Epimysium**
cards.a: The outer layer of fibrous connective tissue covering the body’s more than 430 skeletal muscles. The epimysium is contiguous with the tendons at the ends of the muscle.

cards.q: **Extrafusal fibers**
cards.a: Normal muscle fibers.

cards.q: **Fasciculi**
cards.a: Bundles of muscle fibers located under the epimedium. The fasciculi can consist of up to 150 fibers and each fascicle is individually surrounded by connective tissue called perimysium.

cards.q: **Fast-twitch fiber**
cards.a: The fibers in a fast-twitch motor unit that develops force and relaxes rapidly, resulting in a short twitch time. Fast-twitch fibers are further broken into Type IIa fibers and type IIx fibers. Type II fibers and motor units can produce force rapidly but are inefficient and quick to fatigue. Type IIa fibers are more resistant to fatigue than type IIx fibers due to a greater capacity for aerobic metabolism. Type IIa fibers are still far less aerobically efficient than type I fibers.

cards.q: **Fibrous joint**
cards.a: Joints that allow little to no movement such as the sutures of the skull.

cards.q: **Golgi tendon organ**
cards.a: Proprioceptors located in the tendons attached to extrafusal muscle fibers. Golgi tendon organs relay information regarding tension in the muscle and are though to protect against the development of excess tension in the muscle.

cards.q: **Hemoglobin**
cards.a: The iron-protein molecule carried by red blood cells. Hemoglobin transports oxygen as well as provides an acid-base buffer in the blood to regulate H+ ion concentration.

cards.q: **Hyaline cartilage**
cards.a: The smooth covering on the ends of articulating bones. (ESC p. 2)

cards.q: **H-Zone**
cards.a: The area in the center of the sarcomere containing only myosin filaments. The H-zone decreases during muscle contraction as actin slides over the myosin toward the center of the sarcomere.

cards.q: I-Band
cards.a: The area in two adjacent sarcomeres that contain only actin filaments.

cards.q: **Inferior**
cards.a: The attachment of a trunk muscle closer to the feet relative to the superior attachment. (ESC p. 3).

cards.q: **Intrafusal fiber**
cards.a: Modified muscle fibers that run parallel to normal extrafusal fibers and relay sensory information concerning muscle length.

cards.q: **Left bundle branch**
cards.a: Fibers in the heart that send the contraction impulse to the left ventricle.

cards.q: **Mitral valve**
cards.a: Heart valve that prevents blood flow from the left ventricle to the left atria.

cards.q: **Motor neuron**
cards.a: The nerve cell responsible for innervating the muscle fibers. Each motor neuron can innervate many muscle fibers, sometimes hundreds or even thousands.

cards.q: **Motor unit**
cards.a: The motor neuron and the muscle fibers it innervates.

cards.q: **Multiaxial joints**
cards.a: Joints such and the shoulder and hip ball-and-socket joints that allow movement around all three perpendicular axes that define space.

cards.q: **Muscle fiber**
cards.a: Long, cylindrical cells 50 to 100 micrometers in diameter (about the diameter of a human hair). The fibers have many nuclei situated on the periphery of the cell and have a striated appearance.

cards.q: **Muscle Spindle**
cards.a: Proprioceptors that consist of modified muscle fibers enclosed in a sheath of connective tissue. Muscle spindles provide information concerning the muscle length and rate of change in length.

cards.q: **Myocardium**
cards.a: Heart muscle tissue.

cards.q: **Myofibril**
cards.a: Small fibrils within the muscle fiber that contain the apparatus that contracts the muscle cell.

cards.q: **Myofilament**
cards.a: small strands of protein, primarily either myosin or actin, that are responsible for muscle contraction.

cards.q: **Myosin**
cards.a: a protein that makes up myosin filaments of about 16 nm in diameter. The myosin filament has a globular head, a hinge point, and a fibrous tail. Pairs of myosin filaments form cross-bridges, which interact with actin to produce muscular contractions.

cards.q: **Neuromuscular junction**
cards.a: The junction between the motor neuron and the fibers it innervates.

cards.q: **Parasympathetic nervous system**
cards.a: Component of the autonomic nervous system. Stimulation of the parasympathetic nervous system slows heart rate by slowing SA depolarization.

cards.q: **Perimysium**
cards.a: Connective tissue surrounding each fascicle.

cards.q: **Pleura**
cards.a: The membranes that envelope the lungs and lining of the chest walls.

cards.q: **Pleural pressure**
cards.a: The pressure in the narrow space between the chest wall pleura and the lung pleura.

cards.q: **Power stroke**
cards.a: The pulling action during muscle contraction. Power stroke results from the hydrolysis of adenosine triphosphate (ATP) to adenosine diphosphate (ADP) and phosphate. This reaction is catalyzed by the enzyme myosin adenosine triphosphatase (ATPase).

cards.q: **Proprioceptor**
cards.a: Specialized sensory receptors within joints, muscles, and tendons. Proprioceptors are sensitive to pressure and tension in the muscle and relay information about muscle dynamics to the nervous system. This process allows the CNS to maintain muscle tone and perform coordinated movements.

cards.q: **Proximal**
cards.a: The attachment of a limb muscle that is closer to the trunk. (ESC p. 3).

cards.q: **Pulmonary valve**
cards.a: Valve in the heart that prevents blood flow from the pulmonary artery into the right ventricle.

cards.q: **Purkinje fibers**
cards.a: Fibers in the heart that conduct heartbeat impulse to all parts of the ventricles.

cards.q: **P-Wave**
cards.a: Recordings of electrical depolarization in the heart. The P wave is generated by changes in electrical potential within cardiac muscle cells that depolarize the atria, resulting in contraction.

cards.q: **QRS Complex**
cards.a: Recording of depolarization in the heart resulting in ventricular contraction.

cards.q: **Red blood cell**
cards.a: The major component of blood that contains hemoglobin. Red blood cells transport oxygen as well as other processes such as catalyzing the reaction that facilitates carbon dioxide removal.

cards.q: **Repolarization**
cards.a: The process that occurs as ventricles recover from depolarization.

cards.q: **Right bundle branch**
cards.a: Fibers in the heart that send the contraction impulse to the right ventricle.

cards.q: **Sarcolemma**
cards.a: the membrane surrounding each muscle fiber. (ESC p. 4).

cards.q: **Sarcomere**
cards.a: The smallest contractile unit of skeletal muscle. In a relaxed fiber, sarcomeres average about 2.5 micrometers in diameter and are repeated the entire length of a muscle fiber. Actin and myosin filaments are arranged longitudinally in the sarcomere.

cards.q: **Sarcoplasm**
cards.a: the cytoplasm fluid inside the muscle fiber connotation protein filaments, other proteins, stored glycogen, fat particles, enzymes, and specialized organelles such as mitochondria and the sarcoplasmic reticulum. (ESC p. 4).

cards.q: **Sarcoplasmic reticulum**
cards.a: An intricate system of tubules that surround each myofibril and terminate as vesicles in the vicinity of the Z-lines. Calcium ions are stored in the vesicles.

cards.q: **Semilunar valves**
cards.a: Collective term for the aortic and pulmonary valves.

cards.q: **Sinoatrial (SA) node**
cards.a: Pacemaker of the heart where electrical impulses are initiated.

cards.q: **Sliding filament theory**
cards.a: The theory of muscle contraction that states that actin filaments at the end of each sarcomere slide inwards on myosin filaments, which pulls the Z-lines towards the center of the sarcomere, shortening the muscle fiber. As the actin slides over the myosin, the H-Zone and I-Band shrink. The myosin cross-bridges pull on the actin filaments and are responsible for the movement of the actin filament.

cards.q: **Slow-twitch fiber**
cards.a: Muscle fibers, specifically Type I fibers, with high aerobic efficiency but low maximum force output.

cards.q: **Superior**
cards.a: The attachment of a trunk muscle that is closer to the head relative to the inferior attachment.

cards.q: **Sympathetic nervous system**
cards.a: Component of the autonomic nervous system. Stimulation of the sympathetic nervous system increases the heart rate by accelerating the depolarization of the sinoatrial node.

cards.q: **Synovial fluid**
cards.a: The fluid enclosed inside the joint capsule.

cards.q: **Synovial joints**
cards.a: joints that allow considerable movement with low friction and large ranges of motion (i.e elbow and knee). Sport and exercise movements occur mostly around the synovial joints.

cards.q: **Systole**
cards.a: Ventricular contraction.

cards.q: **Tachycardia**
cards.a: heart rate above 100 beats/minute.

cards.q: **Tendon**
cards.a: Connective tissue that attaches the muscles to the bone periosteum. Muscle contractions pull on the tendon which in turn pulls on the bone.

cards.q: **Tetanus**
cards.a: The process that occurs when stimuli are delivered at such a high frequency that the muscle twitches fuse, resulting in the maximal amount of force a motor unit can develop.

cards.q: **Trachea**
cards.a: The first generation respiratory passage where the air is passed to the bronchi and ultimately the bronchioles for oxygenation by the lungs.

cards.q: **Tricuspid valve**
cards.a: Heart valve preventing blood flow from the right ventricle to the right atrium.

cards.q: **Tropomyosin**
cards.a: A protein that runs along the actin filament in the groove of the double helix. When calcium binds with troponin, a shift occurs in the tropomyosin that results in rapid attachments of the actin filament to the myosin cross

cards.q: **Troponin**
cards.a: A protein situated at regular intervals along the actin filament and has a high affinity for calcium ions. When calcium is released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum, it binds with the troponin.

cards.q: **T-tubule**
cards.a: Transverse tubules that run perpendicular to the sarcoplasmic reticulum and terminate in the vicinity of the Z-line between to vesicles. T-tubules run between outlying myofibrils and are contiguous with the sarcolemma at the cell surface. This results in the action potential reaching all depths of the muscle fiber nearly simultaneously.

cards.q: **T-wave**
cards.a: Recording of the electrical potential generated during repolarization in ventricular muscle.

cards.q: **Twitch**
cards.a: Brief contraction of muscle fibers that occurs when an action potential reaches the neuromuscular junction. To develop force, multiple twitches occur before the complete relaxation of the muscle fiber. When there is resistance (ie from an external weight) to the actin-myosin binding process, multiple twitches will occur back-to-back. The force from the twitches is additive. Multiple back-to-back twitches produce more force than a single twitch.

cards.q: **Type I fiber**
cards.a: Slow-twitch fibers with high efficiency and the ability for aerobic metabolism. Type I fibers are slower to produce force and have a lower maximum force output, but are incredibly efficient.

cards.q: **Type IIa fiber**
cards.a: Fast-twitch fiber with more endurance than Type IIx, slightly less maximum force production, and less endurance than type I fibers.

cards.q: **Type IIx fiber**
cards.a: Fast-twitch fibers that have the greatest ability to rapidly produce force but are the least efficient and least able to use aerobic metabolism compared to Type I and Type IIa fibers.

cards.q: **Uniaxial joints**
cards.a: joints such as the elbow that operate as hinges, essentially rotating around only one axis.

cards.q: **Vein**
cards.a: Tubes that transport blood back to the heart.

cards.q: **Venous system**
cards.a: System of tubes that returns blood from the muscles to the heart.

cards.q: **Ventricle**
cards.a: Chambers of the heart that receive blood from the atria and pump it either to the lungs (right ventricle) or the rest of the body (left ventricle).

cards.q: **Venule**
cards.a: Small tubes that collect blood from the capillaries and converge into the larger veins.

cards.q: **Vertebral column**
cards.a: vertebral bones separated by flexible disks that allow movement to occur. Vertebrae are grouped in the following: Seven cervical vertebrae (C1-C7), the twelve thoracic vertebrae (T1-T12), five lumbar vertebrae (L1-L5), five sacral vertebrae, which are fused together and make up the pelvis, and the three to five coccygeal vertebrae, which form a vestigial internal tail extending downward front the pelvis.

cards.q: **Z-line**
cards.a: A thin dark line running longitudinally through the I-band.

cards.q: A-Band
cards.a: The section of the sarcomere that corresponds with the alignment of myosin and actin filaments.

cards.q: Acetylcholine
cards.a: A neurotransmitter released when an action potential arrives at the nerve terminal. The Acetylcholine diffuses across the neuromuscular junction causing excitation of the sarcolemma.

cards.q: Actin
cards.a: A protein that forms actin myofilaments. Actin filaments consist of two thin strands about 6nm in diameter arranged in a double helix.

cards.q: Action potential
cards.a: An electrical impulse from a motor nerve that signals the release of calcium from the sarcoplasmic reticulum into the myofibril, causing tension development in the muscle.

cards.q: All-or-none principle
cards.a: The phenomenon that a stimulus from the motor neuron will cause all fibers in that motor unit to contract. As such, stronger action potentials do not result in bigger contractions.

cards.q: Alveolar pressure ​
cards.a: Pressure inside the alveoli when the glottis is open and no air is flowing into or out of the lungs.

cards.q: Alveoli
cards.a: The final passages in the respiratory system where gases are exchanged from the lungs.

cards.q: Aortic valve
cards.a: Valve in the heart that prevents backflow of blood from the aorta into the ventricle.

cards.q: Appendicular skeleton
cards.a: Bones of the shoulder/pectoral girdle (left and right scapula and clavicle), bones of the arms, wrists, and hands (left and right humerus, radius, ulna, carpals, metacarpals, and phalanges); the pelvic girdle (left and right coxal or innominate bones), and the bones of the legs, ankles, and feet (left and right femur, patella, tibia, fibula, tarsals, metatarsals, and phalanges). (ESC p. 2)

cards.q: Arterial system
cards.a: System of tubes that carries blood away from the heart. Due to the high pressure of the blood from the heart, arteries have strong walls.

cards.q: Arteriole
cards.a: Smaller branches of the arterial system that deliver blood to the capillaries.

cards.q: Artery
cards.a: Strong tubes that rapidly transport blood from the heart.

cards.q: Atrioventricular (AV) bundle
cards.a: Conducts the impulse in the heart to the ventricles.

cards.q: Atrioventricular (AV) node
cards.a: Node in the heart that slightly delays the impulse from the SA node.

cards.q: Atrioventricular (AV) valves
cards.a: One-way valves that prevent the backflow of the blood from the ventricles into the atria.

cards.q: Atrium
cards.a: Chambers of the heart that receive blood and pump it to the ventricles. The left and right atria pump blood to the left and right ventricle, respectively.

cards.a: Chambers of the heart that receive blood from the atria and pump it either to the lungs (right ventricle) or the rest of the body (left ventricle).

cards.q: **Venule**
cards.a: Small tubes that collect blood from the capillaries and converge into the larger veins.

cards.q: **Vertebral column**
cards.a: vertebral bones separated by flexible disks that allow movement to occur. Vertebrae are grouped in the following: Seven cervical vertebrae (C1-C7), the twelve thoracic vertebrae (T1-T12), five lumbar vertebrae (L1-L5), five sacral vertebrae, which are fused together and make up the pelvis, and the three to five coccygeal vertebrae, which form a vestigial internal tail extending downward front the pelvis.

cards.q: **Z-line**
cards.a: A thin dark line running longitudinally through the I-band.

cards.q: the force a muscle or muscle group can exert in one maximal effort
